faraday-the-bookbinders-apprentice.context_blurb:
Michael Faraday, a blacksmith's son from London who left school at thirteen, became the greatest experimenter of the nineteenth century. He found how to turn electricity into motion and motion into electricity, and nearly every motor, generator and transformer in the world runs on what he discovered with homemade apparatus.

His apprenticeship began in 1805 with George Riebau, a bookbinder on Blandford Street. His science came off the workbench: he read the books customers brought in to be bound. One was Jane Marcet's Conversations on Chemistry, written as a friendly chat for young readers. Faraday did not simply believe it; he tried her chemistry out with cheap experiments of his own, and when they agreed with the book he felt he had caught hold of an anchor. All his life he would trust a fact but cross-examine a claim.

In 1812, at twenty, he sat through four of Humphry Davy's lectures at the Royal Institution. He wrote up his notes, expanded them, bound them himself into a book of more than three hundred pages, since binding was his trade, and sent it to Davy asking for work. In March 1813 he became Davy's chemical assistant.

In September 1821 Faraday stood a magnet in wax inside a basin of mercury and let a hanging wire dip into the mercury beside it. When current flowed, the wire swept around the magnet in circles, on and on for as long as the current ran: the first machine to turn electricity into continuous motion. He rushed it into print without naming William Wollaston, who had tried something similar and failed, and talk of plagiarism followed, some of it from Davy. Faraday went to see Wollaston, who told him that what others thought of his conduct was Faraday's own business, not his.

Then he hunted for the reverse, electricity from magnetism, for about ten years. On 29 August 1831 he wound two coils onto an iron ring, using copper wire bought from an ordinary London shop that sold it for shaping ladies' bonnets. He joined one coil to a battery and the other to a galvanometer. A steady current did nothing; the needle jumped only at the moment he connected the battery and again when he disconnected it. Only a changing magnetic field drives a current. That ring, the first transformer, survives at the Royal Institution.

Weeks later he spun a copper disc between the poles of a great magnet, with sliding contacts at its rim and centre. This time the galvanometer needle swung right over and stayed there for as long as he turned the handle: a steady current, made from motion alone. That disc is the ancestor of every power-station generator.

In 1836 he built a twelve-foot wooden box, covered it in copper mesh and tin foil, and climbed in with lit candles while an electrical machine charged its outer skin until sparks flew. The candle flames stood perfectly still and an electrometer inside never stirred, because electric charge gathers on a conductor's outer surface, never inside it. Test it at home: bag up a phone in plastic, cover the whole bundle with foil and call it, and it stays silent. Skip the bag so the foil touches the phone, and the call can get through, because the foil then works as an extra piece of the phone's own antenna.

Faraday never learned mathematics beyond simple algebra. Instead he drew lines of force curving through the empty space around magnets and wires, and he treated them as real, as if space itself carried the push and pull. That was the birth of the field. James Clerk Maxwell turned the drawings into the equations physicists still use and wrote that Faraday had been in reality a mathematician of a very high order, one whose methods future mathematicians could learn from.

Fame never moved him. A devout Sandemanian, he believed the Bible forbade piling up riches and honours; he refused a knighthood, twice declined to lead the Royal Society and wished to stay plain Mr Faraday. He died in 1867 and was not buried in Westminster Abbey; he lies in the dissenters' part of Highgate Cemetery. One favourite story has the statesman William Gladstone asking what use electricity could be, and Faraday replying that one day he might tax it. No account from Faraday's lifetime records it, and a date breaks it: Gladstone first became Prime Minister in 1868, the year after Faraday died.

faradays-candle-a-whole-course-hiding-in.context_blurb:
At Christmas 1860 Michael Faraday, aged sixty-nine, gave the last of his lecture courses for children at London's Royal Institution: six talks about one ordinary candle. There was no better or more open door into the study of natural philosophy, he told his young audience, than the physics of a burning candle.

His showpiece was a cracked tallow candle salvaged in 1839 from the Royal George, a warship lost in 1782. After decades in salt water, it lit at once and burned as evenly as a fresh candle.

Faraday knew how a lecture can change a life. In 1812, as a bookbinder's apprentice, he had heard Humphry Davy at the Royal Institution, bound his notes into a book with his own hands and posted it to Davy with a letter asking for a job; Davy hired him the next spring.

Nobody carries the fuel up to a candle's flame; the solid wax sits below. The flame's heat melts a little pool, and capillary attraction, the same pull that draws water up a paper towel, lifts the melted wax up the wick to where it turns to vapour and burns. The wick is a pump, not the fuel.

Look at the top of a calm candle and you see a neat cup: liquid wax held inside a hard rim. The flame's heat drives a current of air upward around the candle, and that rising air cools the outside edge more than the middle, so the rim stays solid. Send a draught from one side and the cup goes lopsided and spills; that is all guttering is.

He had the children slide a strip of white paper level through the middle of a flame and pull it out. It scorches in two bands with the centre barely marked, because the flame is hollow: its middle is a dark cone of unburnt vapour. Faraday led a bent glass tube from that dark heart to a spot a foot away, set a light to the far end, and a second flame sprang up there, a candle piped like gas.

Blow a candle out gently and a white trail of smoke rises from the wick. Bring a lit taper to the trail a few inches above, and a train of fire runs down it through the air and lights the candle again. The trail is wax vapour, proof that a candle burns vapour, not wick or solid wax.

Why is a candle bright when a hotter gas jet is pale? Not temperature, Faraday said. The flame's heat breaks the wax vapour apart and frees specks of solid carbon, which glow white-hot and give the light before they burn away.

A candle also makes water. Hold a cold glass over the flame and it fogs; Faraday gathered the drops and, refusing to let the children take his word, dropped on a piece of potassium, the metal Davy had discovered. It burst into flame on the surface and burned away, just as potassium does on water.

In the last lecture he put the children in the candle's place: each of them, he said, carried on a slow burning much like a candle's. To prove it he breathed through clear lime-water, which turned milky, exactly as it had with the gas from the flame. Both give off carbonic acid, which we call carbon dioxide. His final words were a wish, not a lesson: that the children might be like a candle by shining as lights to the people around them, and by making their deeds honourable and useful to others.

Faraday never wrote the lectures out. A young chemist in the audience, William Crookes, recorded them, and The Chemical History of a Candle has stayed in print ever since. In Japan a teacher gave a copy to a fourth-grader named Akira Yoshino, who says it first showed him how a candle works; he grew up to develop the lithium-ion battery, sharing the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

A candle on Earth burns as a teardrop because hot gas rises and cool air rushes in beneath it. In orbit nothing rises. When astronauts on the shuttle Columbia lit candles inside a sealed box in June 1992, some seventy times, each flame became a small blue ball, free of soot and standing a little away from the wick.

fever-is-a-weapon-not-a-malfunction.context_blurb:
When you catch a fever, it is tempting to think the infection is simply overheating you. A lizard showed otherwise. A lizard has no inner furnace, so the only way it can raise its temperature is to go and find heat.

In the mid-1970s at the University of Michigan, Matthew Kluger's team gave desert iguanas a bacterial infection and put them in a pen with a heat lamp. The sick lizards went and basked in the lamp's hotter glow until their bodies ran about two degrees above normal. They had given themselves a fever on purpose. In a paper published in Science in April 1975 under the plain title Fever and Survival, Miriam Anver, William Ringler and Kluger reported that infected lizards kept at fever temperatures survived far better than those kept cool.

A reptile makes the perfect test because in a mammal the fever and the infection arrive together and cannot be pulled apart. Fever is the brain deliberately raising its thermostat, which is why you shiver with cold while your temperature climbs.

feynman-the-o-ring-and-the-glass-of-ice-.context_blurb:
On 28 January 1986 the Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart seventy-three seconds after leaving the pad in Florida, and all seven people aboard were killed. A presidential panel, the Rogers Commission, was set up to find out why. Its most famous moment came from one member, the Caltech physicist Richard Feynman, who made the central point with a glass of ice water.

That morning was bitterly cold. No shuttle had ever flown in air colder than 53 degrees Fahrenheit, but a hard freeze had gripped the pad all night, icicles hung from the tower, and at liftoff the air stood at about 36 degrees Fahrenheit, some seventeen degrees below the old record.

The cold mattered because of the boosters. Each solid rocket booster was stacked from segments, and every joint between segments was closed by rubber rings that had to spring outward in a split second when the joint flexed at ignition. The night before launch, engineers at Morton Thiokol, the Utah company that built the boosters, warned in a telephone conference that the freeze would harm the rubber O-rings sealing the joints between the booster segments, and their first written recommendation said no launch. Roger Boisjoly pushed hardest. He showed photographs of soot that had blown past the rings on earlier cold flights, and he warned that in freezing weather the rings would be as hard as rocks, too stiff to spring back and seal the gap in time. Thiokol's managers then met privately, with their engineers shut out, and reversed the call.

The rings failed. A jet of flame burned through the side of the right booster and ruptured the huge external fuel tank. Most people who watched remember an explosion, but the commission was more exact. The tank's hydrogen and oxygen burned in a vast cloud, while the orbiter itself, still whole for a moment, was flung sideways into the onrushing air and torn apart by aerodynamic forces of about twenty g.

Feynman got his lead from a fellow commissioner, the Air Force general Donald Kutyna. Kutyna had been quietly handed NASA test data showing that the rings stiffened when chilled, and to protect his source he wrapped the hint in a story. He talked with Feynman about the carburetor of an old car he was restoring in his garage, whose small O-rings, he said, leaked when the weather turned cold, and asked whether a shuttle could suffer the same thing. Only after the astronaut Sally Ride died in 2012 did the public learn that she had been the source.

On 11 February 1986, in front of the television cameras, Feynman made the point for everyone. He had brought a scrap of rubber cut from a booster O-ring, squeezed it in a small C-clamp and dropped it into a glass of iced water he had asked to have ready on the table. When he fished it out and let go, the rubber stayed squashed instead of springing back.

Feynman also asked how likely it was that a shuttle would be lost on any one flight. NASA's managers said one in a hundred thousand, a number that meant flying a shuttle every day for about three hundred years without a single loss. The engineers who worked on the hardware gave far gloomier answers, from one chance in fifty to one in two hundred, and Feynman's own estimate was near one in a hundred.

Feynman insisted that his own minority report be printed with the commission's findings, as Appendix F. It ends by saying that a technology that works must put reality ahead of public relations, because nature cannot be fooled.

Ten years later the sociologist Diane Vaughan asked how careful people had talked themselves into the launch. Her 1996 book showed that every earlier flight that came home with scorched rings, and did not end in disaster, nudged the line of acceptable damage a little further out. Her name for that slow drift, normalization of deviance, is now taught wherever engineers study failure.

feynmans-cargo-cult-science.context_blurb:
In the summer of 1974 Richard Feynman, one of the great physicists of his century, spoke to the graduating class at Caltech, the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena. He used the speech to warn the new scientists about research that looks like science from the outside, with the instruments, the jargon and the published papers, but has lost the honesty that makes science work.

His picture for it came from the South Seas. After the war, he said, islanders who had watched planes land with supplies tried to bring them back. They cleared runways, lit fires along both edges, built a wooden hut and sat a man inside with two pieces of wood on his head for headphones and bamboo poles for antennas. Everything looked right, and no plane came. Feynman called research of that sort cargo cult science: it copies every outward form of an investigation and misses the one essential thing. The phrase reached a far wider public a decade later, when the speech became the closing chapter of Feynman's bestselling 1985 memoir, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!

The essential thing, he said, starts with one rule. His first principle was a warning about yourself: never fool yourself, since you are the easiest person in the world to fool. Once you stop fooling yourself, he added, it is easy not to fool other scientists.

He showed how quietly self-deception works with Robert Millikan, who first measured the electron's charge by timing tiny drops of oil as they fell between metal plates. Millikan's number came out a little too low, because he had used a slightly wrong value for the viscosity of air, the stickiness that sets how fast a droplet can fall and so reveals its size.

What happened next was the real lesson. Later measurements of the charge did not jump to the true value; each crept a little higher than the one before. Feynman explained why. When experimenters got a number far above Millikan's, they assumed a mistake and searched until they found one, but when a number came out close to his, they did not look so hard. Nobody cheated. Honest people, checking only the results that surprised them, dragged out the error for years.

Feynman's hero was a researcher named Young, who ran rats along a long corridor of doors. His rats kept choosing the door where the food had been even after it was moved, so they had to be using some hidden cue. Young removed one cue after another and found the last: the rats could tell where they were by the sound the floor made under their feet. To kill that cue, he laid the whole corridor in sand.

Feynman's complaint was about what came after. The rat experiments that followed never mentioned Young and never used his sand or his other careful controls, the very steps he had proved were needed. The field kept the outward form of the experiment and dropped the part that made it work.

Feynman asked for more than ordinary honesty. A scientist who reports a result should also report every check that failed, every other explanation, and everything that might prove him wrong. He called this a kind of utter honesty, a leaning over backwards.

He found a warning in advertising. A Wesson cooking-oil advertisement bragged that the oil did not soak through food. That was true, but at that cooking temperature no oil soaks through food, so the boast fit every brand and gave Wesson no real advantage at all. A sentence can be literally true and still mislead.

Feynman knew that such honesty can cost a scientist his job. So he ended with a wish rather than a command: he wished the graduates the good luck of finding a place where they would be free to keep that kind of integrity. The word luck admitted that the freedom to be honest is never guaranteed.

The islanders were not Feynman's invention, though his telling was a parable rather than fieldwork. Cargo movements really did grow up in Melanesia around the Second World War, and one of them, the John Frum movement on the island of Tanna, in Vanuatu, is still alive: its followers march every year on 15 February. It is a serious anti-colonial religion, not the joke his story can make it seem.

flame-tests-the-fingerprint-in-the-fire.context_blurb:
A firework's colour is a signature. Every element heated in a flame gives off its own set of colours, and in 1859 two Heidelberg scientists, Robert Bunsen, a chemist, and Gustav Kirchhoff, a physicist, learned to read them through a prism. Their flame test could name an element from a speck too small to weigh.

Firework makers pack red shells with strontium salts and green ones with barium salts. No dye survives that blast. The heat makes the metal itself glow: its atoms give off light at wavelengths that belong to that metal and no other. Try it on a kitchen gas stove: dust a clean wire with table salt, hold it in the blue flame, and the flame flares yellow-orange with the light of sodium.

Under an old orange street lamp, which runs on that same sodium light, the world loses its colours. Colour is light bounced back from a surface, and a sodium lamp sends out almost nothing but one orange-yellow, so every surface can only return some shade of that single orange.

Bunsen built his famous burner for this work, because the sooty yellow glare of 1850s gas lamps drowned the faint colours he wanted. His burner draws air in through slits at its base, so gas and air are already mixed before they burn; the carbon burns away completely, no soot forms, and the flame is almost invisible. In late 1854 he handed his design rules to Peter Desaga, the university mechanic at Heidelberg, and when the new laboratory opened early in 1855, fifty finished burners stood ready for his students.

The brilliant white stars and the trailing gold sparks shine by incandescence: hot solid particles, magnesium or aluminium powder for the white and specks of charcoal for the gold, glowing at every colour at once.

Sodium is the saboteur: a trace from a fingerprint floods a flame with yellow. To find potassium's faint violet behind it, a chemist looks at the flame through a pane of cobalt blue glass, which swallows sodium's yellow and lets the violet through.

To prove how sensitive the test was, Bunsen and Kirchhoff burned three milligrams of a sodium salt in a corner of a sixty-cubic-metre room and watched a flame at the other end. Within minutes that distant flame turned yellow and stayed yellow for about ten minutes, so air carrying less than a twenty-millionth of its weight in sodium was enough.

Of all firework colours, blue gives makers the most trouble. Copper's blue comes from a molecule, copper(I) chloride, and that molecule falls apart above roughly 1500 degrees Celsius. Force a blue star hotter for brightness and the heat tears the copper chloride into copper and chlorine, leaving a washed-out whitish glow.

For two years Bunsen and Kirchhoff varied everything they could: the compound carrying a metal, the kind of flame, the source of the sample. In their 1860 paper they reported that none of it moved a single line. The lines belonged to the metal alone, so a pattern of lines names an element the way a fingerprint names a person.

In May 1860 Bunsen held the residue of spring water from Bad Dürkheim in his flame, and Kirchhoff, at the prism, saw a pair of blue lines that matched no element anyone had catalogued. Bunsen named the newcomer caesium, from the Latin word for sky-blue: the first element ever found by its light alone. Chemists of the day would not take a colour as proof, so Bunsen boiled down some forty tonnes of the water, and from all of it he won about 7 grams of caesium chloride, barely two teaspoons.

The flame test also overturned a philosopher. In 1835 Auguste Comte chose the stars as his example of knowledge forever out of reach: we might learn their shapes, distances and motions, he wrote, but never their chemical composition. Within about twenty-five years Kirchhoff had matched his laboratory lines to the dark lines in sunlight and begun reading the Sun's elements.

For half a century nobody knew why each element paints its own lines. In 1913 Niels Bohr explained it: an atom's electrons can sit only on fixed energy levels, and when one drops from a higher level to a lower one, it gives off light of one exact energy, and so one exact colour. Each element spaces its levels differently, so its lines work as a fingerprint.

flemings-open-dish-and-the-forgotten-hal.context_blurb:
Penicillin, the first great antibiotic, has medicine's most famous origin story: a London scientist, a forgotten dish and a stray mould. Its often-forgotten second half, turning mould juice into a medicine, took a team at Oxford, a hospital's bedpans, a melon from Illinois and a world war.

Alexander Fleming, a Scottish bacteriologist working at London's St Mary's Hospital, came back from a two-week holiday in September 1928 to a pile of old plates of staph bacteria. One plate had caught a fuzzy blue-green mould, and the staph near it had dissolved, leaving a clear ring around the mould.

Fleming kept the plate because he had seen something like it before. In November 1921, nursing a cold, he had let a drop of his own nasal mucus fall onto a bacterial plate and watched the bacteria around it dissolve, the clue that led him to an enzyme he named lysozyme.

He grew the mould on broth for several days, then poured the broth through filter paper. The clear liquid that came through held no mould at all, yet it still destroyed staph and streptococci even when watered down hundreds of times. The killer was a substance the mould released, and in 1929 Fleming named it penicillin.

His 1929 paper pitched it chiefly as a laboratory tool. Its title proposed using penicillin to isolate the influenza bacillus: the drug kills the staph and strep that crowd a culture plate but barely touches that fussy germ, so adding it clears away the rivals and lets the bacillus grow alone.

For a decade almost nobody followed it up. In 1932 the London biochemist Harold Raistrick made a crude extract, but it kept falling apart and he gave up. Medicine's hopes went instead to the sulfa drugs that followed Gerhard Domagk's Prontosil, which were stable, easy to make and reliable.

In 1940 Howard Florey's team at Oxford took up the forgotten juice. Ernst Chain concentrated it, and Norman Heatley found ways to measure and extract it. On Saturday 25 May 1940 they gave eight mice a deadly dose of streptococci and treated only four with penicillin. Heatley sat up all night; by 3:45 in the morning the four untreated mice had died and the four treated ones were alive. A larger run with sixteen mice that Tuesday was more sobering: the treated mice lived several days longer, but all of them were dead by day nineteen. The dose, not the idea, was the limit.

Wartime Britain had no factory to spare, so Heatley grew the mould in hospital bedpans, which made near-perfect shallow trays, then had a pottery make hundreds of stackable ceramic copies.

The first real patient was Albert Alexander, an Oxford policeman. The usual telling blames a scratch from a rose thorn, but his family said the wounds on his face came from a bomb blast when German planes raided the police station in Southampton, where he had been sent to help during the Blitz. Treatment began on 12 February 1941, and within a day his fever fell, but the whole stock was nearly gone. Because penicillin leaves the body largely unchanged, the team collected his urine, pulled the drug back out of it and injected it into him again. Even so, the supply ran out after about five days, and he relapsed and died in March.

In 1941 Florey and Heatley carried the problem to government farm scientists at Peoria, Illinois, where Andrew Moyer fed the mould on corn-steep liquor, the sludge that milling corn leaves behind, and raised its yield about tenfold. In 1943 the lab found a far richer strain growing on a mouldy cantaloupe melon from Peoria itself, though who found it, and where, is still disputed.

Penicillin works by sabotage. A bacterium's wall is a mesh that has to be locked together by cross-links as the cell grows, and the drug jams the enzyme that makes them. Meanwhile the cell's own enzymes, which constantly chew open the wall to remodel it, keep demolishing it from inside, water rushes in, and the growing cell bursts. Human cells have no such wall, which is why the drug can be injected.

In 1945 the Nobel Prize went to Fleming, Florey and Chain. Heatley, whose bedpans, measurements and extraction had made the work possible, was left out because a single Nobel award can be shared by three people at most. Oxford made amends in 1990 with an honorary medical doctorate.

flemings-tears-the-bodys-own-antiseptic.context_blurb:
In late 1921 the Scottish bacteriologist Alexander Fleming discovered that the human body makes its own germ-killer. Years before penicillin, he found an enzyme that dissolves certain bacteria, chased it through the fluids of the body and the foods of the kitchen, and spent years trying to turn it into a medicine.

Fleming had a cold. As he worked over a dish of yellow bacteria, a drop of his own nasal mucus fell onto it, and days later the colonies close to that drop had dissolved into jelly, leaving a wide clear ring.

Fleming and his assistant Allison then hunted for the substance everywhere. They found it in blood serum, saliva, milk and tears, but the richest source of all came from the kitchen: egg white, where a hen packs the enzyme around the yolk to guard the growing chick against bacteria. Fleming named the enzyme lysozyme, from Greek words meaning "dissolving enzyme".

It never became a medicine. Lysozyme cuts a sugar bond in the mesh wall of certain bacteria, and the germs it dissolved best were harmless ones, like the yellow test microbe he named Micrococcus lysodeikticus. The dangerous kinds, such as staphylococci and streptococci, have walls it cannot crack or outer coats that block it, so it left the real killers alone. Seven years of that frustration are why, in 1928, Fleming looked twice at a mould's clear halo.

float-a-steel-paperclip-then-touch-it-wi.context_blurb:
Water has a skin. Its molecules cling to one another so hard that the surface acts like a stretched elastic sheet, strong enough to carry a steel paperclip that ought to sink. That pull, called surface tension, even decides whether a newborn baby can breathe.

Steel is nearly eight times as dense as water, so buoyancy cannot hold a paperclip up. Yet a clip laid gently flat on still water stays there, resting in a shallow dimple, held by the water's top layer, which is pulled taut like a skin.

That top layer is special because of where it sits. Deep in a glass, each water molecule is tugged equally by neighbours on every side, and the pulls cancel. A molecule at the surface has no water above it, so its neighbours pull it only downward and sideways, and the whole surface is drawn tight.

Soap destroys the skin. Dip a toothpick in dish soap and touch the water with it, even across the glass from the clip, and the clip drops to the bottom almost instantly. Each soap molecule has a water-loving head and a water-hating tail. The tails escape the water by crowding into the surface, where the molecules wedge between the water molecules and break their grip on each other.

Sprinkle pepper on a plate of water and touch soap to the middle, and the flecks race to the rim. The soap does not push them. It leaves a weak patch in the middle, and the strong, untouched water all around wins the tug-of-war, hauling the surface, and the pepper riding on it, outward.

A bubble's film pulls the same way: it shrinks until it can shrink no further, and a sphere is the shape that wraps a given puff of air in the least possible film. Water also climbs. It creeps up a paper towel and rises inside a thin glass tube, because water clings to glass harder than it clings to itself, and the surface drags a column up behind it.

On a windy day in 1773 Benjamin Franklin poured a single teaspoon of olive oil onto a wind-ruffled London pond on Clapham Common, and the oil spread until perhaps half an acre lay as smooth as a looking-glass.

The person who worked out what such films are was Agnes Pockels, a young German woman barred from university because of her sex. Working at home from her brother's physics textbooks, she built her own instrument by 1882, when she was twenty: a brim-full metal trough some seventy centimetres long, with a sliding strip that swept the surface clean and squeezed any film into a measured area. To read the surface's pull, she hung a disc the size of a button from a balance and weighed the force needed to tear it free of the water.

Unable to publish in Germany, she sent her results to Lord Rayleigh in England, writing in German early in 1891. Rayleigh had his wife translate the letter and forwarded it to the journal Nature, which printed it that year. A popular story makes her a lucky housewife who stumbled on her results at the sink. In truth she ran her trough for years and policed her own work: when a step in her procedure began skewing her readings, she wrote to Rayleigh herself to report the mistake.

Her trough held a deeper discovery. When she put a trace of oil on the water and slid the strip to crowd the film into an ever tighter patch, the pull barely changed for a long way, then shifted abruptly at one particular area. That was the moment the oil had been pressed down to a layer just one molecule thick.

Surface tension also governs breathing. Each breath ends in millions of tiny liquid-lined air sacs, and the smaller a wet sac is, the higher the pressure inside it. With a lining of plain water, the smallest sacs would carry the highest pressure and blow their air into their bigger neighbours until the lung was a few slack bags.

Healthy lungs make a soap-like surfactant to prevent that. In the 1950s hyaline membrane disease was killing babies born far too early, whose lungs stiffened shut. In 1959 Mary Ellen Avery at Harvard tested lung washings from nine such babies on a balance descended from Pockels's trough. Their washings left the water's pull exactly where it was, which showed that the surfactant was missing and pointed straight at replacing it.

fluorescence-light-that-comes-back-chang.context_blurb:
Some substances drink in light you cannot see and give back light you can. The effect is called fluorescence, and it lights highlighter pens, office ceilings and the inside of living cells. Its rules were first worked out in 1852 at Cambridge University by George Stokes, an Irish-born physicist, with a beam of sunlight and a jar of quinine.

Stokes passed sunlight through blue-violet glass into a solution of quinine, a malaria medicine, and saw a ghostly blue glow appear just where the beam, itself invisible, entered the liquid. Opal had given its name to opalescence, so he named his glow after a mineral that does the same thing, fluorspar: fluorescence.

You can repeat his experiment in five minutes. Tonic water still contains quinine, and under a cheap ultraviolet blacklight a glass of it glows an eerie electric blue.

Stokes also noticed that the trick runs only one way. Ultraviolet light can make a highlighter blaze, but no red lamp, however bright, can make anything glow blue. His rule was that the light a molecule gives back always carries less energy per particle than the light it absorbed, because the molecule loses a little energy as heat before it shines. The light coming out is always redder than the light going in, and that gap is still called the Stokes shift.

The glowing stars stuck to a bedroom ceiling work by a slower cousin. A fluorescent highlighter releases the energy it absorbs within billionths of a second and goes dark the moment the lamp goes off. The ceiling stars are phosphorescent: they trap the energy in a state it can leave only slowly, so they keep glowing for minutes or hours.

Ordinary lighting runs on Stokes's rule. Inside a fluorescent tube, an electric discharge excites mercury vapour, which gives off invisible ultraviolet; the white coating on the glass absorbs that ultraviolet and gives it back as visible light. A white LED does the same with a blue chip under a yellow coating.

Biology took the trick inside the cell. Over many summers the Japanese chemist Osamu Shimomura collected tens of thousands of jellyfish on the coast of Washington state and isolated from them a bright green glowing protein: green fluorescent protein, or GFP. Martin Chalfie showed that its gene, spliced beside another gene, makes a living cell label itself, and Roger Tsien engineered new colours, so biologists can now film a nerve cell firing or a virus entering a cell.

follow-the-science-versus-the-dissent-tr.context_blurb:
"Follow the science" sounds simple, but the history of science is full of people who were right while the experts of their day were wrong. Their stories form a tradition of honoured dissent, and they teach two lessons at once: consensus is not the same thing as truth, and being mocked is no proof of being right. What decides a dispute is a test.

Ignaz Semmelweis, a Hungarian doctor in Vienna, made the doctors on his birth ward scrub their hands in chlorine water in 1847, and deaths fell sharply. Instead of thanks he got ridicule, and he lost his post. In 1865 he was committed to an asylum on the edge of Vienna, and he died there two weeks later, aged forty-seven, of an infected wound.

Alfred Wegener, a German who studied weather, proposed in 1912 that the continents had once fitted together and had since drifted apart. Atlantic coastlines fit like puzzle pieces, and the same fossils turned up on either shore. Geologists refused him for about fifty years for one solid reason: he could name no force powerful enough to push a continent across the globe. The ridicule was unfair, but the objection was legitimate. Vindication came in the 1960s, from matching magnetic stripes on the seafloor, three decades after Wegener died on the Greenland ice.

In 1984 the Australian doctor Barry Marshall could not persuade anyone that a bacterium, not stress and acid, caused most stomach ulcers, and ethics rules barred him from infecting a patient. So he swallowed a broth teeming with the bacteria himself. Within days he was sick with gastritis, and in 2005 he shared a Nobel Prize with Robin Warren.

Calling their critics fools is tempting, and it misses the lesson. Each of the three had the right conclusion but an incomplete argument, with no full account of why that conclusion had to be true. Semmelweis had no germ theory to say what the washing removed, Wegener had no force, and Marshall's bacteria defied the accepted model of the stomach. Real dissent usually looks like that from inside. What finally settled each fight was a test that could have gone against either side, and someone willing to run it. Marshall ran his in his own stomach; Benjamin Franklin's blindfold trial killed Mesmerism in 1784; Arthur Eddington's 1919 eclipse photographs gave Einstein's relativity a chance to fail in the sky.

When a state decides what is true, dissent can cost a life. The botanist Nikolai Vavilov gathered the world's first great seed bank in Leningrad, so that his country would never lose its food supply. As Trofim Lysenko's pseudo-science rose, Stalin's police arrested Vavilov in August 1940, and in January 1943 the man who had given his life to feeding people starved to death in a prison at Saratov. His colleagues in besieged Leningrad starved rather than eat the seeds they guarded.

In October 2020 Jay Bhattacharya of Stanford, Martin Kulldorff of Harvard and Sunetra Gupta of Oxford, all experts on disease, published the Great Barrington Declaration, which argued for a different approach than lockdowns. Within days, in a private email later released under freedom-of-information law, the head of the National Institutes of Health, Francis Collins, called them fringe epidemiologists and asked Anthony Fauci for a "quick and devastating" takedown of the declaration's premises in print. In April 2025 Bhattacharya was sworn in to lead that same agency.

The physicist Richard Feynman put the tradition's first rule into one sentence in a 1974 speech at Caltech: above all, do not fool yourself, because you are the easiest person of all to fool. The rule cuts both ways. It warns the expert who trusts the consensus too easily, and the dissenter who trusts his own cause too much.

foucaults-pendulum-walk-in-and-watch-the.context_blurb:
In 1851 the French physicist Léon Foucault let the people of Paris watch their planet turn. Until then the Earth's daily spin had been worked out from astronomy; nobody had ever seen it happen in a room. Foucault's tool was a pendulum, and the secret of his demonstration is that the pendulum itself does not turn.

In March 1851 he hung a heavy lead ball from a wire sixty-seven metres long beneath the great dome of the Panthéon and set it swinging above a ring of small pegs on the floor. A swinging pendulum keeps its plane fixed in space, but the floor, the building and the city turned beneath it, so hour by hour the line of the swing crept round the ring and the ball knocked the pegs over one after another.

Foucault felt that the pendulum could too easily be explained away, so in 1852 he made the same point with no swing at all. He mounted a fast-spinning wheel so that its axis held steady in space while Paris turned around it, and gave it a Greek name meaning "to see the turning": the gyroscope. Gyroscopes now steer spacecraft and sit inside every phone.

frances-kelsey-says-no.context_blurb:
In 1960 thalidomide was a popular sleeping pill across Europe, and the American firm Richardson-Merrell wanted to sell it in the United States. The application landed on the desk of Frances Kelsey, newly hired as a medical officer by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). She refused to let it through for more than a year, and her stubborn demand for evidence spared American families a catastrophe.

Kelsey, born Frances Oldham, was a Canadian pharmacologist. In 1936 a Chicago professor offered her a laboratory post in a letter addressed to "Mr. Oldham". Her supervisor at McGill, Stehle, told her not to be ridiculous: she should accept, sign her name with "Miss" in brackets after it, and go.

In her first weeks at the agency in 1960, her supervisors gave her two files they expected to be easy. One was for an enema called Lavema; she approved, and it went on sale. The other was thalidomide. Ordinary applications ran to a hundred and fifty volumes or more, but under the law of the day a company had only to show that a drug would not poison you, and the whole thalidomide application filled just four volumes.

Kelsey's first objection was to the kind of evidence. The company's reports from doctors who had prescribed it were, in her words, more like testimonials than well-executed studies, and the claims built on them were too glowing for the support behind them.

Under the 1938 law the agency had to act within sixty days, and if it raised no objection, the drug was approved automatically. Her one weapon was to declare the application incomplete, which restarted the clock, and from November 1960 she did it again and again for more than a year.

The company's contact man phoned her over and over, and on one call he dropped the science and said why the company was in a hurry: it wanted the drug in the shops before Christmas, its best season for selling sedatives.

A Scottish doctor had written to the British Medical Journal on the last day of 1960. Four patients, the letter said, had swallowed the pill every night for more than a year, and a prickling numbness had crept up from their feet. It reached Kelsey weeks late, because a mail strike had held up the FDA's journals, and she found it only because she read the journals herself. Unsure how the pill worked inside the body, she still reasoned that nerve damage was not the kind of side effect a simple sleeping pill should cause.

The company assured the FDA that the drug never reached an unborn child, but during the war Kelsey had studied quinine, a malaria drug, in rabbits. She and a colleague had found that a pregnant mother rabbit broke the drug down poorly and her embryos could not break it down at all.

Three FDA reviewers found problems in the file, among them the chemist Lee Geismar, who had trained in Germany and caught errors where the company had translated German reports into English.

On 30 November 1961 the company's own man telephoned with news from Germany. A Hamburg pediatrician, Widukind Lenz, had linked the drug to a wave of babies whose limbs were badly shortened, and the German maker was withdrawing it. She had never predicted that harm. Her objections had rested on something plainer, the fact that nobody had yet shown any evidence that the drug was safe.

The drug was never approved, yet the company had already handed it out as "investigational" samples, a channel the old law barely covered. Its filed list showed only thirty or forty doctors, but about 2.5 million tablets had gone to more than a thousand doctors.

Congress answered with the Kefauver-Harris amendments, which President Kennedy signed in October 1962. Before, a maker had to prove only that a drug was not poisonous; now it also had to prove, with well-controlled studies, that the drug truly worked as its label promised.

That standard had a price. The economist Sam Peltzman counted the genuinely new drugs launched in America each year and found the number fell from about 43 before the law to about 16 after it. Proof kept thalidomide away, and proof also costs sick people time.

Thalidomide comes in two mirror-image forms, one the sedative and the other the form that harms a growing baby. Making only the safe one would not help, because inside the body each form turns into the other within hours.

franklins-kite-and-the-rod-that-actually.context_blurb:
In the 1740s nobody knew what lightning was. Benjamin Franklin, a Philadelphia printer turned electrical experimenter, suspected it was the same electricity that crackled from rubbed glass, and he designed tests to find out. The kite is the famous one, and its usual picture is mostly wrong. The invention that saved lives was the lightning rod.

Europe's old defence was the church bell. Towns met a thunderstorm by ringing their bells, believing the peal would break the storm apart over the town; many bells carried the Latin motto fulgura frango, "I break the lightning". A Munich study by Johann Fischer in 1784 tallied the price: across thirty-three years, lightning hit bell towers 386 times and killed 103 ringers.

In June 1752 Franklin made his storm kite from two thin sticks of cedar, crossed and tied, with a big, thin silk handkerchief stretched over them instead of paper, because paper would tear apart once the rain soaked it. A sharp wire stood up above the wood to draw charge from the cloud. His instructions told the flier what to watch for. Before the rain even reached the kite, the loose fibres of the hemp twine would bristle outward every which way as charge gathered in the cloud overhead. Only after the rain had soaked the line would fire jump from the key to a finger.

Engravings show a small boy helping him, but his assistant was his son William, then twenty-one and a grown man, and the two were the only people there. The engravings also show lightning striking the kite. No bolt hit it, luckily, since a direct strike could well have killed him. Charge seeped quietly down the wet hemp to the key, and there it stopped, because Franklin, standing under shelter, held not the twine but a dry silk ribbon tied on beyond the key: wet hemp carries charge, and dry silk does not.

One spark proved nothing, so Franklin ran the storm's charge into a Leyden jar, a glass bottle for storing charge, and used it for an ordinary bench demonstration: it lit a dish of alcohol, exactly as charge from a glass globe would.

The kite was not even his first plan. In a 1750 letter to Peter Collinson in London, Franklin proposed a sentry box on top of a high tower, with a man standing inside on an insulating stand beneath a tall pointed iron rod, to test whether storm clouds carry charge.

The plan crossed to France in translation, and Thomas-François Dalibard built it at Marly-la-Ville, outside Paris: a forty-foot iron rod on a platform insulated with wine bottles. On 10 May 1752, a month before the kite flew, a storm arrived while Dalibard was away, and a retired dragoon named Coiffier stood in for him and drew the first sparks any human had pulled from a thundercloud.

In France, Jacques de Romas came up with the kite on his own. In June 1753 at Nérac he flew one with metal wire woven into its string and drew sparks about ten feet long, cracking so loudly they were heard across the town.

Copying these experiments could kill. In August 1753 in St Petersburg, Professor Georg Wilhelm Richmann was watching an iron bar wired to his roof when a fist-sized ball of bluish fire leapt to his forehead and killed him. His apparatus lacked the one thing Franklin's recipe insisted on: a conductor running all the way down into damp earth. Franklin's rod gives a strike a metal path into moist ground, past the building and its people.

Even the rod's tip became political. When lightning hit the Purfleet gunpowder store in Essex in 1777, despite its pointed rods, the painter and electrician Benjamin Wilson argued that blunt ends were safer. He staged a huge show for King George III, then at war with Franklin's America, and the King then had the pointed conductors on his own palace swapped for blunt knobs.

How do we know about the kite? His autobiography is silent. At the time Franklin printed only a brief third-person notice in his newspaper, the Pennsylvania Gazette, in October 1752, telling readers how to build the kite but never saying he had flown one. The vivid scene of key, spark and soaked twine first reached print fifteen years later, in Joseph Priestley's 1767 history of electricity, which he wrote from talks with Franklin. Most historians accept that some version of the flight happened. The rod is documented beyond doubt.

fraunhofers-dark-lines-and-the-philosoph.context_blurb:
Sunlight carries a barcode. In 1814 a Bavarian glassmaker, Joseph Fraunhofer, found that the Sun's rainbow is crossed by dark lines, and nobody could explain them for more than forty years. When Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen finally did, at Heidelberg around 1860, the lines revealed what the Sun is made of, a question a famous philosopher had called forever unanswerable.

Fraunhofer was orphaned young, and his guardians apprenticed him to a Munich mirror-maker who underfed him and would not let him read by candlelight. In July 1801 the workshop collapsed, and the boy, fourteen, was trapped under the rubble for hours before rescuers dug him out alive. The rescue made him famous, and Bavaria's ruler, the Prince-Elector Maximilian Joseph, bought out the rest of his apprenticeship, gave him books and money, and set him free to study.

He grew up to make the finest optical glass in Europe. In 1814 he built an instrument with a narrow slit, a flint-glass prism and a small telescope on a surveyor's stand, for one practical job: he made lenses for observatory telescopes and needed to measure exactly how sharply each batch of his glass bent each colour.

When he aimed it at the Sun, the rainbow was not smooth at all. It was crossed by hundreds of fine dark lines; he mapped some 574 of them and lettered the strongest from A to K. Critics blamed flaws in his glass, but every instrument he built showed the same lines.

You can split sunlight yourself without a prism: tilt the shiny side of an old CD in a sunbeam and it throws a full rainbow onto a white wall. The disc's tightly packed tracks act as a diffraction grating.

Fraunhofer's D pair of lines lies in the yellow, at precisely the colour of sodium burning in a flame. Table salt is sodium chloride, so a few grains in a gas flame show you that very yellow.

Explaining that took a better flame. In Heidelberg around 1854 Robert Bunsen built his burner, a tube whose sliding collars, down at the base, admit air to mix with the gas before it burns. Open the collars and the flame gets hotter and almost disappears, so a sample's own colours are no longer drowned by the fire's.

With it, Bunsen and the physicist Gustav Kirchhoff burned one substance after another and studied the light through a prism. Every element threw its own pattern of bright lines, and however they changed the flame or the sample, those lines stayed in exactly the same places.

Then Kirchhoff turned the experiment around. He heated a platinum wire until it gave a smooth rainbow with no lines at all, and set a cooler, thin gas between the wire and the prism. The gas cut dark lines into the rainbow in exactly the places where its own bright lines appear when it glows: a gas absorbs the very colours it gives off. The Sun is a blazing body shining up through cooler gas, so Fraunhofer's dark lines are a roll-call of the elements in its outer layers, and in 1859 Kirchhoff showed that the Sun contains sodium.

Not every dark line is solar. Fraunhofer could not tell whether his lines were born in the Sun or in our own air, and in fact both happen: his two broad bands A and B, deep in the red, are cut into sunlight in its last moments of travel by the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere.

Kirchhoff's banker was unimpressed: what use, he asked, is gold in the Sun if nobody can bring it down? In 1862 Kirchhoff won the Royal Society's Rumford Medal, paid from London in gold coins. He carried them to the bank and told the banker that here, after all, was gold from the Sun.

The lines also beat a philosopher. Auguste Comte, the Frenchman who tried to chart the limits of human knowledge, had written that we might learn the stars' shapes, distances and motions but never what they are made of. Comte died in 1857, two years before Kirchhoff began reading the Sun's chemistry.

In 1868 William Huggins compared the dark lines of Sirius with the same elements' lines in his laboratory, and the star's lines sat slightly toward the red. Light from a source moving away from us is stretched toward the red, so that small shift gave the first measurement of a star's speed along our line of sight, toward or away from Earth.

from-einsteins-spooky-action-to-the-2022.context_blurb: Make two particles together, carry one to one city and one to another, and measuring the first appears to fix what the second will say, instantly. In 1935 a famous paper argued that if you can predict the distant particle's value with certainty without touching it, that value must have been real all along, so the quantum formalism must be incomplete and the particles must be carrying hidden instructions, like twins leaving home with sealed envelopes. For twenty-nine years the question looked like a matter of taste. Then John Stewart Bell, an accelerator physicist doing foundations as a hobby, published in 1964 a theorem that turned the dispute into a test: any sealed-envelope theory must obey a specific inequality, and the formalism predicts breaking it under specific conditions. Taste became arithmetic. In 2018 the detector settings were randomised using properties of light from distant quasars whose photons had left billions of years ago. In 2022 three physicists shared the Nobel Prize. This does not permit faster-than-light communication, because each side's data alone looks like random noise and the correlation only shows up when the two lists are brought back together.

from-willow-bark-to-the-pill-in-the-cupb.context_blurb: The commonest tablet in the house, traced back to a chewed twig. In 1763 an English clergyman noticed that a specific tree bark tasted as fiercely bitter as the Peruvian bark that was known to break fevers, and reported that dried powder of it brought down fever in about fifty people he gave it to. A bad theory pointed him at the right tree, and only the trial turned it into knowledge. Chemists later took the bark apart, extracted the active compound, synthesised an acid version cheaply, and found it genuinely helped rheumatism, and that patients refused to keep taking it because of what it did to their stomachs. In 1897, in Bayer's laboratory in Elberfeld, a specific chemical modification muzzled the harsh acid until the body released it, so the same medicine stopped chewing the lining. The trade name was registered in 1899. What the drug actually does was not understood for seventy-four more years, when a 1971 discovery of enzyme inhibition won a 1982 Nobel. That mechanism explains the strangest fact on the label: why a tiny baby-aspirin dose keeps blood from clotting for days while a headache dose wears off in hours.

gain-of-function-making-a-pathogen-worse.context_blurb: In 2011 two laboratories, in the Netherlands and in Wisconsin, took a strain of bird influenza that is deadly to humans but almost never passes between them, and ran it through a chain of mammalian hosts until it had evolved to spread through the air from one host to another. They deliberately built the thing everyone was afraid of in order to study it. The pro-research case deserves stating at full strength. If researchers know the specific mutations that turn a bird virus into an airborne mammalian one, surveillance can watch for those changes in wild flocks and vaccine makers can get a head start of months. Serious virologists made that argument and it is answered on its own terms. Laboratory escapes have happened, smallpox from Birmingham in 1978, SARS from several laboratories in 2003-04, and a pathogen engineered to spread better only needs to escape once. The policy record, by date: a 2014 US funding pause, the 2017 P3CO oversight framework, the 2024 cutoff and 2025 debarment of a specific grantee organisation, and the executive order of May 2025 ordering agencies to end foreign funding and suspend domestic funding for this research.

galileos-ramps-the-falling-bodies-experi.context_blurb:
Does a heavy thing fall faster than a light one? Aristotle said yes. Galileo Galilei, in Italy around 1600, set out to measure the truth, and the experiment he really ran was not a drop from the Leaning Tower but a ball rolling down a ramp.

The final word came in August 1971, when David Scott, commander of Apollo 15, stood on the Moon's airless plain and let go of a falcon feather and a geology hammer together, and both struck the dust at once. His lunar module was named Falcon, so the crew had fetched feathers from the bird kept as mascot by the US Air Force Academy.

His last assistant, Vincenzo Viviani, wrote that around 1583 the nineteen-year-old watched a lamp swaying in Pisa's cathedral and timed its swings by the beat of his own pulse at the wrist, finding wide swings and narrow ones equally long. Viviani wrote it seventy years afterward. Guides still show the very lamp, but Antonio Favaro, editor of Galileo's collected works, found in the cathedral records that it was hung only in 1587, years after the scene.

The ramp is real. No clock of the day could time a falling stone, so Galileo slowed gravity down: he cut a straight, smooth groove along the edge of a long wooden beam, lined it with parchment, propped one end up and rolled a hard bronze ball down the slope. The tilt only stretches the fall until a person can watch it; try it with a marble on a tilted board.

To time each roll, he let a thin jet of water run from a raised vessel into a little glass for as long as the ball was moving. Afterwards he put every glassful on a very accurate balance and weighed it. Weights stood in for times.

Then he split one descent into four equal spells of time and measured how far the ball went in each spell alone. The distances came out as 1, 3, 5 and 7, the odd numbers in order. Their running totals, 1, 4, 9 and 16, show distance growing as the square of the time.

Aristotle made speed follow weight. Galileo spelled out what that means: drop an iron ball of a hundred pounds together with one of a single pound from a hundred cubits, and when the big one lands the small one should be only one cubit down.

The documented drop test came first, in 1586, at Delft. Simon Stevin and his friend Jan Cornets de Groot let two lead balls fall together from the Nieuwe Kerk, one ten times the weight of the other, and judged the race by ear: a single knock on the boards below, not two. Nothing Galileo wrote mentions the Leaning Tower. When Vincenzio Renieri, holder of Galileo's old chair at Pisa, finally let wood and lead fall together from it in 1641, the lead won by nearly two metres. In Bologna the Jesuit Giovanni Battista Riccioli tried to overturn the law from a tower nearly a hundred metres tall. Nobody can watch a falling ball and a pendulum at once, so Riccioli had a chorus of fellow Jesuits chant in time with the pendulum.

The historian Stillman Drake proposed another timer. Galileo's father was a professional lute player, and Galileo played well. In Drake's version, Galileo tied gut strings across the beam so the ball bumped over each, then shifted them until the bumps came in a steady, even beat, so the marks showed distances covered in equal times. Galileo never describes this; it is Drake's reconstruction.

Two New Sciences admits that in air the heavy ball does arrive first, ahead by roughly the width of two fingers. His spokesman, Salviati, turns that into an attack: would you hide Aristotle's error of ninety-nine cubits behind my two small fingers? He also breaks the rule by pure thought. Say a big stone falls at eight and a small one at four, and lash them together. By Aristotle's logic the slow stone drags on the fast one, so the pair must fall at less than eight, even though together they outweigh the stone that fell at eight.

Yet around 1590, as a young professor at Pisa, Galileo had drafted a treatise on motion that stayed unpublished. There he dropped wood against lead, saw the lead land first, and explained it with a model borrowed from Archimedes: a body sinks through air according to its density, just as it sinks through water.

galileos-starry-messenger.context_blurb:
In the winter of 1609 and 1610, in the university town of Padua, the mathematician Galileo Galilei spent his nights aiming a tube of lenses at the sky. Within weeks he had seen more new things than every astronomer before him, and in March 1610 he rushed them into a short book, The Starry Messenger.

The tube was not his invention. A Dutch spectacle-maker, Hans Lipperhey, had sought a patent on a "looker" in 1608. Galileo only heard a description of the gadget, reasoned out for himself how its lenses must work, and ground his own.

On the last night of November 1609 he turned it on a crescent Moon, sketching it again and again and later painting the drawings in watercolour. Textbooks called the Moon a flawless, polished ball. His pictures showed ground full of hollows and bulges, rough and cratered just as the Earth's own surface is.

Along the ragged edge of lunar sunrise, bright specks lit up in the dark: mountain tops catching the light before the ground below. Galileo measured how far each glowing peak stood beyond that shadow line, and turned the distance, by geometry, into a height of more than four Italian miles. He also explained the ashen glow that fills the dark part of a young crescent. It is sunlight reflected from the Earth, so our planet shines in the Moon's sky as the Moon shines in ours. Check it yourself on the next thin crescent.

The Milky Way, a soft band that old catalogues could only compare to milk, broke apart in his tube into stars beyond counting, each one separate and faint.

On 7 January 1610 he aimed at Jupiter and saw three dim points beside it, which he took for background stars. The next night they had moved, and soon a fourth appeared. Within a week he was sure: these were four bodies travelling round Jupiter itself. That sight broke a rule all educated Europe had been taught, for here were four objects plainly orbiting something other than the Earth. It could no longer be true that everything in the heavens turns around us.

Galileo had tutored the prince Cosimo II in mathematics years before, so he named the moons the Medicean Stars, after the Medici. The compliment paid off: in September 1610 Cosimo made him court mathematician and philosopher in Florence, at double his old salary, with no lectures to give at all. Galileo himself just numbered the moons one to four. Their modern names, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, were printed in 1614 by a rival astronomer, Simon Marius, who took the idea from Johannes Kepler.

In July 1610 Saturn seemed to have two smaller companions. Unsure, Galileo sent Kepler the claim scrambled into an anagram. Kepler worked at the puzzle on his own, read it as a Latin line hailing the twin children of Mars, and decided Galileo had found a pair of moons around Mars. The real message was that Saturn looked triple; the companions were rings, a puzzle Christiaan Huygens solved in 1655.

Dark spots also drifted over the Sun, which everyone thought perfect. The Jesuit Christoph Scheiner argued that they were swarms of small planets passing in front, leaving the Sun itself unmarked. Galileo answered that they lay on its surface, and his proof was their shape: as each spot neared the Sun's edge it was squeezed into a thin sliver, as a mark painted on a turning ball looks when it swings round the side. A body floating in front would have kept its shape. Never look at the Sun through a lens.

The moons gave him one more idea. Sailors could find how far north they were but not how far east or west, and Spain's king, Philip III, promised a pension for life to whoever solved it. Jupiter's moons slip into its shadow on a timetable that can be worked out years ahead, and everyone sees an eclipse at the same instant. So a sailor and an astronomer at home would each write down the local clock time when the eclipse began, and the gap between the two times gives the difference in longitude.

galileos-trial-when-authority-overruled-.context_blurb:
In 1610 the Italian mathematician Galileo Galilei turned a homemade telescope on the sky and saw things that clashed with the picture of a motionless Earth at the centre of everything, a picture Europe's universities had inherited from the ancient Greeks. Twice, in 1616 and 1633, the Church in Rome called him to answer for it. The real story is stranger than the cartoon.

In January 1610, through a scope that magnified about twenty times, he watched four tiny lights beside Jupiter change places from one night to the next: moons, circling the planet.

From the autumn of 1610 into early 1611 he followed Venus as it grew from a slim sickle to a full, round face and shrank back again. In Ptolemy's Earth-centred system Venus always sits roughly between us and the Sun, so it could never show more than a narrow crescent. The full cycle of phases ruled Ptolemy out, though it still fitted Tycho Brahe's compromise system as well as Copernicus.

Galileo argued in public for Copernicus's idea that the Earth goes round the Sun. In February 1616 Cardinal Robert Bellarmine, the Church's leading theologian, warned him in private. Galileo might use the Sun-centred system as a mathematical device for calculating, but he must not hold or defend it as a true account of the physical world.

Galileo's own best argument was wrong. In his Dialogue of 1632 he claimed that the ocean tides proved the Earth moves, because the seas slosh in their basins as the daily spin and the yearly orbit combine. He brushed off the idea that the Moon pulls the waters as astrology, yet Newton later showed the Moon's pull is the main cause. The heretic was right about his conclusion and wrong about his proof.

The book's tone did more damage than its astronomy. It is a conversation among three characters, and Pope Urban VIII, once Galileo's friend, found his own favourite argument, that God can bring about any effect by whatever means He likes, spoken by Simplicio, the slow-witted defender of Aristotle. The Pope took it as mockery.

In June 1633 the Roman Inquisition sentenced Galileo. It did not convict him of heresy outright but of vehement suspicion of heresy, for having believed that the Sun is the centre and the Earth moves. He knelt and renounced the idea that same day, and the Dialogue went onto the Index of forbidden books. The famous dungeon, torture and muttered defiance are legends with no place in the record.

Galileo spent his last years confined to his villa at Arcetri near Florence. Going blind, he wrote his greatest physics book, Two New Sciences, the foundation Newton built on. The manuscript was smuggled out of Italy, and the printer Louis Elzevir published it in 1638 in the Dutch city of Leiden, beyond the Inquisition's reach.

In 1992 Pope John Paul II closed a commission he had set up to re-examine the case, and admitted that the churchmen who judged Galileo had been mistaken about how Scripture relates to science. Newspapers around the world reported that he had cleared Galileo. He did not: he neither annulled the 1633 sentence nor declared Galileo innocent.

galloping-gertie-the-picture-every-textb.context_blurb:
The Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened over Puget Sound in Washington state in July 1940, among the longest suspension bridges anywhere. Four months later a steady wind tore it apart while a camera rolled, and for fifty years physics textbooks used that film to illustrate the wrong idea.

The deck was startlingly thin. Its designer, Leon Moisseiff, made it 39 feet wide but only eight feet deep, nearly twice as slender as any long bridge before it. In wind the roadway rose and fell in slow swells, so a driver could see the car in front sink out of sight behind a crest. The workmen who built it had already nicknamed it Galloping Gertie.

Then, one November morning, the motion changed. Until then the roadway had simply heaved up and down. Now, in a wind of about forty miles an hour, it began to twist, one lane rising while the other fell, until it tilted as far as 45 degrees. Leonard Coatsworth, caught out on the span, was flung against the kerb and crawled to safety at a tower, leaving his family's cocker spaniel, Tubby, shut in the car. A professor tried to free the dog, but the terrified animal bit him, and Tubby went down with the deck, the only life lost.

For half a century, textbooks offered the film as the classic case of forced resonance: the effect of pushing a swing in time with its own rhythm until it soars. In 1991 two engineers, Robert Scanlan and K. Yusuf Billah, published a paper that named the books and showed they were wrong. The wind that morning was steady, not a rhythmic push.

What really happened is called aeroelastic flutter. As the deck tilted, the way the air peeled away from its solid sides changed, so the air shoved harder in step with each twist, and the bridge's own motion kept drawing energy out of the steady wind. Instead of dying away, each twist outgrew the one before, until the hanger cables broke. The bridge, in effect, shook itself apart.

give-it-away-or-share-it-the-two-ways-at.context_blurb:
Table salt and water, two of the most familiar substances in any kitchen, show the two main ways atoms hold on to each other. In salt, one atom gives an electron away. In water, two atoms share electrons, unevenly.

Salt is made of two dangerous elements. Sodium is a soft silver metal, first isolated by Humphry Davy in 1807 and stored under oil. A lump dropped into water floats on top while it fizzes, because sodium is just a little less dense than water, skating on the gas it makes. Chlorine is a pale green gas that the German army used as a weapon in 1915. Yet combine the two and you get table salt, the white seasoning on every dinner table.

Pour some salt on a dark plate and look through a hand lens: every grain is a tiny cube.

Each sodium atom hands its single outer electron over to a chlorine atom. The shaker holds charged ions, not atoms, and that one moved electron changes every property. The formula NaCl makes salt sound like pairs of atoms, but there are no pairs. X-rays showed that a crystal is an endless grid in which every sodium is surrounded by six chlorines and every chlorine by six sodiums.

Water holds together the other way. In 1916 the Berkeley chemist Gilbert Lewis, who had privately drawn atoms as little cubes for years, proposed that a chemical bond is a pair of electrons shared by two atoms.

In water the sharing is unfair. Oxygen pulls harder on the shared electrons than hydrogen does, and the molecule is bent, so the two pulls do not cancel. Each molecule is lopsided, slightly negative at the oxygen end and slightly positive at the hydrogen end, though its overall charge is zero. Those charged ends let water tug ions out of a salt crystal.

You can test the idea at a tap. Turn it to a thin thread and hold a comb charged by your hair beside it, and the water swerves toward it. It is tempting to decide the water must be positive. Now charge a glass rod positively instead, and the water swerves toward the rod as well, the same way it did for the comb. Water molecules simply turn whichever end suits toward any nearby charge.

The physicists' grid annoyed some chemists. In 1913 Lawrence Bragg and his father had mapped salt's grid with X-rays, the first crystal ever solved that way, and Lawrence declared that salt holds no molecules of NaCl. In 1927 the old-guard chemist Henry Armstrong protested in Nature under the headline "Poor Common Salt!", and he is reported to have dismissed the physicists by insisting that chemistry is neither chess nor geometry.

Even sodium's splash hid a surprise. The old explanation was that heat from the reaction set the hydrogen alight and the lump went bang. Two chemists, Pavel Jungwirth and Philip Mason, used a high-speed camera in 2015 to film a sodium-potassium alloy dropping into water. In the first thousandth of a second, before any flame, spikes of metal burst out of each drop in every direction. Electrons rush from the metal into the water, the positive ions left behind repel one another, and the drop blows itself apart.

In 1932 Linus Pauling gave each element a single figure for its grip on the electrons in a bond, its electronegativity. On his scale the gap between sodium and chlorine is 2.23, and chemists call their bond ionic; the gap in water's oxygen-hydrogen bond is 1.24, and they call it covalent. The dividing line usually drawn at 1.7 is only a convention chemists agreed on, and nothing in nature changes there, because bonds run along a smooth scale from evenly shared to fully handed over.

Industry runs the salt reaction backwards. In the cell James Cloyd Downs patented in 1924, a current passes through molten salt, so chlorine gas bubbles off at a carbon rod and liquid sodium flows off at an iron shell. Two-thirds of the bath is calcium chloride, which keeps it melted at about 600 degrees. Yet almost no calcium metal comes out, because calcium ions take electrons less readily than sodium ions, which collect them first.

goddard-the-vacuum-and-the-correction-th.context_blurb:
In 1920 the New York Times mocked Robert Goddard, a physics professor at Clark College in Massachusetts, for proposing that rockets might one day fly to the Moon. Forty-nine years later, as Apollo 11 headed there, the paper took it back. Between those dates lies a simple puzzle: in empty space, what does a rocket push against?

The trouble began with a sober 1919 Smithsonian paper on reaching extreme altitudes. Near its end Goddard suggested how to prove a rocket had really got to the Moon: send a tiny load of flash powder to the Moon's dark face, where it would flare on impact brightly enough for a powerful telescope to see. Those few lines set the newspapers off. An unsigned Times editorial in January 1920 sneered that Goddard seemed to lack even the knowledge served up every day in any high school.

He kept building. In March 1926, in the snow of his aunt's farm at Auburn, he launched the first rocket ever to burn liquid fuel. It had no ignition switch, so an assistant lit it with a blowtorch fixed to a long pole and ran for cover. In 1929 another Auburn rocket rose some ninety feet before nosing into the ground and setting the field alight, and the fire marshal forbade any more launches there. Yet that flight was a first, because it carried a barometer, a thermometer and a camera, the first scientific instruments any rocket had lifted.

The editorial claimed a rocket in empty space would have nothing to react against. Goddard had already tested that in 1915. At Clark he sealed a loaded pistol inside a chamber pumped empty of air and fired it, and the escaping gas kicked the gun backward exactly as it would in open air. The chamber tests showed something stranger too: with the air gone, the push grew stronger, because the surrounding air had been cutting the thrust all along. Air is not a rocket's partner; it is in the way.

The editorial writer was not simply foolish. He applied to rockets a fact that is true of a jet engine, which dies in a vacuum because it scoops the oxygen it burns out of the air it flies through. A rocket carries its own oxygen supply along with its fuel.

So what does a rocket push against? Its own exhaust. The engine hurls hot gas backward out of its nozzle, and by Newton's third law the gas pushes the rocket forward just as hard. Don't equal and opposite pushes cancel out? No, because the two forces act on two different bodies: one shoves the gas, the other shoves the rocket, and each body speeds up on its own. The same bookkeeping makes a rifle kick against your shoulder.

Goddard had put the proof inside the very paper the Times was mocking. Its early pages give a formula for a rocket's top speed, which depends on only two things: how much of the rocket's mass is fuel, and the speed at which the exhaust gas shoots out of the nozzle. The air appears nowhere in it. A deaf Russian schoolteacher, Konstantin Tsiolkovsky, had worked out the same equation in 1903.

Goddard did not live to see the apology. The paper's correction came on 17 July 1969, the day after Apollo 11 launched. Experiment had confirmed Isaac Newton, it said, and it was now settled that a rocket works in a vacuum just as it does in an atmosphere. The Times, it added, regretted the error.

golden-rice-twenty-one-years-in-a-greenh.context_blurb:
Children who live mostly on white rice can go blind, and many then die, for lack of vitamin A. In the 1990s two scientists set out to make rice carry the missing nutrient inside the grain itself. They succeeded in 1999, and the rice came out golden. More than twenty years later, the poor rice-eating countries were still waiting to grow it.

The rice plant already makes beta-carotene, an orange pigment that our bodies convert into vitamin A, though only in its green leaves. In the starchy core of the grain, the endosperm, the chain of steps that builds the pigment is switched off. So white rice, the staple of half the world, carries almost none.

Two European plant scientists, Ingo Potrykus of ETH Zurich and Peter Beyer of Freiburg, spent about eight years turning that pathway back on, and announced their success in Science at the start of 2000. They borrowed just two genes from outside rice. The first came from a bacterium living in soil, and the other came from the daffodil, the yellow spring flower, which supplied an enzyme called phytoene synthase. Together the two genes woke the pathway inside the grain.

That July, Time magazine put Potrykus on its cover, standing among the rice plants, under a promise that the grain could save a million children a year. The World Health Organization estimated that between a quarter and half a million children went blind from the deficiency every year, and that about half of them died within twelve months.

Critics made one fair point: the first rice held too little beta-carotene for a child to meet the daily need from rice alone. In 2005 a team at Syngenta answered it by replacing the daffodil's phytoene synthase gene with the matching gene from maize, which raised the carotenoid level about twenty-three times. The dose objection was settled nearly two decades before anyone was allowed to grow the plant.

Opponents fought the crop in fields as well as courts. In August 2013 a government trial plot at Pili in the Philippines stood a few weeks from harvest when roughly four hundred protesters walked in and tore the plants out by hand. In June 2016 the biologist Sir Richard Roberts organised an open letter, signed at launch by about 107 Nobel laureates, urging Greenpeace to drop its campaign against Golden Rice. Greenpeace replied that the rice had failed after twenty years; the laureates' point was that twenty years of blocking had caused the delay.

In 2021 the Philippines became the first country to approve Golden Rice for commercial growing. In April 2024 the Court of Appeals revoked that permit under the Writ of Kalikasan, a special order the Philippine Supreme Court created in 2010 for large environmental cases; kalikasan is Filipino for "nature". The judges pointed to the constitution's precautionary principle and to conflicting scientific views on long-term safety.
