how-to-read-the-words-low-confidence.context_blurb:
How did COVID-19 begin? In August 2021 America's intelligence agencies published a one-page summary showing that they disagreed, and each attached a confidence word to its judgement. Reading those words correctly is a skill, and the honest answer to the question is still that no one yet knows.

The national intelligence director's office reported that four agencies plus the National Intelligence Council leaned toward natural spillover from animals, one agency, the FBI, leaned toward a laboratory incident, and three declined to choose. In intelligence work, a confidence word does not mean how sure the analyst feels. It measures the quality and consistency of the evidence behind the judgement, so low confidence means the evidence is thin or contradictory. The spillover camp held its view at low confidence, the FBI at moderate.

Every agency agreed on one point: the virus had not been built as a bioweapon. The argument was between a natural spillover and an accident connected to research. Agencies kept looking. In February 2023 the Department of Energy, previously undecided, came down, at low confidence, on the side of a laboratory-related origin. The CIA followed in January 2025, also at low confidence, saying no new intelligence had driven the change.

In December 2024 a committee of the House of Representatives concluded that a Wuhan laboratory was the virus's most probable source. One of its central arguments was a furin cleavage site, a short stretch in the virus's spike protein that lets a common human enzyme activate it, which has not been found in the virus's closest bat relatives. The strongest evidence for spillover is a co-location. Swabs from the wildlife stalls of Wuhan's Huanan market, taken on 1 January 2020, held the virus's RNA alongside DNA from raccoon dogs, animals that can catch the virus and were sold there alive. That falls short of proof, since no infected animal has ever been found. In 2025 a World Health Organization panel still leaned toward spillover but said a laboratory accident must stay on the table.

hubble-andromeda-and-a-universe-that-mov.context_blurb:
Until the 1920s many astronomers thought the Milky Way was the whole universe and that the faint spiral clouds in the sky lay inside it. Then one star in the Andromeda nebula, and some humble helpers, made the universe immeasurably bigger and set it moving.

On 26 April 1920 the question went on stage in Washington, D.C., in what became known as the Great Debate between Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis. Shapley argued that the spirals lay inside a huge Milky Way; Curtis argued they were separate island universes. Shapley's strongest card was Adriaan van Maanen's comparison of photographs of spirals taken years apart, which seemed to show them visibly rotating within a few years. Anything turning that fast had to be close by, or its edges would outrun light. The measurements later proved spurious.

On the night of 5 October 1923 Edwin Hubble photographed the Andromeda nebula through the 100-inch Hooker telescope on Mount Wilson in California, then the largest in the world. He had labelled three possible novae with an N. Older plates showed one of them brightening and dimming on a schedule, so he crossed out its N and wrote VAR! in red ink.

It was a Cepheid, a star whose pulse reveals its true brightness by Henrietta Leavitt's law. Hubble's one star put Andromeda about 900,000 light years away, far beyond any Milky Way then imagined: Andromeda was a galaxy of its own. Modern measurements put it nearer two and a half million light years away.

The universe also turned out to be moving. From 1912 Vesto Slipher at the Lowell Observatory measured the spectra of spirals. Andromeda was approaching us at about 300 kilometres a second, but almost all of the 25 others he had measured by 1917 were racing away from Earth. Hubble's partner in the 1929 paper that matched distances to speeds was Milton Humason, who had left school at fourteen with no schooling past the eighth grade. He had driven mules up Mount Wilson and worked as the observatory's janitor before joining its scientific staff.

Two years before that paper, the Belgian priest and physicist Georges Lemaitre had shown that Einstein's own equations implied an expanding universe with a beginning. When Lemaitre explained it to him in Brussels, Einstein, by Lemaitre's later memory, replied that the calculations were correct but the physics abominable.

Hubble's early numbers gave the universe an age of only about two billion years, less than the age of rocks on Earth. In 1952 Walter Baade showed why: Cepheid variables come in two populations with different true brightnesses, and Hubble had read one kind against the other's calibration. Correcting it roughly doubled every distance beyond our galaxy.

The argument is not over. The Planck satellite's reading of the cosmic microwave background gives an expansion rate of about 67, while the local distance ladder of Cepheids and supernovae gives about 73, and the gap is now too large to be chance. Nobody yet knows why: it may be a hidden error in one method, or genuinely new physics.

hubbles-flawed-mirror-when-the-test-rig-.context_blurb:
In April 1990 NASA launched the Hubble Space Telescope with a 2.4-metre main mirror polished more smoothly than any before it, and the first pictures came back blurred. The mirror had been made beautifully to the wrong shape. How that happened is a lesson in testing the test.

Aimed at one star, each of the telescope's two sharpest cameras returned the same image: a little bright centre swamped by a broad glow that held most of the light. That is the mark of spherical aberration. The rim of the mirror had been left too flat by about 2.2 micrometres, roughly a 450th of a millimetre, so light from the rim and light from the centre never met at one focus. A 1991 Naked Gun comedy hung a picture of Hubble on a bar wall of famous disasters, between the Titanic and the Hindenburg.

NASA's investigating board, led by Lew Allen, read the polishing records: the glass matched its target shape better than the contract demanded, all across the disc. The grinding was superb; the target was wrong. Precision means hitting the same spot every time; accuracy means hitting the right spot. The polishers had judged the shape with a null corrector, a rig built from a pair of small mirrors plus a lens, which shows a plain, clean picture once the mirror is correct. The board measured the rig and found its field lens sitting about a millimetre out of position, 1.3 millimetres where the tolerance was ten micrometres. Mismark the ruler, and every measurement comes out wrong.

Technicians had set that spacing by bouncing a laser off the polished end of a metal rod, which wore a small protective cap. Some of the cap's non-reflecting coating had flaked off around its central hole, and the laser bounced off the bare metal of the cap instead. When the lens then would not reach the position their measurement demanded, because the screws had run out of travel, the technicians wedged spacers in to make room rather than ask why.

Two simpler instruments, an inverse null corrector and a corrector made only of lenses, flagged a problem, the first in 1982, yet the optics division brushed both aside because it trusted no instrument but its reflective corrector. The board later confirmed that the dismissed instruments had been right. In July 1990 the board took a fresh picture of the mirror's shape that showed the flaw plainly, and found a virtually identical one from 1982 tucked in a Perkin-Elmer employee's private notebook. There was an even cheaper check. At NASA's direction the rival firm Eastman Kodak had polished a spare mirror, tested with instruments of a different design, and it came out the correct shape. Simply checking Kodak's finished mirror against Perkin-Elmer's would have exposed the error, and nobody did it.

Hubble was not useless meanwhile. Because the blur was known exactly, Sandra Faber and others used deconvolution, working backward through the blur, and restored pictures in which one blob came apart into separate stars. No one could reshape the mirror in orbit, so any repair had to correct the light downstream. The engineer Jim Crocker needed to fit ten small mirrors into a bay the size of a phone booth, and found the answer in a German hotel room: a showerhead on a rod, folded flat against the wall. In December 1993 astronauts installed the folding package, COSTAR, and a new camera whose optics carried an equal and opposite error, cancelling the mirror's. The telescope's own bad pictures had written its prescription.

hutton-at-siccar-point.context_blurb:
One spring day in 1788 the Scottish geologist James Hutton sailed along the Berwickshire shore with two friends and stepped ashore at Siccar Point. There, in a few metres of cliff, he showed them rock that could only mean the Earth is vastly old.

His companions were Sir James Hall, from whose family estate the boat set out, and John Playfair, a mathematician who had spent nine years as a Church of Scotland minister serving two country parishes before giving it up in 1782 to study mathematics. At Siccar Point grey layers of rock stand almost on end, with flat beds of reddish sandstone laid across their worn-off ends. Hutton explained that the grey rock had been laid down flat on an ancient sea floor, hardened into stone, tilted on end, worn down to a stump and drowned again, long before the red sand arrived.

The rock itself proves the wearing-down. At the base of the red sandstone lies a rubble of round pebbles and angular fragments, and they come from the grey rock lying directly beneath, the old rock's own wreckage cemented into the rock that buries it. A buried surface of erosion like this is called an angular unconformity. Sailing on, the party found more upright grey beds, and on their surfaces were ripple marks like those on a sandy sea bed. Ripples form under water on flat sand, so these beds had been laid down flat and tilted later.

Radiometric clocks now date the grey rock to roughly 440 million years ago and the red sandstone to about 375 million: some 65 million years are missing at a seam no wider than two fingers. In that time an ocean closed between what are now Scotland and England, and mountains the size of the Himalayas rose and wore away; the red sand is their debris. The site is so famous that New York's American Museum of Natural History copied it. A crew on scaffolding hanging off the cliff painted the rock with thick liquid latex and peeled off the mould to cast a replica.

Hutton had been hunting for such evidence. In 1785, in Glen Tilt in the Highlands, he found veins of granite cutting clean across the layers of the surrounding schist, so the granite had arrived molten and forced its way in. That refuted Abraham Werner's teaching that every rock, granite too, had precipitated from a single world ocean. On the Isle of Arran in 1787 he met tilted rock under flat rock in a poor exposure, and wrongly assumed that below the surface the two sets lined up parallel once more. Others had seen such junctions before. Nicolas Steno and Horace-Benedict de Saussure had read them as original formations deposited by a worldwide ocean as it receded; Hutton was the first to read one as a vast stretch of time.

Hall took three years of arguing to be won over, then tested the theory with fire. Hutton scorned furnace work, saying you could not judge the mineral kingdom from a little crucible, so Hall kept all his results unpublished until Hutton's death in 1797. Limestone heated in an open fire burns to quicklime as its gas escapes. Hall heated limestone fiercely inside a sealed gun barrel, and out came crystalline marble: rock cooked deep underground behaves differently.

Hutton's own book ran to more than two thousand murky pages. After his death Playfair spent nearly five years rewriting Hutton's whole theory as a clear book of his own, published in 1802. In 1805, eight years after his friend's death, Playfair printed an account of Hutton's life, and there, not at the outcrop, he recalled how their minds grew dizzy, gazing so far down into the abyss of time.

Hutton closed his 1788 paper by declaring that he could find no trace of a beginning and no sign of an end. He meant only that rocks preserve no starting point, and he could not measure time at all. In 1956 Clair Patterson did, measuring the lead that had built up inside a handful of meteorites to fix the Earth's age at 4.54 billion years.

hwang-woo-suk-the-cloned-cell-hero-unrav.context_blurb:
In the mid-2000s Hwang Woo-suk, a veterinary scientist in Seoul, was the brightest star of Korean science. Writing in the journal Science, he reported cloned human embryos and stem-cell lines tailored to individual patients, cells that might repair tissue without rejection. Nearly all of it was fake, and the people who caught him were not the journal's reviewers.

Hwang was a national hero. The state gave him a bodyguard, free first-class flights and even a postage stamp issued in his honour. The post office withdrew it the day after investigators reported.

The trouble began with ethics. In November 2005 the television programme PD Notebook reported that Hwang's human eggs had come from his own junior researchers and from paid donors, though his paper had claimed unpaid volunteers. The public at first sided with Hwang, but the report proved accurate. In December, unnamed researchers posting on a Korean science forum laid the paper's photographs side by side and spotted the same colony of cells printed twice, passed off as two different lines.

In January 2006 a university panel found every one of the eleven claimed cell lines to be faked. It also found that Hwang's team had used at least 2,061 human eggs, more than ten times the number his paper reported.

One claim survived. Snuppy, an Afghan hound born in 2005, really was the world's first cloned dog. The panel settled it with one straightforward check: Snuppy's DNA matched that of the donor dog, Tai, so the cloning was real.

The medical problem Hwang claimed to have solved was real, and it was solved honestly a year later without cloning or embryos. In 2006 the Japanese researcher Shinya Yamanaka reprogrammed ordinary adult cells back into stem cells using four genes, and he shared a Nobel Prize for it in 2012.

in-search-of-the-engram.context_blurb:
Where in the brain does a memory physically live? It must leave some physical trace, which scientists call an engram, but finding one took most of the twentieth century and ended with mice remembering things that never happened.

The word came first. The German biologist Richard Semon coined engram in his 1904 book Die Mneme, arguing that memory must leave a physical change in nervous tissue, long before anyone could look for one.

Karl Lashley, an American psychologist, devoted some thirty years from the 1920s to the hunt. He trained rats to run mazes, cut out pieces of their cortex, then tested them again. He found nothing: the maze memory was never in the piece he removed. The rats got only somewhat worse the more cortex he took, wherever he cut. From that failure he proposed, in 1929, two principles now called mass action and equipotentiality: damage depends on how much cortex is lost, and other areas can take over a missing part's role.

Donald Hebb, a Canadian psychologist, proposed a simple learning rule in 1949: when two neurons fire together again and again, the link between them strengthens. It survives as a rhyme about cells that fire together wiring together.

In 2012 Susumu Tonegawa's team at MIT tagged the hippocampus cells that were active while a mouse was learning that one box meant danger, fitting them with a light-switched protein. In a different, completely safe box, a flash of blue light delivered through an optical fibre reactivated those cells, and the mouse froze as if a shock were coming. The memory lived in a findable set of cells.

In 2013 the same lab planted a false memory. A mouse explored a harmless box while its active cells were tagged. Later, in a second box, the team reactivated those tagged cells with light at the very moment the mouse received a shock. Back in the harmless first box, the mouse froze in fear. How a memory outlasts the proteins in its cells, which are replaced within weeks, is still unknown.

ioannidis-counts-the-false-positives.context_blurb:
In August 2005 John Ioannidis, a Stanford doctor whose field is the failures of medical research, published a short essay in the journal PLoS Medicine with no new experiments and no data tables. Its title made a blunt claim: most research findings that get published are false. Few papers in modern science have been argued over more.

The essay was arithmetic. Ioannidis built a single equation from probability to work out a finding's positive predictive value: the chance that a result marked statistically significant is actually true. What mostly sets that number is the ratio of true to false hypotheses in a field, multiplied by the study's power, its chance of detecting a real effect. A field testing long shots with weak studies publishes mostly noise.

Many readers misread the famous cut-off, p less than 0.05. It does not mean a 5 per cent chance that the finding is wrong. It means that if there were really no effect, data at least this extreme would turn up less than 5 per cent of the time.

From the model Ioannidis drew corollaries. The first says that a field running mostly small, weak studies fills its journals with flukes that later studies cannot repeat, because only the lucky swings of small samples clear the significance bar. Another is shown by his example of searching 100,000 genetic sites for schizophrenia links when only about ten matter: the more relationships a field tests, and the less carefully it selects them, the less likely its findings are to be true. A third says the hotter a field, the worse its record, because of a race. When many teams test the same shaky idea, the first to clear the significance bar publishes, so the race picks out the lucky, noisy runs while the null results stay in drawers. Years later, Ioannidis and David Chavalarias found that nearly all medical papers citing p-values reported results below 0.05, an impossible success rate unless failures were filtered out before print.

What the paper did not say matters too. Ioannidis never claimed that science is worthless or that its findings should be ignored; he argued that the filter is weaker than people think, and named repairs such as larger studies and registering trials in advance. His numbers have been challenged. In 2014 Leah Jager and Jeffrey Leek estimated the false-discovery rate across medical journals at about 14 per cent, far below the headline claim, and the argument continues.

james-lind-and-the-first-controlled-tria.context_blurb:
Scurvy made sailors' gums bleed, teeth loosen and old wounds reopen, and in the 1700s it killed more British seamen than enemy guns did. In 1747 James Lind, a naval surgeon from Scotland, ran a test aboard HMS Salisbury that is now celebrated as the first controlled clinical trial. Then he misread his own result.

The cost of scurvy was staggering. In 1740 Admiral George Anson sailed with about 1,854 men to raid Spain's Pacific colonies. He captured a treasure galleon in a battle that cost one life, yet disease, above all scurvy, so ravaged the voyage that only 188 men came home aboard his flagship, the Centurion. The diet of salt beef and hard biscuit was hard to convict, because sailors on it remain healthy for at least a month before bleeding gums appear.

On 20 May 1747 Lind took twelve sailors with scurvy, as alike as he could find, and kept them together in one sick berth on one identical diet. Then he gave every pair its own remedy, each one something serious doctors of the day recommended: cider, vinegar, sea water, dilute sulphuric acid, a spicy paste, or oranges and lemons. Only one thing changed between the pairs. The cider, a quart daily, brought a slight improvement, and four of the remedies did nothing. The pair on citrus, a couple of oranges and one lemon daily, recovered fastest. When the fruit was gone after six days, one man was fit for duty and the other was well enough to nurse the rest.

Lind did not know what he had. His Treatise of the Scurvy of 1753 ran to some four hundred pages and gave the trial roughly five paragraphs, buried some two hundred pages into the book. Instead of naming citrus as the cure, he argued that scurvy had several causes at once, such as damp and cold, and so needed several remedies. His practical fix made things worse. Fresh fruit rots, so Lind recommended a "rob", juice simmered for hours down to a sixth of its volume. The heat destroyed most of the vitamin C, leaving a syrup that could not cure.

On Anson's voyage a sailor saw a wound from the Battle of the Boyne, healed for more than fifty years, break open again. Scars and the callus that knits broken bone are made of collagen, and the body constantly tears collagen down and rebuilds it; without vitamin C it cannot rebuild, so old repairs come apart. The cure needs astonishingly little. A ration of lemon juice under an ounce a day, stirred into the grog, holds barely ten milligrams of the vitamin, yet that much daily reverses every obvious symptom, even in a man far gone.

The Admiralty was slow. Rear Admiral Alan Gardner issued lemon juice aboard HMS Suffolk on a long run to Madras that arrived free of serious scurvy, with Gilbert Blane arguing for it. Only then, in 1795, did the Navy order lemon juice for the whole fleet, forty-eight years after Lind's trial.

Then the Navy undid its own cure. In the 1860s it switched from Mediterranean lemons to lime juice, which fights scurvy only a quarter as well, because limes could be bought from British colonies. Scurvy returned to the fleet by the mid-1870s and haunted polar explorers.

In 1931 Joseph Svirbely gave guinea pigs boiled food, half of them with Albert Szent-Gyorgyi's newly isolated substance mixed in; only the others fell sick and died. Guinea pigs work as stand-ins for sailors because, like humans, they carry a broken gene for making their own vitamin C. The substance was renamed ascorbic acid, the acid that prevents scurvy.

jan-hendrik-sch-n-the-noise-that-was-too.context_blurb:
At Bell Labs around 2000, the young German physicist Jan Hendrik Schön published a new paper every week or so, reporting exactly the breakthroughs his field most wanted, and was talked of as a future Nobel winner. Readers caught him by noticing that graphs from different experiments carried identical random noise, which real measurements cannot share.

In 2002 Bell Labs asked Malcolm Beasley of Stanford to lead an outside inquiry. In September his committee reported that, of twenty-four charges of scientific misconduct, sixteen were proven, including data reused across unrelated experiments and curves generated from mathematical formulas instead of instruments. The committee cleared all of his roughly twenty co-authors of misconduct; they had trusted samples and figures that Schön produced alone.

About two dozen of his papers were withdrawn. The University of Konstanz revoked his doctorate in 2004, and a Freiburg court restored it in 2010. The final word came from Germany's Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe, which in 2014 upheld the revocation.

jenner-james-phipps-and-the-farmer-who-g.context_blurb:
Smallpox killed roughly thirty of every hundred people it infected. In 1796 Edward Jenner, a country doctor in Berkeley, Gloucestershire, tested a safer protection taken from a mild cattle disease, cowpox. His work gave the world the vaccine, though a Dorset farmer had tried the same idea twenty-two years earlier.

Jenner knew what the older protection cost. As a boy of about eight, around 1757, he underwent variolation, deliberate infection with a mild dose of smallpox, after six weeks of preparation in which he was bled again and again, purged, and starved on a vegetable drink. He was hunting not a first method but a safer one.

Country people said that milkmaids who caught cowpox never got smallpox. On 14 May 1796 Jenner took matter from a sore on the hand of a dairymaid, Sarah Nelmes, and rubbed it into two shallow cuts on the arm of James Phipps, his gardener's eight-year-old son. The boy stayed well, but that proved nothing yet. On 1 July Jenner scratched matter from a smallpox sore into the boy's arm, and no disease followed. Jenner vaccinated the poor without charge from a hut in his garden he called the Temple of Vaccinia, and he let Phipps and his family live in a Berkeley cottage rent-free on a lease.

Jenner never named the cow behind his cowpox, but tradition calls her Blossom, and a London medical school, St George's, keeps her hide on its library wall.

In 1797 Jenner sent his case to the Royal Society, which refused to print it and warned him not to risk his reputation on something so at odds with established knowledge. He paid to publish it himself in 1798, as the Inquiry. He was right that cowpox protected and wrong about where it started: he traced it to a horse's diseased heel, a sore called the grease, carried to the cows by farmhands who dressed the horse and then milked without washing. Oddly, the virus in the vaccine that finally ended smallpox turned out to be closest to horsepox. He also promised that a single dose of cowpox would guard a person for life. Before his century of use was out, testing showed the protection fades and people needed vaccinating again.

Jenner was not the first to try it. In 1774, with smallpox in his Dorset village, the cattle farmer Benjamin Jesty led his wife and two little boys seven miles to a farm whose cows had cowpox, and scratched the matter into their arms with a darning needle. Neighbours pelted him at market. In 1805 a London vaccine institute questioned him, and in front of its officers his eldest son Robert let them inoculate him with live smallpox; he showed no disease. Jenner's real first was the science: he published his evidence and sent vaccine out freely.

Jenner named cowpox Variolae vaccinae, from the Latin vacca, a cow. In 1881 Louis Pasteur proposed, in Jenner's honour, that the word vaccine should cover every protective inoculation, so that today even a flu jab bears the cow's name. The name spread by proposal; each new vaccine still had to earn its own evidence.

john-snow-and-the-broad-street-pump.context_blurb:
At the end of August 1854 cholera exploded around Broad Street in London's Soho, killing more than six hundred people. Most doctors blamed bad air, a foul miasma. John Snow, a London physician, suspected the water, and the way he tested that idea founded the science of epidemiology.

Snow walked the district and marked every death as a short black bar at the address where it happened, stacking bars where several had died in one house. The bars piled up around the public water pump on Broad Street. Yet the water looked innocent. When the local doctor Edwin Lankester examined a glass during the outbreak, it was clear, odourless and pleasant to drink, and people thought it the best water in the area. Only the pattern of who fell ill could convict it.

Snow studied the places that escaped. A brewery stood near the pump, yet none of its seventy-odd workmen died; the owner, Mr Huggins, told him his men had a daily allowance of beer and never drank water. The Poland Street workhouse, almost surrounded by stricken houses, lost only five of its 535 inmates, because it had a well of its own in its yard and never sent to Broad Street.

The strongest clue lay miles away. On 2 September a widow died of cholera in Hampstead, in a district free of cholera. A cart had brought her a large bottle of Broad Street pump water every day, because she liked its taste, and a niece who drank it on a visit died too. Bad air does not travel by cart.

The curate Henry Whitehead knocked on hundreds of Soho doors because he trusted the bad-air theory and expected to demolish Snow's case. His survey converted him instead, and it found the first victim, a baby in the house at number 40, whose mother had washed dirty nappies and tipped the water into the cesspit by the door. The pit's brick lining had rotted, and the shallow well beside it stood in loose gravel, so the filth seeped straight in.

On 8 September the parish board removed the pump's handle. Snow himself would not claim that this ended the outbreak. Deaths were already falling as people fled, and he wrote that it was impossible to say whether the well's water was still poisonous by that date. His 1855 map also carried a single line, which he thought the heart of his argument. It enclosed every spot lying nearer to the Broad Street pump than to any other pump, and the deaths sat inside it.

Three inspectors from the government's General Board of Health rejected the pump, citing the very brewery and workhouse Snow relied on. They blamed the new sewers, laid too flat to drain and choked with butchers' waste, and the foul air rising off them. The same facts, read through a different theory, gave the opposite verdict. Critics had one fair point. Reviewing Snow's 1855 book, the physician Edmund Parkes noted that Snow could not show any impurity in the pump water itself, since his own analysis found almost nothing. Snow won on pattern, not on a specimen.

His strongest evidence was what he called a grand experiment. In south London two water companies piped water down the same streets. Lambeth took its water from upstream, above the city's sewage, while Southwark and Vauxhall pumped from the filthy tidal river. Counting deaths house by house over seven weeks, Snow found roughly eight and a half times the death rate per house among Southwark and Vauxhall's customers.

Even the other side came round. William Farr, the government statistician, had linked cholera to low ground near the Thames. When cholera returned to east London in 1866 and killed over five thousand, Farr went house by house and traced the deaths to the reservoir of one of the water companies. Snow had died eight years earlier.

joseph-black-and-the-heat-that-hides.context_blurb:
Joseph Black, professor of chemistry at Glasgow in the late 1750s, wondered why snowdrifts linger for days after a thaw begins. Warm air keeps pouring heat into them, so they ought to melt in minutes. His answer uncovered heat that thermometers cannot see.

The incoming heat is spent turning ice into water, and the temperature does not budge. In December 1761 Black tested it. He timed a lump of ice melting in a warm room, then compared an equal mass of ice-cold water warming by the same amount. The ice took many times longer, soaking up heat while the thermometer stood still. Black named this hidden heat latent heat, from the Latin for lying hidden.

You can see it at the stove. Put a thermometer in fiercely boiling water and turn the burner to full, and the reading stays stuck at about 100 degrees, because every extra bit of heat goes into turning water into steam. That hidden heat explains why steam burns worse than boiling water at the same temperature: steam condenses on your skin and dumps its latent heat there all at once. It is also why sweating cools you.

Black also showed that the same weight of two different materials can demand very unequal quantities of heat to warm by the same amount, which he called specific heat. Water had an unusually big appetite, soaking up more heat, ounce for ounce, than almost anything else he tested. That is why the sea moderates coastal weather.

Black's friend James Watt was the university's instrument maker. Repairing a model Newcomen engine in 1763, Watt saw that it wasted most of its coal warming the cylinder back up after cold water had been sprayed in to chill it on every stroke. In 1765 he hit on the separate condenser, which kept the working cylinder hot and cut fuel use to about a quarter.

joseph-blacks-fixed-air-the-gas-you-can-.context_blurb:
Before the 1750s, chemists treated air as one single substance. Joseph Black, a young chemist in Edinburgh, showed that a gas could be a definite chemical with its own weight on the balance, and the gas he found is one you can pour.

In 1754 Black weighed a white powder called magnesia alba, now known as magnesium carbonate, heated it strongly, and weighed what was left. The residue was lighter, because a particular gas had been driven out of it. He called it fixed air, since it had been fixed inside the solid; today we call it carbon dioxide.

Carbon dioxide is about one and a half times as dense as air. Let baking soda fizz with vinegar in a jug, then pour the invisible gas toward a burning candle, keeping the liquid in the jug. The gas flows down over the flame, pushes away the oxygen the flame needs, and the flame dies.

The same physics kills. Carbon dioxide is colourless and odourless, and it collects at the lowest point of a farm well, a grain silo or a brewery's fermenting cellar, so a worker who climbs down can be starved of oxygen without warning; the American workplace safety agency lists it among the worst killers in such confined spaces.

joules-paddle-wheel-the-exchange-rate-be.context_blurb:
In the 1840s James Prescott Joule, a brewer from Salford near Manchester with no university post, showed that work and heat are one thing in two forms, exchanged at a fixed rate. His proof was a paddle wheel in a can of water, and the leading scientists of the day did not believe his thermometer.

Joule let weights drop on cords that spun a brass paddle wheel inside an insulated copper can of water. Each time the weights fell, the water warmed a little, and the warming matched the heaviness of the weights multiplied by how far they fell, the quantity physicists call work. A wheel in a smooth can would just carry the water round, so Joule bolted fixed vanes to the inner wall, forcing the water to rub and turn the fall into heat. The effect was tiny: four-pound weights fell twelve yards, sixteen times over, to warm the water by about one degree Fahrenheit.

Joule distrusted everything, starting with himself. A big wooden screen stood around the apparatus during every run, shielding it from the warmth of his own body. And for every trial he went through every step with the weights left still, measured the small rise the room caused on its own, and subtracted it: a control run.

His day job was his training. Critics said serious physics could not come from a brewhouse, but brewing is a trade in which a fraction of a degree decides what the beer becomes, so Joule had habits of fine temperature measurement that professors lacked. The critics attacked exactly that: they said no one could read a thermometer to a two-hundredth of a degree, as Joule claimed. The objection was reasonable, and it was wrong.

Most physicists then held that heat was caloric, an invisible, weightless fluid flowing from hot things to cold. A believer in caloric would say the stirring merely squeezed out caloric the water was already holding. What caloric could not explain was the fixed rate: the same fall always bought the same heat, and the water never ran out.

Joule read his work to the Royal Society in June 1844, and it refused to publish the paper, so he settled for the Philosophical Magazine. Years later the Society printed his work only after its committee struck out his third conclusion, that friction converts mechanical power into heat. The unnamed reviewer who insisted on it was Michael Faraday, impressed by the numbers but unwilling to make that jump.

Joule's 1847 talk at Oxford converted a doubting young listener, William Thomson, the future Lord Kelvin. The two began a long collaboration around 1852, and the Joule-Thomson effect is named for them: a gas cools when it is forced to expand through a porous plug, the principle behind every refrigerator. Joule even predicted that falling water heats itself, so a waterfall should be warmer at the bottom. On his Alpine honeymoon in 1847 he and Thomson planned to test it at the Cascade de Sallanches, but the attempt proved impractical, and he never got a figure from the waterfall.

His certainty that energy is never made or unmade did not come only from his thermometer. It rested on faith: only the Creator, he wrote, has the power to destroy, so any theory demanding the destruction of force must be wrong. A copper paddle-wheel barrel of Joule's, about the size of a kitchen bin, sits in London's Science Museum, but it is not the one from the 1840s. He made this one with his own hands in Salford in 1876, long after the original runs.

keelings-stubborn-curve.context_blurb:
In 1958 Charles David Keeling, an American chemist, began measuring the air's carbon dioxide at an observatory high on Mauna Loa, a volcano in Hawaii. His graph, the Keeling Curve, is the longest direct record of the gas, and it was built on one man's refusal to be approximate.

Earlier published readings of the gas varied so much that chemists thought the figure was purely local. From 1955 Keeling carried a home-built instrument to forests in California, Washington and Arizona and sampled around the clock. Night readings swung wildly, but every site's afternoon reading came out near 310 parts per million: there was one real background number worth measuring.

Precision was the point. He trapped air samples in five-litre flasks, froze out the carbon dioxide with liquid nitrogen, and measured what he had trapped by how hard it pressed on a mercury column. Today the Mauna Loa analyser is held to the original scale by cylinders of reference gas traced back to primary standards, and it is rechecked against them every half hour.

Keeling's first Mauna Loa reading, in March 1958, was 313 parts per million. Recent monthly readings stand at about 429, and anyone can look up the latest figure, which Scripps and the US agency NOAA post every month. The line does not climb smoothly. Instead it zigzags, rising and falling about six parts per million each year. That rhythm is the planet breathing. Land plants in the Northern Hemisphere, where most of the world's seasonal forests and fields lie, pull carbon in as they grow each summer and release it as they decay.

The climb has sped up. During the 1960s the yearly rise was under one part per million, around 0.7; the rate has since more than tripled, passing 2.5 parts per million a year.

The record is not quite unbroken. For roughly three months in 1964 there are no readings, because the analyser failed and the budget had no money to pay a technician to mend it, after Congress trimmed federal spending. To keep Mauna Loa going, Keeling gave up the continuous monitoring station he had been running at the South Pole, which did not restart until 1974.

Critics ask whether the volcano spoils the readings. Volcanic gas arrives in jumpy, noisy bursts, so NOAA's analysts discard any hour whose readings jitter past a set limit. They also discard afternoon air carried up from lower slopes, where island plants have already drawn the gas down. And volcanoes are small sources. Mount St Helens' 1980 eruption released some ten million tons of the gas over nine hours, but the US Geological Survey calculates that humanity now emits that much in roughly two and a half hours.

By itself the curve cannot reveal the source of the extra carbon, but two other measurements can. Plants prefer the lighter form of carbon, so carbon that has passed through living plants, and the fossil fuels made from them, is unusually light. The air's carbon has been drifting lighter since industry began, pointing at that source rather than at volcanoes, whose carbon is heavier. In 1989 Keeling's son Ralph began measuring the air's oxygen, which has fallen in step with the rising carbon dioxide. Burning consumes oxygen and ocean or volcanic gas does not, so the drop points to the extra carbon dioxide coming from burning fuel.

Measuring the gas is not the same as predicting the warming. Its warming effect grows with the logarithm of its concentration, so each extra fifty parts per million warms a little less than the fifty before; a rise added now does less than the same rise did in 1958. How much warming each doubling brings, the climate sensitivity, is where the genuine scientific argument lies.

kekul-s-ring-and-the-dream-he-told-25-ye.context_blurb:
Benzene is a clear liquid whose molecule holds six carbon atoms but only six hydrogens, far fewer than a chain of six carbons should carry. For decades it baffled chemists. In 1865 the German chemist August Kekulé proposed that its carbons join in a ring, and the story of how chemists proved him right is better than the legend that surrounds it.

Michael Faraday found benzene in 1825 at the Royal Institution in London, which lit its rooms with a gas made by dropping whale oil into a hot furnace and squeezed into iron cylinders. Faraday distilled the dark residue at the bottom of spent cylinders and drew off a clear new liquid. Its name has nothing to do with its shape. In 1833 Eilhard Mitscherlich made it on purpose by heating benzoic acid with quicklime. That acid came from gum benzoin, a sweet-smelling resin that oozes from a tree, so he called his product benzin.

Then there is the famous dream. On 11 March 1890, at a celebration in Berlin's city hall a quarter-century after the benzene paper, Kekulé told for the first time of a fireside daydream around 1862: atoms wheeling before his half-closed eyes, until a snake seized hold of its own tail. Nobody but Kekulé ever vouched for it, and he told it long after the fact. Before he sat down he urged the young chemists to dream, but to beware of announcing a dream in print until it had been tested.

The ring was settled at the bench. A hexagon makes a testable prediction: put two chlorine atoms on it and only three truly different compounds can exist, with the chlorines on neighbouring carbons, one carbon apart, or straight across. A chain would permit more. Chemists made dichlorobenzene every way they could and found exactly three. Benzene also behaves strangely. Bromine water instantly loses its colour on a compound with a double bond, because the bromine attaches itself there, but benzene leaves it untouched. Forced with a catalyst, benzene finally reacts by swapping one hydrogen for a bromine and keeping its ring intact.

Getting the structure right paid off. In 1868 Carl Graebe and Carl Liebermann, seeing that the red dye alizarin was a cousin of a ring compound in coal tar, made it in the laboratory, and within a few years the centuries-old trade in madder roots, dug from the ground for their red, collapsed.

Kekulé had a rival. In 1858 the Scot Archibald Scott Couper independently showed that carbon atoms link to one another, and invented the straight line between letters that every student now draws for a bond. The Paris chemist who was supposed to submit his paper delayed it, so Kekulé's appeared first, and Couper returned to Scotland and published no more science for the rest of his life.

In 1869 Albert Ladenburg, once Kekulé's own student, attacked the hexagon. If single and double bonds alternate around the ring, two neighbouring groups could straddle either kind of bond, giving two different compounds, yet chemists only ever found one. In 1872 Kekulé repaired his own picture: the two kinds of bond flip places so fast that no one can tell them apart.

Nobody measured the ring until 1929, when Kathleen Lonsdale fired X-rays through crystals of hexamethylbenzene. All six carbon-carbon bonds were the same length, in a flat, regular hexagon. Each bond lies between a single and a double bond in length. The reason is that each carbon uses three electrons in bonds lying in the ring's plane, and the six left over spread into a single cloud that belongs to the whole hexagon, above and below it. Chemists draw that shared cloud as a circle inside the hexagon.

Historians still argue whether the dream happened. A single dated scrap proves the tale was already going round before the 1890 speech: in 1886 a joke edition of a chemistry journal, made for a beer evening, drew the benzene ring as six monkeys gripping one another tail to paw. Priority is argued too. In 1861 the Viennese schoolteacher Josef Loschmidt printed a booklet in which he drew benzene as a single big circle ringed by six little hydrogen circles, and whether that circle means a ring is disputed.

keplers-question-why-six-corners.context_blurb:
In the winter of 1611 Johannes Kepler, the astronomer who had shown that planets move in ellipses, walked over the Charles Bridge in Prague as snow settled on his coat. The flakes gave him a question that took science three centuries to answer.

He set down his thoughts in a little booklet, a New Year's present for his patron, built around one question: why does every snowflake seem to have six corners? He compared the flakes with seeds packed in a pomegranate and with the cells of a honeycomb, and then he ended by confessing honestly that his own question had beaten him.

The answer lies in the water molecules. As water freezes, its molecules link into a puckered hexagonal cage, so an ice crystal grows fastest in six equal directions, and a flake's six arms are that atomic pattern showing at a size you can see.

On 15 January 1885 Wilson Bentley, a nineteen-year-old on a Vermont farm, used a camera he had joined to a microscope and made the first-ever photograph of one snow crystal. He went on to photograph more than 5,000. Ukichiro Nakaya, working in a frozen laboratory in northern Japan in the 1930s, was first to grow snow crystals artificially, and showed that heat and humidity decide a flake's form. He called a snow crystal a letter sent from the sky, recording the air the flake fell through.

Are no two snowflakes alike? In 1988 Nancy Knight photographed two identical crystals from a research plane, and doubters of the old saying quoted her widely, usually leaving out that the pair were plain hollow columns, not elaborate six-armed stars. The picture-book star is rare anyway: the Caltech physicist Kenneth Libbrecht finds that fewer than one natural flake in a thousand is a clean, symmetric six-armed star. Catch flakes on a dark sleeve and look with a hand lens to see for yourself.

kochs-four-step-test-for-a-killer.context_blurb:
A microbe found in a dead body might be the killer, a harmless passenger, or a scavenger that arrived after death: being present is not being guilty. In the 1870s Robert Koch, a country doctor in the Prussian town of Wollstein, worked out how to prove which germ causes which disease.

He had no laboratory and no colleagues. A curtain split his consulting room in two, and behind it he made his own apparatus; the one real instrument he did not build was the microscope his wife Emmy had given him for his birthday. He also taught himself to take photographs through the microscope, and his 1877 anthrax paper carried them, because a rival can check a photograph but must take a drawing on trust.

Earlier researchers had spotted tiny rods in the blood of cattle killed by anthrax. Koch infected mice with rods taken from dead animals, using splinters of wood, and they all died. That same day a second batch of mice got blood from healthy animals instead, so the two groups differed in one thing only. A critic could still say a poison in the sick blood had done the killing. So Koch grew the bacilli for generation after generation outside any body, in the watery fluid taken from an ox's eyeball, and bacteria that had never been near a diseased animal still killed. Under his microscope he also watched the rods, when conditions turned against them, form rounded spores inside themselves, which later became rods again. Spores can wait for decades: in 2016 a Siberian heat wave unfroze the body of a reindeer dead since around 1941, and its anthrax infected a boy.

In April 1876 Koch, still an unknown, claimed he could prove the cause of anthrax. Ferdinand Cohn, professor of botany at Breslau, made him run the whole proof at Cohn's own bench, which took three days; by the end the room was convinced, and Cohn published the paper.

Koch then turned to tuberculosis, which killed about one person in seven. Since Hippocrates, respectable medicine had held that it was inherited, running down through families. On 24 March 1882 Koch showed the Berlin Physiological Society that a bacterium causes it, having isolated it from patients, cultured it, infected guinea pigs and recovered it. The room barely reacted, but Paul Ehrlich, who called that evening the greatest scientific moment of his life, set to work that night refining Koch's method for staining the germ.

Pure cultures needed a solid surface on which one germ grows into a visible speck. Potato grew anything, and gelatin melted at body warmth. In 1881 Fanny Hesse, married to a member of Koch's team, suggested agar, a setting agent boiled out of a red seaweed that she knew from fruit jellies; it stays solid when warm, and no bacterium can digest it. She received no credit. In 1887 Julius Richard Petri, another assistant, swapped the bulky bell jar for a flat dish with a slightly wider lid, and titled his paper, in German, a small modification of Koch's plating method.

Koch's four rules, drawn up with Friedrich Loeffler, demand that the suspect be present in every patient and absent from healthy people, be grown pure, cause the disease, and be recovered again. Koch himself found healthy people carrying cholera and typhoid germs, and he said so in public and loosened the first rule. Viruses break the second: a virus copies itself only inside a living cell, so it can never be grown alone on a plate.

Koch once broke his own standard. In 1890 he announced a secret remedy for tuberculosis before testing it properly. Patients died, and in January 1891 Rudolf Virchow showed autopsies proving that the remedy had woken tuberculosis lying dormant in them. Koch withdrew the claim, and the substance survives today as a skin test.

koonin-reads-the-report-himself.context_blurb:
Steven Koonin is an American physicist whose 2021 book Unsettled asked a plain question: what do the big climate assessments actually say in their technical chapters, and does the summary match? He accepts that the climate is changing and that humans influence it. His quarrel is with certainty, and his method is one anyone can copy: open the document and read it.

He was no outsider. He taught physics at Caltech from 1975 and served as its provost, and from 2009 to 2011, under President Obama, he served as the Energy Department's Under Secretary for Science. Nor is he a stranger to computer models. He wrote a textbook on computational physics, and simulations like his served the Energy Department's programme for confirming, without test explosions, that the country's nuclear weapons still function.

He had punctured hype before. In 1989, when two chemists in Utah, Stanley Pons and Martin Fleischmann, claimed to have achieved fusion in a simple jar of water, Koonin told a meeting of the American Physical Society that their result came from incompetence and self-delusion, and the room applauded.

In 2014 Koonin wrote an essay for the Wall Street Journal under the title Climate Science Is Not Settled; an annotated version carries twelve numbered notes. Each note points to a numbered figure or section of the IPCC's own report, so any reader can check whether he quoted it honestly. His ninth note, about the sea ice around Antarctica, shows the whole method in one paragraph: it quotes the summary's wording and then prints, right next to it, what the chapter itself says. The summary is what officials and journalists read; the chapters underneath are what almost nobody opens.

Many summaries say the essay calls man-made warming fake. It does not. In its fourth paragraph Koonin wrote that human influence is no hoax: greenhouse gases from burning fossil fuels are influencing the climate. His argument is about how certain anyone can be.

The fifth IPCC assessment relied on roughly fifty-five models, each trying to match the past century's temperatures. Koonin reported that their descriptions of that century differ from one another by more than three times the warming actually measured, so no more than one of them can be right. The key number is climate sensitivity, the warming that follows a doubling of carbon dioxide. Koonin noted that the fifth assessment's figure, between 1.5 and 4.5 degrees, came from the panel's own expert judgment rather than from a measurement, and was no narrower than thirty years before. Applied to Koonin himself, the same checking habit shows that claim was soon overtaken. In August 2021 the sixth assessment gave a best estimate of 3 degrees, with a likely range of 2.5 to 4.

Unsettled also points to the years 1940 to 1970, when greenhouse emissions climbed but global temperature did not rise. Models can reproduce that pause only if they include a cooling influence, also human: aerosols, the fine particles of pollution that factories and furnaces send into the air. Aerosol cooling is real, but its size is uncertain, which leaves models room to fit a known answer.

Koonin reads every paragraph to the end. The 2021 report's single paragraph on tropical cyclones is unsure whether such storms are becoming more frequent overall and judges that a larger fraction now reach the top categories. It reserves its most confident label, very likely, for a finding hardly anyone repeats: the latitude at which north-west Pacific cyclones reach their peak has shifted north.

He wants the arguments held in public. In January 2014 he chaired a day-long American Physical Society workshop that set three scientists known for questioning mainstream projections against three of their defenders, and the society put the complete transcript online for anyone to read. In 2025 he and four other scientists wrote a review for the US Energy Department that said carbon dioxide warms the climate but found no clear long-term rise in American extreme weather. Over eighty climate researchers answered with a joint rebuttal, charging cherry-picking and misquotation. It is a minority position, defended in print and contested hard.

Uncertainty, Koonin wrote, is no excuse for doing nothing. His 2014 essay closes by calling it well-justified prudence to accelerate low-emissions technology and cost-effective energy efficiency, and it refuses to call climate science either settled or a hoax.

kwoleks-cloudy-batch.context_blurb:
Stephanie Kwolek, a chemist at the DuPont company, invented Kevlar, a fibre that is about five times stronger than steel, weight for weight. Her discovery began with a batch of liquid that looked ruined, and with her refusal either to throw it away or to believe her own results too quickly.

She joined DuPont in 1946 meaning to work a few years and save enough to pay her way through medical school and become a physician. She stayed forty years. In 1964 DuPont set her group to replace the steel cord inside car tyres with a lighter fibre. The worry was a coming gasoline shortage: lighter tyres stretch a gallon further.

Her polymer batches always came out clear and thick as molasses. Then one batch was thin and cloudy, with the look of buttermilk. A cloudy batch was normally thrown away. Cloudiness usually means solid specks floating undissolved, so the obvious verdict was contamination, and Kwolek tested that first: she pushed the batch through a fine filter, and nothing was caught.

She asked for it to be spun into fibre. Charles Smullen, who ran the spinning machine, refused at first for a sound reason: he thought the cloudy liquid held grit that would block the tiny holes of his spinneret. After much discussion he gave in, and it spun without trouble. She ran the first test with her own hands, pulling on the new fibre, and it would not break. The strength numbers were far beyond anything DuPont had spun, so she had the tests repeated again and again before she would believe she had made a discovery.

The cloudiness was the secret. Ordinary polymer molecules are floppy tangles, but Kwolek's were stiff rods, and in the flask they lined up side by side into liquid-crystal patches that scattered light. Rods already aligned in the liquid stay aligned in the fibre, and alignment is strength: the reason the batch looked wrong was the reason it was strong. Along the fibre, Kevlar's chains lie stretched and parallel, and what grips neighbouring chains sideways are hydrogen bonds, each N-H group on one chain reaching to a C=O group on the next. The strength runs one way only: Kevlar resists pulling but buckles when bent or pushed, and sunlight weakens it.

Police vests stack twenty or thirty layers of Kevlar cloth and are rated to stop pistol bullets. They are bullet-resistant, not bulletproof: to stop a rifle round, a hard ceramic plate must be slid into the vest. Kevlar armour is credited with saving more than 3,000 officers' lives.

Kwolek also gave classrooms a demonstration. In 1959 she and Paul Morgan published the Nylon Rope Trick: pour two liquids into one beaker and nylon forms at the line where they meet, so a solid strand can be drawn out like thread. Kevlar went on sale in 1971 and has earned DuPont billions. The 1974 patent names Kwolek as inventor, but as a DuPont employee she signed it over to the company and earned nothing from it.

lamarcks-ghost-what-a-body-can-and-canno.context_blurb:
Jean-Baptiste Lamarck's 1809 book Philosophie Zoologique offered the first full theory of how species change. His famous example was the giraffe: each giraffe stretched its neck reaching for high leaves, and its calves inherited the longer neck. The idea, called the inheritance of acquired characteristics, says that a trait a parent works into its own body during life is handed down to its young.

In the 1880s the German biologist August Weismann tested the claim bluntly. He docked the tails of white mice and of their descendants for five generations, and among 901 offspring he found not one shortened tail. Weismann argued that body cells cannot write back to the cells that make the next generation.

A modern twist is the study of children conceived during the Dutch famine of 1944 and 1945, who carried chemical marks on their genes decades later. Whether such marks pass reliably down the human generations is still unknown.

landsteiner-ends-the-transfusion-lottery.context_blurb:
Until 1900, giving a patient someone else's blood was a lottery. One patient recovered quickly while the next developed a raging fever and died, and doctors could not tell why. In Vienna the young pathologist Karl Landsteiner solved the mystery with a few drops of his colleagues' blood.

The idea of transfusion was old. In Paris in 1667 Jean-Baptiste Denys transfused a fifteen-year-old boy with a lamb's blood, and the boy survived; a later patient, given calf's blood, died, and the practice was soon banned.

In 1900 Landsteiner mixed serum and red cells from himself and his colleagues on a plate. Some pairs clumped and some stayed smooth, and the pattern revealed that humans fall into distinct blood types, and that blood from one type can clash with another. He labelled the three groups he found A, B and C; C was later renamed O. Six donors were too few to catch a rarer group. In 1902 two of his students, Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli, tested a much larger set of samples and found the fourth, later named AB. Rare types appear only when you test enough people.

The clumping is a chemical fight. Red cells carry sugar markers called antigens, and the plasma carries antibodies, each built to fit one kind of marker; the antibodies grab any red cells bearing their matching sugar and pull them into clumps. That is why a mismatched transfusion can kill. Emergency rooms therefore keep O-negative red cells, which lack the A, B and Rh markers, since in an emergency there may be no time to test a patient's type, and they suit nearly everyone.

lavoisiers-sealed-vessel-and-the-death-o.context_blurb:
For most of the 1700s chemists explained burning with phlogiston, a fire-substance that burning things were supposed to release. The French chemist Antoine Lavoisier overthrew it with the balance: he weighed everything, before and after, and let nothing escape.

Set fire to some steel wool balanced on a scale and the beam tips down on the burnt side, because the crust outweighs the wool: the metal has taken something out of the air.

Phlogiston was no foolish idea. It explained the smelter's trick of heating a calx, the ashy powder left when a metal is roasted, with charcoal to get shiny metal back: the charcoal, thought to be nearly pure phlogiston, was handing its own phlogiston over to the starved calx. But roasted metals got heavier, not lighter. Jean Rey, a French physician, had explained in 1630 why a tin powder weighed more than its tin: air, thickened by the long heat, had attached itself to the metal. Nobody listened. In 1764 Jean-Baptiste Chardenon rescued phlogiston by proposing that it has negative weight, so a body that loses it gets heavier. A theory that needs such patches has stopped predicting.

Lavoisier's answer was the sealed vessel. He shut tin and air together in a glass vessel, weighed it all, then heated it till a crust formed on the tin. The sealed vessel weighed exactly what it had before. Opened, the tin was 3.12 grains heavier, and the air had lost the same 3.12 grains. The extra weight had come from inside the jar.

The key gas was caught in England. On 1 August 1774 Joseph Priestley heated a red mercury powder with a burning lens and collected the gas it gave off. In that gas a candle's flame flared five or six times as bright as in ordinary air. Priestley called it dephlogisticated air and died believing in phlogiston. Lavoisier named it oxygen, from Greek words meaning acid-maker, because he believed it was the ingredient behind every acid.

Lavoisier kept mercury hot for twelve days in a closed vessel of air. Red crust formed, the air shrank by about a sixth, and a lit taper lowered into the leftover air died at once, as if dunked in water. Heated alone, the red crust gave back running mercury and exactly the air the jar had lost. The books balanced in both directions, which phlogiston could never do.

His wife, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, worked in the laboratory and translated the strongest defence of phlogiston, Richard Kirwan's essay, into French. Her 1788 edition printed Kirwan's case with Lavoisier and his allies answering it, note by note, at the foot of each page.

Reformers carry their own errors. The table of thirty-three elements in Lavoisier's 1789 textbook begins with light and caloric, the weightless fluid he believed heat was: two unweighable substances heading the list of a man who had beaten phlogiston for being unweighable. His oxygen name was wrong too. In 1810 Humphry Davy showed that muriatic acid, now called hydrochloric acid, is made of hydrogen and chlorine, with no oxygen at all. And the famous French slogan about nothing being lost or created was coined by later writers and appears nowhere in his own works; what he wrote was that in every operation nothing is created and equal matter exists before and after.

Lavoisier paid for his science as a member of the Ferme générale, the company that collected France's taxes. In 1794 the Revolution tried him with other tax farmers and guillotined him the same day, aged fifty. Among the charges was soaking tobacco to make it heavier, the very cheat he had long worked to detect. France cleared his name in 1796.

Even his great law is very slightly false. Burn carbon in a sealed vessel and the whole really does lose a tiny amount, roughly a third of a billionth of the carbon's mass, because the mass left with the heat and light: energy has mass. No balance could ever catch it, so for chemistry Lavoisier's law is exactly right.

leeuwenhoeks-animalcules-and-the-royal-s.context_blurb:
Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a shopkeeper in Delft in the Netherlands, had no university training and never learned Latin, yet in the 1670s he was the first human being to set eyes on bacteria and other single-celled life. The learned men of London did not simply believe him. They checked.

His first lenses were tools of the cloth trade, which he learned in Amsterdam from 1648: a draper used a small magnifying glass to count the threads per inch in a weave. He went on to make far stronger lenses of his own. His microscope was a single tiny lens riveted between two metal plates; he held the plate flat against his eye and aimed it at a candle flame, with the specimen on a pin moved by screws.

In September 1674 he examined a drop from a lake outside Delft and saw green spiral streaks, and among them a crowd of tiny creatures swimming about. So that readers without a lens could picture the scale, he wrote that some were over a thousand times smaller than a cheese mite, the tiny creature on cheese rind and the smallest most people had ever seen. He wrote in plain Dutch, calling them by an everyday word that his translators rendered as little animals.

In September 1683 he looked somewhere nobody had thought to: the soft whitish film he scraped from between his own teeth, mixed with clean rainwater. His sketches of what he saw are the earliest known images of bacteria. He wrote that more animals live in the scum on one man's teeth than there are men in a whole kingdom, especially in those who never clean their teeth. He even tried vinegar on them, and when that kill-test was printed, some readers were so disgusted that they swore never to use vinegar again.

London hesitated. Henry Oldenburg, the Royal Society's secretary, had printed Leeuwenhoek's letters promptly, but once they claimed invisible creatures in water, he printed only three of the next twelve, and none of those three touched the creatures. Leeuwenhoek sent sworn statements from a notary, ministers, a lawyer and a physician who had seen them. In November 1677 the Fellows heard them out and were still not satisfied: they told Robert Hooke, their curator of experiments, to repeat the observation with his own eyes. Hooke failed twice. On the third try he saw great numbers of tiny animals swimming, because this time he had let his pepper-water steep for nine or ten days instead of two or three. A failed repeat is not always a refutation.

Leeuwenhoek kept his best lens-making method secret, and people long assumed a lost technique. Researchers in Delft in 2021 used beams of neutrons to see inside two of his surviving microscopes without opening them, and found his high-power lens was a tiny blown glass globule, made by a method Robert Hooke himself had published. His real edge was patience, preparation and lighting. He worked to the end: dying of pneumonia at ninety in 1723, a day and a half before his death, he was still dictating a letter about sand that a director of the East India Company had brought him to test for gold.

lenskis-twelve-flasks.context_blurb:
In February 1988 Richard Lenski, an American biologist, set out to watch evolution happen. He started twelve identical flasks of E. coli bacteria from one ancestor, all on the same thin broth, and the experiment has run ever since, past 80,000 generations. It began at the University of California, Irvine, and moved to Michigan State University a few years later.

No machine keeps it going. Every morning a person moves a drop from each flask into fresh broth by hand, weekends and holidays included. The broth carries only 25 milligrams of glucose per litre, so the cells use up the sugar in about six hours and spend the rest of the day starving. The routine has broken only once, when a COVID-19 lockdown emptied the building in 2020 and the populations waited in the freezer for months.

What makes it an experiment is the freezer. Every 500 generations a sample from each flask goes into a freezer at minus eighty degrees, and when the oldest tubes are thawed, the 1988 cells start dividing again and rebuild a full population: a fossil record that is still alive. That lets the lab race descendants against their own ancestors. To measure fitness, it puts an evolved strain and its thawed ancestor into one flask together and compares how fast each multiplies. The ancestor needed about an hour to double on the thin broth; its descendants now double in about forty minutes. To tell two mixed strains apart, six populations carry a single harmless change in a sugar gene called araA, so on a special indicator plate the two versions form colonies of different colours, one red and one white.

The biologist Stephen Jay Gould wondered what would happen if life's tape were rewound and played again. Lenski's flasks are twelve replays, and one change appeared in all twelve independently: the cells grew steadily larger.

Around generation 31,500 one population, Ara-3, began eating citrate, which had sat in the broth all along but which E. coli cannot use when oxygen is present. Its genome showed why: an existing citrate carrier gene had been copied and placed next to a switch that runs in air. Lenski's team then replayed history, reviving Ara-3 from thirteen moments of its frozen history and screening trillions of cells. The ability evolved again only in cultures started from samples frozen after roughly generation 20,000, because earlier mutations had to be in place first.

Six populations broke their own DNA-proofreading genes and began piling up mutations roughly a hundred times as fast. Careless copying costs a cell about one per cent of its growth, but each such cell has a far better chance of producing the next winning mutation, and once it wins it is hard to displace. In one of those populations, two separate lineages later made the same change: both reduced their mutation rate by roughly half rather than restoring it fully.

Will improvement ever stop? In 2013 Wiser, Ribeck and Lenski fitted 50,000 generations of data, and the curve was still climbing, though more and more gently, with no upper limit in sight.

lgm-1-the-signal-that-was-too-regular.context_blurb:
In 1967 a Cambridge graduate student, Jocelyn Bell, found a radio signal from space so regular that her team half-jokingly called its source LGM-1, for Little Green Men. It was the first pulsar: the spinning, collapsed core of a dead star, sweeping radio waves across the sky like a lighthouse beam.

Bell had spent two years helping build the radio telescope at Lord's Bridge near Cambridge, about 2,048 antennas spread over four acres. Her supervisor, Antony Hewish, designed it to study how quasars twinkle as their radio waves pass through the turbulent solar wind, which is why it recorded fast flickers at all.

In August 1967, reading roughly thirty metres of chart paper each day, Bell noticed a scrap of untidy trace, barely a quarter of an inch long, that recurred whenever one patch of sky passed overhead. She called it a bit of scruff. In November she ran the recorder at full speed over that patch, and the scruff resolved into crisp, evenly spaced pulses: one every 1.337 seconds, regular to about one part in a million. No natural source then known kept time that well.

The team tested the alien idea honestly. If a civilisation on a planet were broadcasting, the planet's orbit around its own sun would shift the pulse rate up and down, but the pulses showed no such Doppler shift; only the Earth's own motion appeared. Then Bell found a second pulsing source in another part of the sky with its own, quite different period, and two alien broadcasters on one frequency was too much to believe.

The object had been predicted on paper. In 1934, two years after the neutron was discovered, Walter Baade and Fritz Zwicky proposed that some massive stars collapse into balls made almost wholly of neutrons, and in the same work gave us the word supernova. Almost nobody expected one to be seen.

The 1974 Nobel Prize for the discovery went to Hewish and Martin Ryle, not to Bell. In a 1977 speech she herself said it would demean the Nobel Prizes to award them to research students except in very exceptional cases, and that hers was not one of them. When a $3 million Breakthrough Prize came to her in 2018, she gave every penny to the Institute of Physics to fund physics doctorates for women, minorities and refugee students.

limits-to-growth-and-the-deadlines-that-.context_blurb:
In March 1972 a slim book called The Limits to Growth warned that the world was heading for collapse. With some thirty million copies sold worldwide, it became the best-selling environmental book ever. Its forecasts, its critics and its afterlife are a lesson in what a computer model can and cannot tell you.

The study was paid for by the Club of Rome, a circle of European business leaders, financiers and scientists founded in 1968. A team at MIT led by Donella and Dennis Meadows built a computer model of the whole planet, called World3. It turned five interacting dials: population, food output, industrial output, pollution, and the consumption of non-renewable resources. Its warning was that if growth continued at 1970s rates, the world would run out of resources and collapse within about a century.

Critics pounced. In the New York Times the economist Peter Passell called it an empty and misleading work and dismissed its graphs with the programmers' proverb, garbage in, garbage out: a model can be no better than the assumptions fed into it. The sharpest attack came in 1973 from two economists, Ronald Riker and Allen Kneese. The modellers, they said, had let resource use and pollution grow exponentially while technology improved only linearly, which builds collapse in before the machine starts.

Resource deadlines have a way of expiring. In 1956 the geologist M. King Hubbert predicted that American oil output would top out around 1970, and for decades he seemed right. Then horizontal drilling paired with hydraulic fracturing unlocked oil trapped in shale rock, and by 2017 American output passed ten million barrels daily.

Yet the book cannot simply be called refuted. Its standard run, in which the world carries on as before, dates a serious downturn to the middle of this century. When Graham Turner in 2008 and Gaya Herrington in 2020 compared decades of real data with it, they found the real data tracking the standard run so far. That part of the forecast has not yet been tested.

Models can also do harm. In 1980 the Chinese engineer Song Jian, trained in missile-guidance control theory, picked up the book in Europe and applied its logic to China's population, helping to fix the one-child rule in place. A model built for one problem became a lever on a billion lives.

listers-carbolic-and-the-coat-he-stopped.context_blurb:
In the 1860s an operation was often deadlier than the injury, and about half of those who lost a limb died afterwards of wound infection. Surgeons wore coats stiff with old blood to show their experience. The Scottish surgeon Joseph Lister changed that, and later had the honesty to drop his own most famous device.

Lister reached for a chemical used to treat sewage in the town of Carlisle: carbolic acid. In August 1865 his first test case at the Glasgow Royal Infirmary was James Greenlees, eleven, whose leg had been crushed by a cart so that the bone stuck out through the skin. Instead of amputating, Lister dressed the wound with carbolic acid and splinted it, and six weeks later the boy walked out on both legs.

Ignaz Semmelweis had cut deaths in a Vienna maternity ward with handwashing in the 1840s and was laughed out. Lister succeeded where he had failed because he had a mechanism: Louis Pasteur had shown that rotting is caused by living microbes. If wound rot came from microbes arriving from outside, then instruments, stitches, hands and dressings all had to be treated.

The resistance was not stupid. Critics pointed out that nobody could see the organisms he blamed, and that carbolic burned patients and cracked surgeons' hands. One claim sometimes attached to the story, that carbolic fumes threw patients under chloroform into fatal spasms, is an invention: nobody raised it at the time.

Lister tested his own methods too. His most photographed device was a brass spray that hissed carbolic mist over the operating table. In 1887 he abandoned it, concluding that germs in the air mattered far less than what touched the wound.

His revolution ran on past him, from killing germs in the wound to keeping them out altogether. At Johns Hopkins, William Halsted asked the Goodyear Rubber Company to make thin rubber gloves for his scrub nurse, Caroline Hampton, whose skin had been wrecked by the disinfectant; infections fell when the whole team wore them. And in 1879 a St Louis chemist, Joseph Lawrence, and the pharmacist Jordan Wheat Lambert named a new antiseptic Listerine in his honour. It was first marketed for surgery and for scrubbing floors, and became a mouthwash only in the 1920s.

lorenzs-rounding-error.context_blurb:
In 1961 Edward Lorenz, a weather scientist at MIT, found that a tiny difference in starting numbers could change a whole forecast. His discovery, chaos, explains why no one can forecast the weather for a particular day more than about two weeks ahead.

Lorenz wanted to rerun part of a simulation on his room-sized LGP-30 computer, so he typed in numbers from an old printout. The new run drifted until nothing matched, and he first suspected a weak vacuum tube in the machine. The computer was fine. It held six decimal places but printed only three, so he had typed 0.506 where the machine held 0.506127, an error of roughly one part in four thousand. That rounding rewrote the weather, the discovery now called the butterfly effect.

His equations contained no random numbers at all; given exactly the same start, they give exactly the same answer forever. That is what chaos means: not randomness, but a system that stretches tiny differences until they are the whole answer. Plotted in three dimensions, the path his three equations trace makes a famous two-lobed shape said to resemble a butterfly.

Lorenz was not the first to meet the problem. In the 1890s Henri Poincaré, working on the restricted three-body problem, wrote that small differences at the start can produce very great ones at the end, making prediction impossible, but no one could grind through enough hand calculation to watch it happen. In 1922 Lewis Fry Richardson worked out a weather forecast by hand and got an impossible pressure rise. When Peter Lynch reran the method decades later, the real problem turned out to be that his initial pressure readings were too rough; smoothed, they gave nearly the right answer.

Because tiny errors grow, modern forecasters run the same model many times from slightly different starting conditions. A forecast of 40 per cent chance of rain means that 40 per cent of those computer runs produced rain at your location.
