The sting at the end is that the same year he mailed the cheque, 1990, Ehrlich received a MacArthur Fellowship and the Crafoord Prize from the Royal Swedish Academy. Prestige and accuracy are awarded separately.

the-electron-sea-why-metal-bends-where-s.context_blurb: Bend a paperclip back and forth and it gets warm, stiffens, then snaps; drop a lump of rock salt or a china plate and it splits into flat-faced pieces instead. Both are orderly stacks of particles — the difference between them is the glue. The picture is a MODEL; its original classical form, written by Paul Drude in 1900, is crude, fails on specific tested properties, and has been replaced by quantum band theory — and still gets every one of these ordinary facts right. A model can be wrong in its foundations and still be the right picture to think with.

the-ether-dome-16-october-1846.context_blurb: On 16 October 1846, in a Boston operating theatre packed with sceptical surgeons, a dentist named William Morton held a glass inhaler to the face of a young man with a tumour on his neck while surgeon John Collins Warren made the cut. The patient did not scream, thrash, or need holding down — and the world in which speed had been a surgeon's chief virtue and amputations were timed in seconds ended that morning. Humphry Davy had written in 1800, in print, that nitrous oxide might be used during surgical operations; instead it, and ether, became fairground entertainments and student party games for most of a human lifetime while surgeons kept cutting into screaming patients. Horace Wells, Morton's former partner, had tried a public demonstration in the same hospital in January 1845 and was jeered out of the room when the dose fell short. Morton tried to own the discovery through a trade name, and the attempt collapsed quickly because the drug behind it was easy to identify. Crawford Long of Georgia had actually done it first, in 1842, and simply did not publish; the PUBLIC demonstration, not the first use, is what changed the world. The grim sequel is that painless surgery arrived before germ theory, and infection deaths rose until Lister caught up.

the-file-drawer.context_blurb: In 1979 the Harvard psychologist Robert Rosenthal gave a specific thing that eats the evidence its own name: the studies that found nothing, were never written up, and sit forgotten. The consequence is structural, not moral — a journal shelf is not a record of what was tested, only of what worked, and no reader can see the difference. A 2008 New England Journal of Medicine paper by Erick Turner and colleagues did something a little bit radical: they went to the FDA's advance registry of a particular class of drug trials covering more than twelve thousand patients, where every trial had been registered before anyone saw its results, and compared what the registry said about outcomes to what the published literature said.

the-filter-that-caught-nothing-what-a-vi.context_blurb: In 1892 the Russian botanist Dmitri Ivanovsky pressed sap from mosaic-diseased tobacco plants through an unglazed porcelain filter so fine that no known bacterium could pass through, and found that the filtered juice still carried disease. Ivanovsky himself assumed something ordinary — one of two conventional categories — had slipped the pores. It was the Dutchman Martinus Beijerinck who did the next experiments in 1898 and gave the mystery its new category, calling the agent 'contagium vivum fluidum,' a living contagious fluid. The conceptual leap, not the filtration, was the discovery, and the credit for it belongs to Beijerinck rather than Ivanovsky. In 1935 Wendell Stanley took the strange thing one further and purified tobacco mosaic virus into needle-like crystals, a bottle of dry crystals that could sit on a shelf like table salt. A virus has no ribosomes and runs no metabolism of its own; it is instructions wrapped in a protein coat, and it does nothing at all until it gets inside a cell and borrows its machinery. A late addendum from a 1992 Bradford cooling tower is a good lesson in how categories get rewritten: the thing was misfiled for over a decade because it was too big to fit the box.

the-forgotten-organ-counting-the-hidden-.context_blurb: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a Delft cloth merchant who ground his own lenses, was the first human being to see the hidden half of life, and he found it in his own mouth: he scraped the film off his teeth, put it under a single-lens instrument of his own making, and watched living things swimming about. He wrote to the Royal Society in the 1670s and 1680s about his observations in extraordinary numbers. A famous ratio that was repeated in textbooks and lectures for about forty years about how much of 'you' is actually bacterial traces to a single back-of-the-envelope estimate in a 1972 paper that nobody rechecked. A careful 2016 arithmetic by Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo actually did the organ-by-organ count and said the previous ratio should be retired. A particular community does jobs no human cell does, from fermenting fibre to training immune tissue, and the causal test is the germ-free mouse, raised in a sterile isolator, which grows up wrong in specific ways and is largely corrected by giving it a defined community of microbes. The gut-brain claim is an open question whose mouse evidence is strong and whose human extrapolation is not.

the-francis-field-trial-what-a-good-test.context_blurb: In 1954 almost two million American schoolchildren rolled up their sleeves as 'Polio Pioneers,' and the ones who were not getting vaccine did not get nothing — they got an injection designed so that no child, parent or doctor knew which group each child was in. Thomas Francis Jr., who had been Jonas Salk's own mentor at Michigan, agreed to evaluate the vaccine only on his terms, which required randomization, double-blinding, and a particular comparison condition that Salk sincerely objected to on ethical grounds. Francis did not get his design everywhere; some health districts refused and ran a looser alternative, and that arm turned out to be the weaker evidence because the families who volunteered differed from the ones who did not. On 12 April 1955, Francis read the result at Ann Arbor's Rackham Auditorium — ten years to the day after Franklin Roosevelt died — and deliberately reported it broken out by poliovirus type rather than as a single rounded headline. That evening Edward R. Murrow asked Salk about ownership of the discovery on See It Now.

the-full-shell-and-the-evening-xenon-bro.context_blurb: A whole column of the periodic table was taught for sixty years to combine with nothing at all. Balloons, signs and sealed light bulbs lived off their refusal to react, and the reason is a particular detail of their electron count: nothing to give away and no room to take. That picture is reinforced by a measurable number — the energy it takes to pull off one of their outer electrons — and by the opposite behaviour of their neighbours one row down and one column over. The reversal is a specific evening in late March 1962 at the University of British Columbia, working alone. A chemist named Neil Bartlett noticed that one colourless element's electron-removing energy sat almost exactly on the same number as a diatomic gas he had just shown his red platinum hexafluoride could grab an electron from. He broke the seal between the red gas and the colourless one and an orange-yellow solid precipitated immediately. Within months Rudolf Hoppe and others had made simple fluorides of that same element, and textbooks that had called the group 'inert' were rewritten to say 'noble.' The sharpest twist is that the century's most famous chemist had predicted compounds of this exact kind in 1933 and had written in 1961 that the same element was completely unreactive — the same man on both sides of the question. Bartlett's own product turned out not to be the clean compound he first wrote down, and the rule still holds where it should. A rule with exceptions is still a rule, and the exceptions are where the chemistry is.

the-furnace-we-can-never-open.context_blurb: How did we learn what is happening inside a star without ever going in? Lord Kelvin, the greatest physicist of his age, calculated the Sun's possible age by assuming it shone from a specific gravitational process and got at most a few tens of millions of years — then told geologists and Darwin their slow Earth was impossible. He was wrong because a power source existed that nobody had yet imagined. Arthur Eddington's 1920 proposal, built on a precise mass measurement by Francis Aston, pushed the right picture into print; critics who said the Sun's interior was not hot enough got a famously brief reply. Hans Bethe worked out the actual reaction chains in 1938–39. Fred Hoyle's reasoning around carbon production is one of the strangest successful predictions in astrophysics: a particular intermediate step is so unstable that carbon seemed almost impossible to build, and Hoyle argued that since we are made of carbon, the nuclear physics had to permit it — a prediction tested and confirmed by Fowler's Caltech lab within months. The B2FH paper of 1957 mapped where every element comes from.

the-great-barrington-takedown.context_blurb: In October 2020 three well-known epidemiologists — Martin Kulldorff of Harvard, Sunetra Gupta of Oxford and Jay Bhattacharya of Stanford — signed a one-page open letter at Great Barrington, Massachusetts, proposing a strategy for shielding the elderly and sick hard while letting lower-risk people resume ordinary life. Its factual basis was the age gradient the pandemic had revealed by that autumn, in which the measured infection fatality rate ran from near zero in children to much higher in the oldest patients, a spread wide enough that uniform policies spent protection where risk was not. The then-Director of the NIH wrote privately to Anthony Fauci and Eric Green describing the authors as 'three fringe epidemiologists' and calling for a 'quick and devastating published take down' of the declaration's premises; the emails surfaced later under FOIA. The response was a smear operation rather than a scientific one, AND the legitimate scientific rebuttal that followed (the John Snow Memorandum of 14 October 2020) was a real argument. The declaration has NOT been vindicated as a whole, but one of its lead authors now holds the post the email writer once held. No sneering and no cartoons of Fauci or Collins.

the-great-dying.context_blurb: About 252 million years ago, Earth came as close to a full reset as anything in the fossil record — a mass extinction that wiped out the great majority of marine species and most land vertebrates, and that finished a particular, instantly recognisable arthropod lineage that had been crawling through the seas for something like 270 million years and never returned. The wonder is that we can read a 252-million-year-old crime scene at all. A widely repeated number for how much of marine life was lost came from an older genus-level extrapolation and has been revised downward; the current figure is still by far the worst in the record. The murder weapon is written into one particular Siberian volcanic province that erupted across exactly this interval, and the lethal part was not the lava but the gas, which cooked carbon out of the rocks it rose through. Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen; a strange absence in the global rock record — no coal forms anywhere in the world for millions of years — testifies to what the peat-forming forests had become. High-precision uranium-lead dates on zircons from volcanic ash beds squeeze the main extinction pulse to a geologically instant duration a human can picture. The honest open question at the top is the ranking of the kill mechanisms, which real researchers still argue. This is deep-time history, not modern climate policy.

the-green-flash-at-sunset.context_blurb: This is a real phenomenon written off for a long time as an illusion of the observer. In the last second or two before the Sun's upper edge disappears into a clean sea horizon, the top sliver can flare vivid green. The atmosphere acts as a weak prism: it bends short wavelengths slightly more than long ones, so the Sun's blue-green image sets a fraction of a second later than its red image, and for an instant only the greenish edge remains. For a long time the serious competing hypothesis was that there was no 'out there' at all — a plausible explanation drawing on well-known behaviour of the human eye after staring at a bright coloured patch. The French astronomer Lucien Rudaux published one in 1925, and instruments do not have retinal fatigue. The honest limit is that even though the refractive effect always happens, the flash is rare because the pure effect is far too thin to see, and it needs a particular atmospheric condition to magnify the separation. That is why a stable sea horizon or a high desert horizon gives the best odds, and why the blue bent even further gets scattered away before it reaches you (which is also why 'blue flashes' are much rarer).

the-greening-nobody-forecast.context_blurb: Since the early 1980s, two satellite instruments — NOAA's AVHRR and NASA's MODIS — have measured how much leaf each patch of ground carries. A 2016 study in Nature Climate Change led by Zaichun Zhu reported that a substantial fraction of Earth's vegetated land had greened significantly over roughly 35 years. The satellites were not looking for good news; they were counting leaves. In richer air a leaf can take in the same raw material while giving up less water, which is why the greening shows up most strongly at dry margins. The direct test — Free-Air CO2 Enrichment experiments that ring real forest and cropland and fumigate them for years — tends to produce smaller effects than sealed-greenhouse studies promised, and is limited where soil nitrogen or water runs short. The other half of the honest ledger: a sizeable chunk of the new green reflects land management, not the chemistry; and crops grown under elevated CO2 have been measured with lower nutrient density. Greening is a real negative feedback already counted in carbon budgets, not a cancellation of warming.

the-hard-problem-why-anything-feels-like.context_blurb: Every day, in ordinary operating theatres, somebody switches a person's inner experience off and then back on, and nobody can say what physical thing is being switched. David Chalmers named the split at a 1994 Tucson conference and published it in 1995 — the EASY problems are hard engineering but ordinary science, and the HARD problem is why performing any of those functions is accompanied by experience at all. Thomas Nagel's 1974 essay about an animal that uses echolocation set the shape: you can know every detail of how a sense works and still not know what it is LIKE from the inside, and that residue is what the science has to explain. Two rival theories — one associated with Giulio Tononi, one with Stanislas Dehaene and Bernard Baars — make different and testable brain predictions, and the COGITATE adversarial collaboration had both camps pre-register what their theory predicted before the scanning started. The result, published in Nature on 30 April 2025, vindicated neither cleanly.

the-herrick-twins-kidney-23-december-195.context_blurb: On 23 December 1954 in a Boston hospital, Ronald Herrick gave a kidney to his dying identical twin brother Richard — the first organ transplant that lasted. Every earlier attempt had ended within days when the recipient's body attacked another person's tissue, and the surgeon Joseph Murray had already watched the same thing on a wartime burn ward, where grafted skin from a donor would take hold, look healthy for a while and then be destroyed. The dinner-table surprise is the test the team ran BEFORE the operation to prove the immunology was in their favour: they exchanged small patches of skin between the two brothers and watched the result, so they knew they were betting on a known equation and not on hope. The moral problem the surgery raised was new: to save one brother they had to cut a healthy organ out of a healthy man who did not need surgery at all, and the family meetings around that decision — the team refused to advise for or against — are the ethical heart of the story. Richard Herrick lived eight more years, married and had two children. Making the operation work for people who are NOT twins took another decade through immunosuppressive drugs (azathioprine, developed with Roy Calne and George Hitchings), and the standing trade is that a transplant buys a working organ at the price of a lifetime of higher infection and cancer risk.

the-higgs-a-forty-eight-year-wait-for-on.context_blurb: In 1964 Peter Higgs wrote a short paper that the journal Physics Letters, edited at CERN, turned down as of no obvious relevance. He revised it, adding one extra consequence pointing to something the paper's physics implied that nobody had yet seen, and sent it to Physical Review Letters, which printed it. That added material is why the particle carries his name rather than somebody else's — but it is not the whole credit story. Three groups got there independently within months of each other in 1964: a Belgian pair, Higgs in Edinburgh, and a British trio in London, which is why the theory is properly the Brout-Englert-Higgs mechanism and never 'Higgs predicted it' alone. The quick popular story — 'the Higgs is what makes things heavy' — is wrong by about two orders of magnitude for ordinary matter: most of the proton's mass is binding energy among its quarks and gluons, not the Higgs field. On 4 July 2012 CERN announced the particle's discovery, with two deliberately independent collaborations finding the same bump near 125 GeV. Peter Higgs, aged 83, was in the seminar room. The question the discovery OPENED — the hierarchy problem, why the measured mass sits where it does — remains open. Grade-10 ceiling: no gauge theory and no symmetry-breaking jargon.

the-hiss-the-pigeons-could-not-explain.context_blurb: In 1964 at Bell Labs in Holmdel, New Jersey, Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson pointed a twenty-foot horn antenna at empty sky and heard a faint hiss from every direction, day and night, every season. The wonder is a methodical one: a step-by-step elimination of every candidate they could think of, from New York City's radio racket and military radar to fallout from a 1962 high-altitude nuclear test, to the glow of the Milky Way, to the metal joints of the antenna itself. Even a pair of nesting pigeons was dealt with and did not account for the signal. What remained was an excess antenna temperature at a specific microwave frequency that refused to go away. Forty miles away at Princeton, Robert Dicke's group was building an antenna to hunt for exactly this relic heat, and a telephone call connected the two labs. The prediction had been in the published literature since 1948, and there was even an unrecognised 1941 clue from certain interstellar molecules that were gently excited as if bathed in something a few degrees above absolute zero. Penzias and Wilson were not looking for the Big Bang; they were calibrating an antenna.

the-hoax-papers-sokal-1996-and-the-griev.context_blurb: In 1996 the NYU physicist Alan Sokal published an article in the cultural-studies journal Social Text whose argument was deliberately absurd, and three weeks later announced in Lingua Franca that he had written it as a test. Sokal's own stated claim was narrower than the headlines it produced. Twenty years later a group of three authors — Peter Boghossian, James Lindsay and Helen Pluckrose — ran a much more ambitious sequel, submitting twenty fabricated papers to genuinely peer-reviewed journals.

the-hockey-stick-fight.context_blurb: In 1998 and 1999 Michael Mann, Raymond Bradley and Malcolm Hughes published Northern Hemisphere temperature reconstructions combining tree rings, corals, ice cores and documentary records; the IPCC's 2001 Third Assessment Report put the resulting graph in its Summary for Policymakers and used it as a poster-sized backdrop at the televised launch, which turned a research figure into an emblem. Two outsiders to climate science — one from industry, one an economist — could not reproduce the published result from the published description, asked for data and code, and ran their own audits whose statistical findings the 2006 US National Research Council panel accepted on specific technical points while concluding that the broad recent-warmth picture survived when other methods were used. The NRC graded its own confidence in tiers: high for the last four centuries, less back to AD 900, very little before. A published result should arrive with data and code a stranger can rerun. Replication as a right, not a favour.

the-human-genome-project-and-the-20-000-.context_blurb: The Human Genome Project officially began on 1 October 1990 with a fifteen-year plan and a three-billion-dollar budget, with its working draft declared essentially complete on 14 April 2003 — a date deliberately timed to a famous fiftieth anniversary. There was a race alongside the public consortium, with Craig Venter's Celera Genomics claiming it could do the job privately with a smash-and-reassemble strategy against the public side's slower map-first method. The public consortium bound itself to release every finished stretch into a public database within twenty-four hours (the Bermuda Principles agreed in 1996), and the political truce arrived on 26 June 2000 with Bill Clinton announcing a joint 'working draft' at the White House with Tony Blair on a satellite link. Before the project the working guess ran into six figures — one for roughly each protein people thought the body needed — and a betting pool run by Ewan Birney had taken more than 460 wagers. The settled answer is dramatically lower, counted as protein-coding genes to avoid the sloppy comparison that drifts across RNA genes, and roughly matches small worms and rice; complexity is not gene count. The 'finished' 2003 genome was not finished; the gaps were only closed in 2022 by the Telomere-to-Telomere consortium's ultra-long-read sequencing. Promised cures have arrived unevenly.

the-immortal-chicken-heart-that-wasnt.context_blurb: For many years at the Rockefeller Institute, a scrap of chicken heart tissue was fed daily and its birthdays were reported in the newspapers; Alexis Carrel's famously 'immortal' culture was celebrated as proof that cells, given enough good food, never age at all. Nobody has ever reproduced it. In 1961 Leonard Hayflick and Paul Moorhead found the opposite result for ordinary human cells: they divide a limited number of times and then stop dividing but stay alive, a stage the field now calls senescence. The field's first reaction was that they must have been sloppy. Hayflick and Moorhead mixed cells from one source that had done many doublings with cells from another source that had done fewer, in one flask sharing everything, and watched which cells survived. Whatever was counting had to be inside each cell, not in the shared medium. The most likely explanation for Carrel's immortal culture is embarrassingly ordinary and does not require accusing him of fraud. The mechanism was predicted on paper by Alexei Olovnikov in 1971 from the arithmetic of DNA replication, and the enzyme that undoes the counter was found by Carol Greider and Elizabeth Blackburn in 1984 (Nobel 2009). The field name 'Hayflick limit' came along later from Macfarlane Burnet in 1974.

the-immunity-that-was-already-there.context_blurb: Natural immunity is what immunology textbooks say it is: the trained response left behind by surviving an infection, the same machinery a vaccine is designed to imitate. Protection against SEVERE disease stayed high at 40 weeks across variants, including Omicron BA.1; protection against catching the virus AGAIN faded far faster. Alongside the Lancet number sits an older institutional document — the CDC's own MMWR of 28 January 2022 (Leon and colleagues) — on California and New York data from May through November 2021, which reported during one specific pandemic period that unvaccinated people with documented prior infection had lower case rates than vaccinated people without it. Through 2021 and into 2022, mandates in most jurisdictions counted a documented prior infection as worth nothing.

the-knee-jerk-a-decision-your-brain-neve.context_blurb: The experiment takes only a chair with a free-swinging edge, a loose leg, and a small reflex hammer or the side of a hand. Tap the tendon just below your kneecap and your leg kicks before you could have decided anything about it. The whole loop takes about eighteen thousandths of a second, because the signal never travels up to your brain at all. It turns around in your spinal cord. The hammer is not hitting a nerve, and the tendon is not a trigger. The real trigger is something inside the muscle that responds to a sudden stretch, and the standard answer the spinal cord sends back is to contract. The circuit exists so that your knees do not buckle every time your weight shifts.

the-law-of-small-numbers.context_blurb: Flip a coin ten times and you will fairly often get eight heads. Flip the same coin a thousand times and you will almost never get eight hundred. Small samples do not merely carry more error than large ones. They manufacture extreme results, at both ends. In 1971 the Israeli psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman handed a questionnaire to professional psychologists at their own conference and found experienced researchers trusting small samples the way a gambler trusts a streak. The paper they wrote has a diagnosis in its title. A famous US map of county kidney-cancer rates shows the counties with the lowest rates in the same places as the counties with the highest rates, because rural counties have very few people in them and swing further at both ends. A twenty-person study is a ten-coin-flip study, and only lucky swings get published.

the-laws-that-outlived-the-science.context_blurb: The first compulsory sterilization law in human history was not passed in Germany. It was passed in the American state of Indiana in April 1907, and it allowed the superintendents of state prisons and asylums to sterilize inmates judged insane, idiotic, imbecilic, epileptic, or criminal. By the 1930s roughly thirty US states had such laws, and tens of thousands of Americans had been sterilized under them, about two thirds of them women. The most important fact is that these programs did not shrink after the Second World War, when the Nazi record became public. The busiest American state program continued into the late 1970s. One state board kept reviewing cases on IQ scores and social histories decades after the hereditary theory behind them had collapsed, and did more of its work after the war than before. The programs were eventually stopped on legal and civil-rights grounds, not scientific ones.

the-lockdown-meta-analysis-that-correcte.context_blurb: The question is a narrow and checkable one. Taken as a whole, did mandated spring-2020 lockdowns reduce COVID-19 deaths, and if so by how much? Three economists, led by Jonas Herby with Lars Jonung and Steve Hanke, worked through a huge pile of candidate studies, kept only the ones that used a specific apples-to-apples comparison method, and worked out an average effect. Their first widely circulated paper on this question gave a far smaller headline number. Better data and a tighter method moved their own answer substantially, and they published the revision under their own names.

the-loudest-sound-ever-recorded.context_blurb: On a Monday morning in late August 1883, the volcanic island of Krakatoa in the strait between Java and Sumatra exploded. The sound of it carried across an enormous fraction of the earth's surface. The chief of police on an island thousands of miles away heard it as heavy guns firing somewhere to the east and wrote it in his logbook. On a British ship closer in, the captain recorded that the eardrums of more than half his crew had been shattered. The reason we can quote a specific loudness in modern units for an event that predates the microphone is that a sensitive barometer at a gas works about a hundred miles away recorded a pressure spike that can be converted into a decibel figure for its distance. Beyond a certain amplitude a pressure wave in ordinary sea-level air stops being a sound wave at all and becomes a blast wave.

the-machinery-the-trusted-news-initiativ.context_blurb: There are two specific institutions here, one private and still in operation, and one federal and stopped within four months of being announced. The private one was founded in 2019 by the BBC and seats the leading news organisations of several countries together with the major technology platforms that distribute news. It extended its remit during the pandemic and again before an American election. In 2022 it was sued, not under free-speech law but under American antitrust law, by a party arguing that competitors had agreed among themselves to suppress rival reporting. The federal one was announced by the US Department of Homeland Security to a congressional subcommittee in the spring of 2022, provoked an immediate public reaction, and was formally terminated within four months on the recommendation of the department's own advisory council.

the-magic-bullet-hunt-from-a-dye-that-st.context_blurb: In the early twentieth century a German physician and chemist named Paul Ehrlich noticed something ordinary. Some laboratory dyes stain one kind of cell and leave its neighbour completely untouched. If a dye could single out one cell on a glass slide, he reasoned, a chemical might in principle single out one kind of invader inside a human body. He gave the dream a name, meaning a magic bullet, and he gave the search for it a word that is still used, meaning the chemical treatment of disease. Ehrlich's lab synthesised and tested hundreds of arsenic compounds against the organism that causes syphilis in infected rabbits, one after another, until one worked. A generation later, a different German laboratory ran the same brute-force screening on industrial dyes against a specific bacterial infection in mice. The breakthrough came with a twist. The dye they picked did nothing at all in a test tube. The drug the body produced from it was the one that worked, and nobody would have found it by screening in glassware alone.

the-measurement-problem-the-part-no-one-.context_blurb: The question is a strange one. Quantum mechanics is the most carefully tested theory in the history of science. It predicts the results of ordinary measurements with astonishing precision, and it has done so for a century. But the theory in its ordinary mathematical form does not say what actually happens when a particle meets a measuring device. It describes a smooth evolution of possibilities right up until the moment of measurement, and then one specific outcome is simply there. The experiments that pinned the ghostly correlations of entangled particles to the wall closed the question of whether some hidden local variable was quietly deciding things in advance. They did not say which of the several surviving pictures of what measurement actually is turns out to be right. Several very different interpretations reproduce every laboratory result anyone has ever obtained, and no experiment has yet separated them. Some objective-collapse theories make specific predictions that are already being narrowed by ongoing experiments. The honest state of the question is a live argument, not a resolved one.

the-mesmer-commission-of-1784.context_blurb: In the 1780s in Paris, a Viennese physician named Franz Mesmer ran one of the most fashionable medical practices in Europe. He claimed there was an invisible universal fluid called animal magnetism that flowed between all bodies and dammed up in the sick. His patients gripped iron rods sticking out of a tub of what he said was magnetized water, while music played, until they fell into convulsive crises that were counted as the cure working. Louis XVI appointed a royal commission to investigate the claim. The commission included several of the most famous names in Enlightenment science. Its most senior member hosted some of the trials in his garden at Passy. The experiment they ran there, with a blindfolded boy and four trees, is the first clearly blinded medical experiment in recorded history. The commission concluded that the effects on patients were real but produced by their own expectations rather than by any invisible fluid. That conclusion is generally credited as the first scientific description of what we now call the placebo effect.

the-metal-that-melts-in-your-hand.context_blurb: There is a specific chemical element you can buy today as a small silvery ingot and watch melt in your open hand within a minute. Its melting point is below human body temperature. On a hot day it is below room temperature. The same metal boils above two thousand degrees Celsius, which gives it one of the widest liquid ranges of any element and makes it useful in thermometers for furnaces where mercury would long since have boiled away. In 1871 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev left a deliberate gap in his new table of the elements and described in detail the properties of a missing element that should fit there, including its density, its atomic weight, and the fact that it should have a low melting point. In 1875 a French chemist found an element with the predicted properties in a specific zinc ore from the Pyrenees. Shortly after the discovery, Mendeleev wrote to the Frenchman to tell him his sample must be impure. He was right.

the-missing-mass-zwicky-rubin-and-an-hon.context_blurb: In the early 1930s, a Swiss-American astronomer named Fritz Zwicky measured how fast individual galaxies were flying around inside a specific cluster of galaxies, applied an ordinary piece of physics called the virial theorem, and found that the cluster needed far more mass than its light could account for just to avoid flying apart. He coined a name for the missing stuff and his colleagues largely left it alone for about forty years. Around 1970 the American astronomer Vera Rubin and her colleague Kent Ford, using a new kind of image-tube spectrograph, measured how fast stars and gas clouds orbit at different distances out from the centres of several spiral galaxies and found that outer stars were moving just as fast as inner ones. In the solar system the opposite is true, because gravity weakens with distance.

the-molecule-nobody-believed-in-nuclein-.context_blurb: In the winter of 1869, in a converted kitchen laboratory in a castle in southern Germany, a young Swiss physician named Friedrich Miescher collected pus-soaked surgical bandages from the town hospital, washed the white blood cells off them, dissolved away the proteins with an enzyme, and precipitated out a strange new substance from the cell nuclei. He called it nuclein. His supervisor was so skeptical of the finding that he insisted on his own students repeating the whole procedure before letting Miescher publish, which took almost two years. For roughly the next seventy years, nearly every serious biologist assumed that genes could not possibly be made of this stuff. Nuclein had only four kinds of building block, and it looked far too monotonous to spell out an organism. Proteins, with twenty amino acids, looked like the only alphabet rich enough to do the job.

the-molecules-that-wouldnt-stop-stauding.context_blurb: In the 1920s the German chemist Hermann Staudinger argued that natural substances like rubber, cellulose, and starch are not loose clumps of small molecules held together by weak physical forces, as the reigning view assumed, but single molecules thousands of units long, joined by ordinary covalent bonds. A Nobel laureate wrote to him urging him to drop the idea, saying such a thing could not exist, and comparing it to an impossible tower. Staudinger answered the objection by chemistry rather than by argument. He modified rubber at the molecular level and showed that the product was still a giant molecule, which it could not have been if rubber were a loose aggregation of small ones. A kid can run a version of the experiment on a plastic grocery bag.

the-mpemba-effect-a-schoolboys-question-.context_blurb: In the early 1960s, in a cookery class at a secondary school in Tanzania, a boy named Erasto Mpemba put his ice-cream mix into the freezer while it was still hot, because the freezer was crowded and he wanted a space, and his mix froze before his classmates' cooled mix did. His teacher told him he had confused himself. When a visiting physicist named Denis Osborne came to the school, Mpemba asked him the question anyway. Osborne, openly skeptical, went back to his laboratory and tested the claim rather than dismissing it. He published the result jointly with the schoolboy. Ancient and early-modern writers from Aristotle onward had reported something similar and been forgotten. Careful experiments have failed to find a reproducible effect at all, while other groups continue to report one.

the-muons-that-should-never-have-reached.context_blurb: A muon is a short-lived particle that forms about fifteen kilometres up when a cosmic ray smashes into the top of the earth's atmosphere. Its average lifetime in its own rest frame is about two millionths of a second. Even at nearly the speed of light that would only let it travel a few hundred metres before decaying. Yet muons from the upper atmosphere arrive at the ground in huge numbers. Roughly one is passing through your hand every minute as you read. In 1963 two American physicists climbed Mount Washington in New Hampshire with a muon counter and spent hours counting arrivals at that altitude, then drove the detector down to Cambridge, Massachusetts, and spent hours counting arrivals at sea level. The ratio of the two counts is a specific, measurable prediction of Einstein's special relativity. The particle itself does not experience its own lifetime running slow. From the muon's point of view the fifteen kilometres of atmosphere are squashed to a few hundred metres.

the-nuremberg-code-ten-rules-written-in-.context_blurb: The founding document of modern medical research ethics was not written by a medical society. It was written by three American judges at the end of a criminal trial of German physicians in the summer of 1947 and handed down as part of a verdict. Its first line is the one most people have heard. One of its provisions gives the research subject a power nobody had thought to write down before, that the subject may end the experiment at any moment, for reasons of the subject's own, and nobody may argue. Another contains a strange, deliberate hole that the judges carved for the scientist willing to run the risk on his own body. The Code was not law anywhere. It was treated widely in the United States as a rule for barbarians rather than a rule for ordinary doctors, and some of the studies it should have stopped kept running for decades after it was written. The Code acquired real force only when later documents translated it into things that had teeth.

the-patent-clerks-miracle-year.context_blurb: In 1905 a twenty-six-year-old examining electrical patent applications at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern sent to the leading German physics journal four papers in six months, any one of which would have made a career. His job title was technical expert, third class. He did not yet hold a doctorate. He had argued the ideas out in his evenings with two friends in an informal reading group he called the Olympia Academy. The paper everyone remembers today, on special relativity, was not the paper for which this patent clerk was eventually given the Nobel Prize, and the Nobel citation does not actually mention relativity at all. Most people have met his famous equation in the wrong form. The 1905 paper does not contain the modern three-letter version. He wrote the result as a question and he suggested a specific experimental test using salts of a particular radioactive element the Curies had recently discovered.

the-peppered-moth-re-tested.context_blurb: In the middle of the nineteenth century, around the city of Manchester in industrial Britain, dark-coloured individuals of a particular common moth began appearing. Within a few decades they made up almost all the moths caught in the region. The cause looked unmysterious. Industrial coal soot had blackened the bark of local trees and killed the pale lichens that the original speckled form of the moth matched. Birds eating the moths off those darkened trees had a specific preference. In the 1950s the English biologist Bernard Kettlewell tested this bird-predation explanation head-on, with mark-release-and-recapture experiments in a polluted wood and in a clean one, and the survival advantage flipped depending on which wood he was standing in. The result became the textbook case of natural selection in action, and in the 2000s it came under heavy attack. The answer was not an argument. A different biologist spent seven years re-running the experiment properly on natural resting positions, dying before he could publish, with his colleagues finishing the paper on his behalf.

the-periodic-table-in-your-pocket.context_blurb: A modern smartphone contains something close to two thirds of the stable elements on the periodic table, in a slab you can hold in one hand. The touchscreen works because of a specific chemistry in a particular transparent conductor. The speakers and the vibration motor use permanent magnets built around rare-earth metals, with others added so they do not lose their strength when the phone heats up. The red and green colours on the screen come from phosphors that use particular rare earths because ordinary materials cannot give pure enough reds and greens. The reason the whole device fits inside a thin case at all is a specific metal whose oxide layer is such a good insulator that one of the smallest components stores far more charge per unit of volume than any alternative. The glass is a specific aluminosilicate that has been soaked in a molten salt so that large ions swap into sites left by smaller ones and jam the surface into permanent compression.

the-phases-of-venus.context_blurb: The planet Venus, viewed through a telescope, runs through the same shape-cycle that the Moon does, from thin crescent through half and gibbous to nearly full, and back again, over a specific period. Galileo first saw and reported this early in 1611, less than a year after he had seen the four largest moons of Jupiter. He wrote to a leading Jesuit mathematician about it, telling him that Venus had already reached a half-moon shape and predicting that it would go to crescent next. The prediction was kept, and the result mattered for a very specific reason. The ancient earth-centred arrangement by Ptolemy puts Venus on a particular small circle whose geometry keeps the planet always between the earth and the sun. If Ptolemy had been right, Venus's lit face could never fully turn toward us. A gibbous Venus is fatal to that arrangement. The phases do not prove that the earth moves. They refute Ptolemy, and they leave an alternative old arrangement standing.

the-piccards-a-balloon-turned-upside-dow.context_blurb: In 1931 a Swiss physicist named Auguste Piccard climbed to roughly sixteen kilometres above a Bavarian town inside a pressurized aluminium sphere hanging under a hydrogen balloon, becoming the first human beings to reach the stratosphere. The pressurised cabin he invented for that trip is the ancestor of every airliner cabin anyone has ever sat in. He then had a specific second idea. A balloon is a heavy cabin hung under a light fluid rising through a heavier one. Turn the whole arrangement upside down and you get a heavy steel cabin hung under a tank of a light liquid sinking through seawater. He called the result a bathyscaphe. Thirty years later Auguste's son Jacques and an American naval officer rode a bathyscaphe to the floor of the deepest trench in the ocean.

the-placebo-and-why-blinding-exists.context_blurb: The strength of a fake treatment scales with how impressive the ritual around it looks. Two dummy pills work better than one. An injection of nothing works better than a capsule of nothing. The honest consequence is that the question in a medical trial is not whether the people on the real treatment got better. The question is whether they got better than the people on the fake. The placebo mostly moves the patient's reported pain and nausea. It barely moves measurable disease. Expectation leaks into the measurement exactly as it did in the famous horse experiment.

the-playbook-they-had-already-written-wh.context_blurb: In September 2019, several months before anyone had heard of COVID-19, the World Health Organization published its standing pandemic-influenza guidance. The document is a public PDF. A parent can download it today and open it beside a child. Its summary table carries a column headed in specific words meaning that the measures listed under it are not recommended in any circumstances. The 2019 guidance was for influenza, which is not the same thing as the virus that caused COVID-19. School measures were in a different column of the same table than quarantine. The quality of evidence behind nearly every line was rated as very low. A standing recommendation was reversed in 2020 without the reversal being argued out in the open.

the-price-tag-and-the-private-jet.context_blurb: At some point the physics of climate stops being a physics question and starts being an argument about politics, money, and persuasion. The physics does not change from year to year. The response to it does. A French government announced an increase in a fuel tax weighted toward one kind of fuel; weeks later people in high-visibility vests were in the streets, and shortly after that the increase was cancelled. In an American state, a proposed carbon tax lost at the ballot box, with part of the opposition coming from environmental and labour groups who objected not to taxing carbon but to the proposal to return the revenue to taxpayers. An analysis of chartered aviation around a well-known annual meeting in a Swiss ski resort counted more than a thousand private-jet flights during the event week. A survey of ten thousand young people found that close to sixty percent reported being very or extremely worried about climate change.

the-prophecys-price-sterilisation-quotas.context_blurb: In the late 1960s, a popular book by a well-known American biologist forecast mass famines in the near future and recommended specific coercive policies, including the compulsory sterilization of men with three or more children in India, with the United States supplying helicopters and surgical instruments. In India during the 1976 Emergency, roughly eight million sterilisations were performed in one year under quotas handed down to officials, teachers, and clerks. The policy ended with an election, in which the government that pushed the quotas lost power. In China, a control engineer trained on missile-guidance mathematics ran the country's population through control-theory equations and his group concluded that a specific national population target justified universal one-child restrictions. The one-child policy ran for more than three decades. Scholars dispute how much the mathematics mattered to the Party's decision. The record carries the moral weight. No planner was ever graded the way the author of the book was.

the-quantum-tech-already-in-your-pocket.context_blurb: In 2001 a famous Scientific American article estimated that something like thirty percent of the United States economy rested on inventions that quantum mechanics made possible, and identified two main families carrying most of the load. The invention of a certain kind of switch in 1947 at Bell Labs, demonstrated by its inventors to management by using it to amplify an audio signal they could all hear, led to the semiconductor age. The specific reason it works is a purely quantum result about allowed and forbidden energy bands in a crystal that has no classical version. The same band physics explains why a light-emitting diode of a particular colour exists at all, and why the blue version of it took thirty years longer than the red one and finally produced a Nobel Prize in the 2010s.

the-radium-craze.context_blurb: For roughly three decades after its discovery in 1898, the element radium was sold to the public as a health product. Factory workers painted the glowing numbers on watch dials with a radium-and-zinc-sulfide paint, pointing their brushes with their lips between strokes. Drinks were sold with radium dissolved in them. Face creams and toothpastes advertised their radium content. A specific wealthy Pittsburgh industrialist drank a particular radium tonic by the bottle because it made him feel wonderful. Radium sits directly below calcium in a specific column of the periodic table, so the body cannot tell them apart and files the element away permanently in bone, where it goes on emitting alpha particles for the rest of a life. The same property that makes radium lethal in a drink makes it a usable targeted therapy for specific cancers today.

the-radium-girls-and-the-element-that-fi.context_blurb: At a watch-dial factory in a town in New Jersey in the late 1910s and early 1920s, young women were trained to paint luminous numbers on watch and instrument faces with a paint that contained a tiny amount of a specific radioactive element. Their supervisors taught them in three words, pointing the brush between strokes, which meant that each dial painter swallowed a small amount of radium with every stroke. Some of them painted their fingernails and teeth with leftover paint for the glow before a night out. Several years later their jaws began to crumble. Radium sits one column over on the periodic table from calcium and the body files it away in bone just as it would file away calcium, where it carries on emitting alpha radiation for the rest of a life.

the-rainbow-you-can-build-with-a-garden-.context_blurb: The bow is always centred exactly on the shadow of your own head. Every rainbow anyone has ever seen is aimed personally at the viewer. Every drop that sends red light to your eye sits on a cone of one specific angular width around the shadow of your head, and that fixed angle is the reason every rainbow in history is the same size.

the-repairs-that-actually-work.context_blurb: The answer to the replication crisis in modern science is not less science or more cynicism. The answer is more and better checking, done in the open. The simplest of them is a piece of paper on which researchers write down their hypothesis, their sample size, and their analysis plan in advance, publish it with a timestamp, and then run the study. A stronger version lets a journal peer-review the question and the method before the study is run, and commits to publishing the result either way. One specific comparison of positive-result rates between ordinary psychology papers and these pre-committed papers is startling.

the-river-in-the-sky-nobody-would-read.context_blurb: In the 1920s and 1930s, a Japanese meteorologist named Wasaburo Oishi was tracking balloons high above a specific observatory north of Tokyo. In the winter profiles he found something nobody expected. A persistent band of extremely fast westerly wind, far above the ground, blowing many times harder than ordinary surface winds. He published his findings in a series of nineteen reports between the mid-1920s and the mid-1940s. The reports ran to over a thousand pages. He published them in Esperanto, an invented international language he had adopted in the hope of reaching foreign scientists who were not reading his Japanese papers. The result was that almost nobody outside Japan read a word of it. The same wind was rediscovered the hard way by American bomber crews flying high over Japan in 1944, who found their bombing runs unusable because the aircraft were being pushed along at speeds that no bombsight could handle.

the-same-machine-run-backwards-motor-and.context_blurb: This is one piece of physics read in two directions. The piece of physics is a specific law found by Michael Faraday in 1831, which says that a wire moved through a magnetic field has current pushed along it, and a wire that already has current flowing in it feels a sideways push when it sits in a magnetic field. In 1873 at an industrial exposition in Vienna, an assistant carelessly wired one dynamo's output into a second dynamo, and the second machine's shaft started turning. A generator running backwards is a motor, and nobody had meant to demonstrate it. Drop a small strong neodymium magnet down a copper or aluminium pipe. Copper is not magnetic, yet the magnet sinks in slow motion, because its own motion induces circulating electric currents in the pipe whose fields push back on it. Lenz's rule made visible in three seconds.

the-schedule-vaers-and-the-study-nobody-.context_blurb: The question is a narrow and honest one. How would we actually know, with the specific numerical confidence science demands elsewhere, whether the complete modern American childhood vaccination schedule, as a whole, is as safe as a direct alternative? The answer is not obvious. Individual vaccines are tested against controls before they are licensed, and most of them have genuinely good evidence of safety and effectiveness. The complete schedule, with all its doses in a specific order at specific ages, has not been tested against an unvaccinated control group in a randomised trial. The strongest piece of evidence on the other side is a very large Danish national cohort study of a specific adjuvant.

the-shipyards-flaw-detector-in-the-mater.context_blurb: The first ultrasound images of a tumour and an unborn child came off a machine built to hunt cracks in boiler plate. In 1957, in Glasgow, an obstetrician named Ian Donald borrowed an industrial metal flaw detector from a boiler-making firm and used it to scan patients. Within a few years, working with a clinical colleague and an engineer, he had turned a dockyard tool into a diagnostic method. The physics underneath it is older than that. In 1880 the brothers Jacques and Pierre Curie had found that squeezing certain crystals produces a voltage, and that feeding a voltage into those crystals makes them squeeze back. That is still exactly how every ultrasound probe both makes its pings and hears the returns. A decade of promising images turned out to be an artefact. The real method is reflection, not transmission.

the-sky-does-fall-tunguska-chelyabinsk-a.context_blurb: On the morning of 15 February 2013, a rock about the size of a double-decker bus entered the earth's atmosphere over the Russian city of Chelyabinsk at roughly nineteen kilometres per second and blew apart high in the sky with the energy of several hundred thousand tons of TNT. Nearly fifteen hundred people needed medical attention. Almost all of them were cut by flying window glass, because the flash came first in silence and people crowded to their windows to look at it, and the shock wave took about two minutes to arrive.

the-superconductor-nobody-can-explain.context_blurb: In 1911, in Leiden, a Dutch physicist named Heike Kamerlingh Onnes cooled a sample of mercury below a specific low temperature and found its electrical resistance did not merely drop to a very small value. It fell to zero. This is a hard cliff rather than a slow slope, and it is accompanied by a dramatic effect in which a magnetic field is actively expelled from the interior of the material. The mechanism that explains superconductivity in ordinary metals was worked out in 1957 by three American physicists and seemed to put a ceiling on how high the critical temperature could ever go. In 1986 two IBM researchers in Zurich found superconductivity at a far higher temperature in a specific brittle ceramic. Within a year, other groups pushed the temperature above the boiling point of liquid nitrogen, which is a cheap coolant. Forty years later nobody has an accepted explanation of why these ceramics superconduct.

the-tell-what-actually-gives-a-faked-res.context_blurb: In every one of the four specific cases here, the fraud was not caught by an authority. It was caught by someone doing something concrete to a physical thing. A Viennese biologist published spectacular evidence for the inheritance of an acquired characteristic in a particular amphibian. A Sloan-Kettering researcher presented mice supposedly carrying accepted skin grafts from unrelated donors. A British psychologist published twin-study correlations. Two Texas statisticians tried to reproduce a specific Duke University cancer analysis. The lesson is a single transferable habit: the catch is always something physical that was checked.

the-terrella-a-model-earth-on-the-bench.context_blurb: In the year 1600, the English physician William Gilbert, personal physician to Elizabeth I, carved a particular magnetic mineral into a sphere he called a little earth. He walked a tiny compass across its surface and the needle did exactly what sailors' compasses do at sea. From that, by a specific argument about scale models, he reasoned to the claim that the earth itself must be a giant magnet, and he published that argument in the first great book of modern experimental science. Three centuries later, a Norwegian physicist named Kristian Birkeland built a different little earth. He put a magnetised sphere coated in phosphorescent paint inside a vacuum chamber, fired a beam of electrons at it, and glowing rings appeared around its poles. From that he argued that the real aurora in the real polar sky must be particles coming from the Sun, funnelled down the earth's own magnetic field lines. He was ridiculed for decades on a specific point about the physics of space, and died without an answer. In 1967 a satellite flying through the auroral zone found exactly the currents he had predicted.

the-three-millimetre-shield.context_blurb: In 1913, two French physicists named Charles Fabry and Henri Buisson were not hunting for a shield. They were simply measuring the Sun's spectrum carefully. They found that the Sun's output in a specific range of ultraviolet wavelengths below about three hundred and ten nanometres was simply missing by the time it reached the ground. Something in the earth's atmosphere was eating it. The missing band matched the absorption fingerprint of exactly one known chemical.

the-tides-the-moons-grip-on-the-ocean.context_blurb: Twice a day in a specific bay on the eastern coast of North America, the sea rises and falls by as much as sixteen metres, which is roughly five storeys of water, on a published timetable. The hard puzzle in the physics is a particular one. If the Moon pulls the ocean toward itself, why is there also a high tide on the far side of the Earth at the same moment? The answer is a specific gradient argument that a kid can picture. The near water is pulled hardest, the solid Earth next, and the far water least, which leaves the far water effectively behind as a second bulge. Even Galileo got the tides wrong in his famous Dialogue, insisting they were water sloshing from the Earth's double motion and dismissing the Moon's role as astrological superstition. Newton fixed it in a specific later book.

the-transplant-that-beat-squeamishness.context_blurb: A specific common and sometimes fatal infection of the gut, caused by an organism called Clostridioides difficile, usually comes not from the arrival of the bug but from the clearing out of the gut's resident microbial community by a course of antibiotics given for something else. The commonest trigger for the infection is the treatment for a different infection. Because the problem is a vacancy, a specific obvious-sounding fix exists: refill the vacancy. In the late 1950s a Denver surgeon named Ben Eiseman and his colleagues treated four critically ill patients using faecal enemas from healthy donors and reported a rapid recovery in a surgical journal. The treatment then sat almost unused for about fifty years. The obstacle was not the evidence. The obstacle was disgust. In the early 2010s a careful randomised trial by a Dutch team compared the treatment against a standard antibiotic and the results were so lopsidedly in favour of the stool infusion that the trial was stopped early.

the-twelve-letters-that-shouldnt-be-ther.context_blurb: The spike protein of the virus that causes COVID-19 must be cut by a specific human enzyme at a specific site before the virus can enter a human cell. The site is called a furin cleavage site. The closest known natural relative of the virus, a bat coronavirus matching it over about ninety-six percent of its genome, is missing exactly that short stretch of twelve letters. So are the two hundred-plus other closely related natural coronaviruses that have been sequenced. The site is not alien to coronaviruses in general. Some other coronaviruses have one. But its absence in this virus's own nearest wild cousins is unexplained. The proposal was rejected. The honest status is that no one has shown where those twelve letters came from.

the-twitching-frog-galvani-versus-volta.context_blurb: In the 1780s in the Italian city of Bologna, an anatomy professor named Luigi Galvani noticed that the dissected legs of frogs hanging from a specific kind of hook twitched as if alive, with no obvious electrical cause nearby. He concluded that he had found a special fluid stored inside living tissue, the force of life itself, carried by the nerves. A different Italian physicist named Alessandro Volta disagreed. He argued that the twitching had nothing to do with the frog. It came from the fact that two different metals were being joined through a moist conductor, and the frog's leg was simply the most sensitive detector anyone had of a tiny current. To settle the argument Volta did something specific. He built the alternative. His stack of alternating zinc and copper discs separated by brine-soaked cardboard was announced to a Royal Society Fellow in London in 1800 and became the first battery. The first battery was literally a rebuttal. The frog-leg experiment was explained by the metals, and real electrical signals in nerves were measured by other researchers decades later.

the-unseen-graveyard-right-to-try-and-th.context_blurb: In 2018 the United States Congress passed a law whose common name does not carry the name of any legislator. It carries the names of four patients, three of them dying of a specific neurological disease and one of them a boy with a specific muscular disease who had lobbied for the law in person. The law lets a dying person try a medicine that has already cleared its first safety trial without first needing a federal regulator's permission. In the early 1970s an American economist named Sam Peltzman worked out that a particular 1962 amendment to federal drug law, which added a requirement to prove effectiveness and not only safety before approval, had roughly halved the rate of new drug introductions without a matching gain in quality. The 1962 amendment exists because of thalidomide, and a specific FDA reviewer named Frances Kelsey saved thousands of American children from severe birth defects by refusing to approve it. Both columns need to be counted.

the-volunteer-detectives-elisabeth-bik-a.context_blurb: A Dutch microbiologist named Elisabeth Bik began a specific kind of volunteer work in 2013, after discovering that one of her own papers had been plagiarised. She started reading published biology papers in the evenings and looking for a specific telltale sign in their figures. The sign is that the same photograph of the same patch of cells has been reused in two experiments that should have produced different pictures. Rotate it, mirror it, stretch it, drop it into another figure, and the random pattern of specks still matches. Fabrication that would be invisible in a table of numbers is visible as a visual fingerprint in a picture, to a patient reader. She flags suspected duplication. Findings of actual misconduct come from institutions afterwards.

the-wall-that-wasnt-there-the-sound-barr.context_blurb: On 14 October 1947, over the California desert, an American test pilot named Chuck Yeager was dropped out of the belly of a bomber inside a stubby orange rocket plane he had named for his wife and pushed past the speed of sound. He was flying with two cracked ribs. The project engineer sawed off a length of broom handle for him to use as a lever to latch the cockpit door, which he could not have done without it. The sound barrier was not a wall hanging in the sky. The specific trouble aircraft of the previous decade had faced as they approached the speed of sound in steep dives involved a shock wave forming on the horizontal tail, making the elevator useless. The fix was not more thrust but a specific mechanical change. A sonic boom is not a one-off bang at the moment of crossing. It is a specific conical shock trailing behind an aircraft the whole time it stays supersonic, sweeping a carpet along the ground.

the-war-of-the-currents-told-honestly.context_blurb: In 1882, Thomas Edison lit a section of lower Manhattan from a power station on Pearl Street using direct current. The system had a specific physical limit baked in: at usable household voltages, direct current fades out quickly over distance, so a city needed a power station every mile or so. A rival approach used alternating current, which can be transformed up to a very high voltage for long-distance transmission and then back down for household use. Heating loss in a wire goes as the square of the current it carries, so a given amount of power sent at high voltage loses far less in the wire than the same power sent at low voltage. Edison's associates ran specific unpleasant demonstrations to associate alternating current with danger. George Westinghouse, who is the person who actually built the grid, underbid the direct-current camp to light a specific exposition in Chicago and later to transmit power from a specific American waterfall.

the-whales-that-walked.context_blurb: In 1834 an American anatomist named Richard Harlan was handed an enormous fossil skeleton from the American South and named it something meaning king lizard, because he mistook it for a sea reptile. It was in fact a whale, and by the rules of scientific naming the wrong name has stuck to it forever. Decades later another anatomist caught the error by looking at the specific shape of the molars.

the-wrong-strength-glue.context_blurb: In 1942, at a Kodak laboratory in Rochester, a research team was trying to cast clear plastic gunsights and kept running into a specific chemical that instantly welded itself to everything it touched. The project rejected it as a nuisance. Nine years later, in a different Kodak laboratory in Tennessee, a researcher spread a small sample of the same chemical between the glass prisms of an expensive instrument to measure its refractive index and permanently glued the instrument shut. This time somebody recognised what the property actually meant. Separately, in 1968 at a different American company, a researcher aiming at a stronger aerospace adhesive produced a weak one instead, consisting of tiny microspheres that touch a surface at points only and let the bond peel away cleanly. He called it a solution waiting for a problem and spent years pitching it inside his company with no takers.

theranos-show-me-the-machine-working.context_blurb: A specific American company promised a revolution in medical testing, reached a valuation of about nine billion dollars at its peak, and turned out to be running most of its blood tests on ordinary commercial analysers bought from a specific other medical-device maker. The company's claim was that a single drop of blood from a finger prick could run hundreds of tests on its own proprietary machine. One finger-prick drop is a tiny volume, and if you split it hundreds of ways each test gets less than a microlitre, which is below the detection limit of the chemistry involved. The claim broke chemistry before it ever broke the law. The people who caught it were not the famous board of former generals and statesmen, and not the regulators and investors. It was two junior lab employees who watched the quality-control failures from inside the laboratory and went to a reporter. A serious investor should have made a specific demand: run the test in front of me, start to finish, on this machine, right now.

thomsons-corpuscle-and-the-model-built-t.context_blurb: In the final years of the nineteenth century, at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge, a British physicist named J.J. Thomson showed by a specific series of deflection experiments on so-called cathode rays that these rays consisted of a particle more than a thousand times lighter than a hydrogen atom. He had found something smaller than an atom, which many of his contemporaries did not believe at first. He later recalled a senior physicist telling him he had been pulling their legs. A few years later Thomson proposed a specific detailed model of the atom in which these negatively charged particles circulated in stable rings inside a sphere of positive charge, and he tried to use the ring configurations to explain the periodic table. The model made a specific numerical prediction about what should happen when positively charged particles were fired at thin metal foil. When the test was run, a small fraction of the incoming particles came straight back toward the gun. The specific model was killed by its own prediction, which is a compliment to a scientific model, not an insult.

tiktaalik-they-knew-where-to-dig.context_blurb: In the early 2000s, a team of palaeontologists led by Neil Shubin at the University of Chicago did something specific. They worked out in advance exactly what kind of fossil they needed to find to fill a famous gap in the evolutionary record, which is the gap between water-living lobe-finned fish and the earliest land-walking four-limbed animals. They worked out the age the rock would need to be. They checked a geology map for exposed freshwater sediment of that age. The map pointed to Ellesmere Island, deep inside the Canadian Arctic. A specific later discovery of fossil footprints in a Polish quarry, which turned out to be older than Tiktaalik, means that the word ancestor is the wrong word, even though the prediction method still worked.

time-really-runs-slower-down-here-and-yo.context_blurb: Every GPS satellite's clock runs about thirty-eight millionths of a second a day faster than a clock on the ground. If engineers did not correct for that specific discrepancy, your phone's map would drift off by miles within a single day, because a GPS receiver turns clock time into distance at the speed of light. Gravity is weaker up there, which makes the satellite's clock run faster relative to the ground. Motion is faster up there, which makes it run slower. Gravity wins, and the net adjustment is a specific number of microseconds per day. The very first GPS prototype in orbit carried a correction circuit that could be switched off, so the engineers could watch the clock drift against the predicted amount before activating the correction.

tonegawa-and-the-genome-that-cuts-itself.context_blurb: Your body can build a specific matching antibody against a molecule that did not exist on Earth until some chemist made it last week. You can only do this because your immune system can produce an astonishing number of different antibody shapes. The problem is that you carry only about twenty thousand genes in total, which looks like a severe mismatch. For decades, the leading explanation was that the invader itself acted as a kind of mould, and the antibody somehow folded itself around the invader like clay pressed onto a coin. That explanation came from one of the greatest chemists of the twentieth century. It turned out to be wrong. In the mid-1970s a Japanese biologist named Susumu Tonegawa took the extraordinary step of cutting the DNA from mouse embryo cells and from antibody-producing tumour cells with the same enzyme, and showed that the gene pieces for the antibody sat in different places in the two kinds of cell. The B cell had physically cut its own chromosome and stitched the pieces back together, producing diversity by a specific internal shuffle.

torricellis-ocean-of-air.context_blurb: In the early seventeenth century, Florentine well-diggers found that no matter how carefully they built a suction pump, they could not lift water higher than about ten metres. Nobody knew why. In 1644 one of Galileo's assistants, Evangelista Torricelli, worked out the explanation by running the same trick with a much denser liquid, mercury, in a sealed metre-long tube inverted into a dish. The mercury column always fell back to about seventy-six centimetres and stopped there. The reigning explanation at the time was that nature abhors a vacuum. Torricelli's rival explanation, written in a specific letter in 1644 to a friend, was that we live submerged at the bottom of an ocean of air whose weight presses down on everything. In 1648, with Blaise Pascal too ill to climb himself, Pascal's brother-in-law carried a specific identical pair of barometers up a particular French volcano.

transhumanism-a-programme-not-a-prophecy.context_blurb: The modern meaning of the word transhumanism was given to it in a 1957 essay by the biologist Julian Huxley, who defined it as the idea that the human species can, if it wishes, transcend itself. Across the same stretch of decades he was an officer of the British Eugenics Society, serving as its vice-president in the late 1930s and early 1940s and later as its president in the early 1960s. He was also the first director-general of UNESCO. He was Aldous Huxley's older brother.

tungsten-the-filament-that-would-not-mel.context_blurb: The useful light that a hot wire gives off is produced at a temperature not far from the temperature at which almost all metals have already boiled away into vapour. Thomas Edison's early light bulbs used carbon filaments, which evaporate too fast at the temperature of useful brightness, which is why those bulbs were dim and short-lived. The answer turned out to be a specific metal with the highest melting point of any element on the periodic table, which can be run white-hot without boiling itself off the wire. The real obstacle turned out not to be melting at all. The real obstacle was brittleness. A particular American industrial researcher named William Coolidge spent years working out how to make the metal ductile enough to be drawn into a wire fine enough to light a room, and another specific GE researcher solved the last problem by filling the bulb with gas instead of evacuating it.

turbulence-the-swirl-in-your-coffee-no-e.context_blurb: Stir milk into coffee once, and watch what happens. The ribbon of milk breaks into curls, and inside those curls are smaller curls, and inside those are smaller curls still. No physicist alive can write an equation that predicts where any individual curl will go. The equations describing the flow of a fluid have existed since the mid-nineteenth century, and they are called the Navier-Stokes equations. Nobody has proven that their solutions in three dimensions always stay smooth rather than blowing up. That specific question is on the list of unsolved Millennium Prize problems in mathematics, with a million dollars attached to its answer. Weather forecasts decay after about a week because of what we cannot do with those equations.

tuskegee-forty-years-of-watching.context_blurb: From 1932 to 1972 the United States Public Health Service enrolled six hundred poor black men in a specific county in Alabama into a study it told them was treating them for a vague illness it called bad blood. Three hundred and ninety-nine of the men had latent syphilis. Two hundred and one did not. The researchers never treated the men with syphilis, and they went on watching the untreated disease run its course for forty years. The men were not deliberately infected. They already had the disease when the study enrolled them, and what the researchers did was withhold treatment. Even the painful lumbar punctures were described to them as a treatment. Penicillin cured syphilis from the mid-1940s, and the study continued anyway, publishing results in medical journals.

twenty-years-of-silence-and-wallaces-env.context_blurb: Charles Darwin had the specific mechanism of natural selection worked out in his private notebooks by 1838. He did not publish his book on the origin of species until 1859. He spent much of the intervening time on specific projects that look like displacement activities to a modern reader, including eight years on the taxonomy of barnacles. In 1842 Darwin wrote a brief pencil sketch of his theory. In 1844 he wrote a longer essay and left it in a drawer with specific written instructions to his wife about what to do if he died suddenly. The envelope that finally forced him to publish arrived in June 1858, posted from the Malay Archipelago, written by a specific younger naturalist named Alfred Russel Wallace, enclosing an essay that laid out essentially the same mechanism. Charles Lyell and Joseph Hooker arranged a joint reading at the Linnean Society. Neither Darwin nor Wallace was in the room when it took place. Wallace was in the East Indies. Darwin was at the funeral of his infant son, who had died of scarlet fever a few days earlier.

two-bicycle-mechanics-build-their-own-wi.context_blurb: Behind the famous flight by the Wright brothers at Kitty Hawk was the instrument that made it possible. In the autumn of 1901, in the back of their bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, two self-taught mechanics built a wind tunnel. It was a wooden box about six feet long, with a fan driven by the shop's engine giving a steady wind of around twenty-five miles an hour, and a glass window in the lid to watch through. The cleverest part was the measuring balances inside. The Wrights cut them out of old hacksaw blades and bicycle spoke wire, and designed them to read the ratio of lift to drag directly, so that the result did not depend on knowing the air's density or any of the published numbers they did not trust. The published lift tables of the most famous glider pilot in Europe, reprinted under the Smithsonian's name, had turned out to be wrong. Two men with no laboratory re-measured the foundation of a field in about two months of evenings.

two-pencils-and-a-battery-electrolysis-t.context_blurb: Sharpen a pencil at both ends, stand two of them in a glass of water with a pinch of baking soda dissolved in it, touch them to a nine-volt battery, and watch what happens. Bubbles of gas climb off both leads, and about twice as much gas collects at the negative one. The chemical formula for water is being made visible in a kitchen glass. Within weeks of Alessandro Volta announcing his pile in 1800, two English researchers in London ran its current through water and collected the two gases separately. It was the first time anyone had used electricity to pull a chemical compound apart.
