In 1807 the Cornish chemist Humphry Davy ran a large battery through a specific molten compound in an evaporating dish and extracted a shining metal nobody had ever seen free before, because the metal is too reactive to exist alone on earth.

two-sounds-that-add-up-to-silence.context_blurb: Point two loudspeakers playing exactly the same steady tone into a room. Walk slowly across the room while they play. You will pass through specific places where the tone is loud and other specific places where it nearly disappears. Nothing is absorbing it. Where a push of air from one speaker meets a pull from the other, they cancel each other out, and sound plus sound equals quiet. This is the simplest demonstration of a specific wave phenomenon called interference. A German physician and physicist named Paul Lueg filed a patent in 1933 proposing to kill an unwanted sound by broadcasting the same sound turned upside down. The first working version was built two decades later at a specific American research laboratory.

tychos-data-and-keplers-eight-arcminutes.context_blurb: In the late sixteenth century, a Danish nobleman named Tycho Brahe spent decades building and running the finest observatory in Europe, on a small island between Denmark and Sweden, with the king's money. He worked entirely without a telescope, because telescopes had not been invented. His star and planet measurements were nevertheless accurate to about one arcminute, which is roughly one-thirtieth the width of the full Moon, and about five times better than anyone before him. In the summer of 1600 he hired a poor, short-sighted German mathematician named Johannes Kepler and assigned him the worst planet in the catalogue to work on, which was Mars. Kepler ground through those numbers for years, tested and rejected one geometric model after another, and eventually produced a model that matched Mars to within a specific small residual. Any astronomer before him would have declared victory with that result. Kepler threw it away, because Tycho's data were better than the residual.

tyndalls-ribbon-of-invisible-heat.context_blurb: In 1859 at the Royal Institution in London, an Irish-born physicist named John Tyndall ran a careful experiment. He filled a long tube with a gas, shone invisible heat through it from a specific source, and measured what came out of the far end. The specific gases that make up almost all of the atmosphere let the heat sail straight through the tube as if it were empty. One specific trace gas absorbed enormously more heat than the entire bulk of dry air put together. The reason he could do the experiment at all was that an American scientist named Eunice Newton Foote had already shown in 1856 that cylinders of specific gases warmed differently in sunlight. The underlying physics is settled science to the point where a specific class of modern commercial sensors used in school classrooms today works by measuring exactly the absorption Tyndall first measured in his tube.

unit-731-and-the-data-the-americans-boug.context_blurb: In 1936 the Imperial Japanese Army set up a biological-warfare research unit in occupied Manchuria. It operated under a specific official name whose plain English translation describes the opposite of what it actually did. It was commanded by a specific physician and army officer. It worked on specific diseases including plague, anthrax, and cholera. Its records referred to prisoners by a specific filing word. The unit destroyed what it could not take. A specific American report written at Camp Detrick in 1947 recorded the terms of a specific bargain: the senior scientists were granted immunity from prosecution for war crimes in exchange for turning over their data. The unit was deliberately left out of the Tokyo war-crimes tribunal. A separate trial of twelve of them was held by the Soviets in 1949, which the West dismissed at the time as propaganda. Historians today argue the trial's flaws and its substance both.

van-t-hoffs-tetrahedron-and-the-professo.context_blurb: You can smell handedness. One specific molecule in a mint leaf and its exact mirror image in a caraway seed have exactly the same atoms connected in exactly the same way, but one smells like chewing gum and the other smells like rye bread. The reason was worked out in 1874 by a twenty-two-year-old Dutch chemist. His name was Jacobus Henricus van 't Hoff, and he proposed, independently with a young French chemist, that carbon's four bonds do not lie flat but point to the four corners of a tetrahedron. If you attach four different groups to one carbon atom, there are exactly two ways to do it, and those two are mirror images of each other that you cannot superimpose. One of the most powerful chemists in Germany, Hermann Kolbe, published a scorching attack on the paper, mocking van 't Hoff for abandoning serious chemistry for flights of imagination. A right hand fits a right glove.

vavilov-and-the-seed-bank-that-outlived-.context_blurb: The Russian botanist Nikolai Vavilov crossed sixty-four countries on over one hundred and fifteen collecting expeditions and brought home more than three hundred and eighty thousand seeds, tubers, roots, and fruits, building in Leningrad the largest seed collection on Earth. He had a specific stated reason. He was trying to end famine in Russia. The scientific idea behind his collecting trips was that a crop's variety is not spread evenly over the world but piles up in one region where the plant was first domesticated and where its wild relatives still grow. The specific wild and primitive varieties in those regions carry the disease resistance that improved varieties have usually bred away, so the collection is a library of answers to famines that have not yet happened. His passport was revoked in 1933 by a Soviet state increasingly captured by a different, politically favoured theory of inheritance. He was arrested in a field on a seed-collecting trip in 1940. The man who had built the world's biggest seed bank specifically to end starvation died in a Soviet prison in 1943 of starvation.

vesalius-puts-his-own-hands-in-the-body.context_blurb: In the standard medical lesson of 1540, the anatomy professor sat in a high chair reading the ancient Greek physician Galen's book aloud in Latin while a hired barber-surgeon on a stool below did the cutting and an assistant pointed at parts. The reading authority was fourteen hundred years older than the body on the table. In the mid-1540s a twenty-eight-year-old anatomy professor in Padua named Andreas Vesalius climbed down out of the chair and cut the body himself. He found that Galen's book was systematically wrong in a specific identifiable way, which was that Galen had done most of his dissections on apes, pigs, and dogs because Roman law forbade cutting human corpses. Vesalius catalogued specific discrepancies between what Galen said was in a body and what was actually there. He looked for a specific invisible connection Galen's physiology required, and he could not find it. His book, printed in Basel in 1543 with over two hundred and seventy woodcuts, is one of the first great printed books of modern science.

vestigial-what-the-body-kept-after-the-j.context_blurb: Goosebumps are a response you still own from a furrier ancestor. Tiny muscles yank each hair upright to trap warm air, which worked when there was a full coat on the skin. The muscles and the wiring are still there. The coat is not. A human embryo grows a visible tail in the first weeks of development, which is reabsorbed before birth, leaving the small fused bone at the base of your spine. The word vestigial does not mean that a body part does nothing. It means a body part has lost its ancestral function. The small fused bone at the base of your spine still anchors several specific pelvic muscles. The strongest evidence for the evolutionary reading of these features is not that they are useless. It is that the family tree of the appendix shows it has been independently reinvented in mammal lineages dozens of times, which is a specific fact nobody expects.

vostok-1-the-engineering-nobody-advertis.context_blurb: On the morning of 12 April 1961, a Soviet pilot named Yuri Gagarin flew one orbit around the earth inside a small spherical capsule and became the first human being in space. The specific flight lasted one hundred and eight minutes. For a decade the Soviet press implied that the pilot came down inside his spacecraft. He did not. Nobody knew whether a human being could think straight in weightlessness, so the controls of the capsule were locked. The specific unlock code was sealed in an envelope aboard, with engineers quietly telling Gagarin the digits anyway. The capsule was a sphere on purpose, because a sphere with its mass offset toward the heavy heat shield is passively stable during reentry.

w-hler-makes-urea-without-a-kidney.context_blurb: In February 1828 a German chemist named Friedrich Wohler wrote a specific private letter to his old teacher Jons Jacob Berzelius making an unusual boast. He said he could now make urea, which is the main solid in urine, without the help of a kidney, of either a man or a dog. He had been trying to make a specific dull inorganic salt by mixing two salts in water, and when he evaporated the solution he got the wrong crystals. He proved by careful comparison that his crystals were identical to urea taken from urine. The famous story that gets told around this experiment is that Wohler's result killed a prescientific doctrine called vitalism in a single stroke. That popular story is mostly wrong. Wohler himself pitched the result as something quite different, which is a specific chemical idea about two substances with the same atoms arranged differently, and vitalism survived in various forms for decades.

wakefield-1998-a-warning-that-points-bot.context_blurb: In February 1998, the medical journal The Lancet published a case series by a British physician named Andrew Wakefield and twelve co-authors describing twelve children with bowel disease and developmental regression. The paper itself did not claim to have proven that the MMR vaccine caused autism. The paper actually said the opposite. What set off a national panic was a press conference held by one of the authors alongside the paper's release, at which specific recommendations were given to parents that were not in the paper. Two large Danish studies of over five hundred thousand children, and later over six hundred and fifty thousand children, found no association between the vaccine and autism. The senior clinician on that same paper was struck off and won his appeal in a British court. A tribunal is not a laboratory.

warm-vikings-frozen-thames-the-climate-b.context_blurb: Around the end of the first millennium, Norse settlers led by Erik the Red crossed from Iceland to the south-western coast of Greenland, where for roughly four centuries they kept cattle, sheep, and goats and built stone churches on ground that later froze hard. European farms in Greenland. The last surviving document from the Norse Greenland settlements is from 1412, and then they are gone. From roughly 1300 to 1850, Alpine glaciers advanced onto farmland, Dutch painters filled canvases with frozen canals, and the Thames at London froze in two dozen recorded winters between 1400 and 1831.

wasons-2-4-6-and-the-urge-to-confirm.context_blurb: In 1960 a British psychologist named Peter Wason designed a specific little experiment that most people lose in under two minutes. In its simplest form, the experimenter tells you that the triple of numbers two, four, six fits a hidden rule, and that you may test any other triple you like and be told only yes or no. Almost everyone proposes a triple like eight, ten, twelve, and then another like twenty, twenty-two, twenty-four, and gets yes every time, and announces with confidence that the rule is to add two each time. The real hidden rule is just that the three numbers must be in increasing order. Fewer than one person in ten picks correctly in the abstract version. The same logic problem rephrased as a specific social enforcement question about underage drinking produces almost universal success.

water-the-molecule-that-breaks-the-rules.context_blurb: Drop an ice cube into a glass of water and the cube floats. Freeze a lump of olive oil and drop the lump into a glass of oil and the lump sinks. Water is one of a specific small number of substances whose solid form floats on its own liquid. The reason is specific. Each water molecule hooks into the next through a specific weak bond, and in the solid state the molecules lock into an open hexagonal cage that spreads them further apart than they are in the liquid. Freezing pushes them apart instead of packing them tighter. The consequence of this specific property is that a lake freezes from the top down and the ice lid insulates the water beneath, so the pond does not freeze solid and its life survives.

webb-unfolds-344-steps-with-no-second-tr.context_blurb: The main mirror of the James Webb Space Telescope is too wide to fit inside any rocket fairing, so it had to fly folded, with the outer wings hinged back, inside the rocket that launched it on Christmas Day 2021. On the way out to its destination, more than a million miles from Earth, the telescope had to unfold itself. The specific number that captures the engineering difficulty is three hundred and forty-four, which is the count of single-point failures in the deployment, where a single failure in a specific mechanism would have ruined the mission. Every one of them worked. The sunshield is five kite-shaped layers of a specific thin material, each separated by vacuum gaps, so that heat is radiated sideways out of the gaps and the temperature falls in five steps from blazing hot to extremely cold.

what-a-mask-trial-can-and-cannot-prove.context_blurb: In January 2023 the Cochrane Collaboration, which is the organisation whose whole purpose is pooling randomised controlled trials, published an updated review of physical interventions to reduce the spread of respiratory viruses. It is not a new experiment but a careful pooling of the randomised trials that already exist, with weak studies weighted down. The randomised trials of masks did not randomise whether particles pass through cloth. They randomised whether people were asked to wear masks. Adherence in the trials was often poor. That is a real limit, and it is also exactly the question a government policy asks.

what-a-vaccine-actually-does-to-the-immu.context_blurb: On Christmas night in 1891 in Berlin, the German physician Emil von Behring injected a dying diphtheria child with the clear serum taken from the blood of an immunised animal, and the child lived. The specific protection was in the serum, which was something the animal's own body had manufactured. A specific picture of the immune system was worked out in the mid-twentieth century by two researchers named Macfarlane Burnet and David Talmage. In their picture the vaccine does not instruct the body to build a new weapon. The body already carries a specific one-shaped-match for essentially any invader. All the vaccine does is show the body a preview of the invader, so the matching cell can multiply before the real invader arrives.

what-actually-settles-a-scientific-fight.context_blurb: The famous slogan about Galileo being laughed at is not an argument, and the pattern of real scientific reversals is specific and worth learning. The pattern runs claim, then objection, then a test that could have come out either way, then verdict. In each real case the objection was not stupid, and the resolution came through a specific later measurement that could have gone the other way. For every one of these specific vindicated outsiders, there are many more confidently defiant outsiders who were simply wrong. What separates vindication from crankery is never defiance. It is a specific test other people can run that comes out the same way in their hands.

what-glass-actually-is.context_blurb: Drip molten glass into cold water and you get a specific tadpole-shaped lump called a Prince Rupert's drop. You can strike the fat head with a hammer and nothing happens. Snap the thin tail with your fingers and the entire drop disintegrates into powder instantly. A widely-repeated schoolroom claim is that old cathedral windows are thicker at the bottom because glass is a very slow liquid that has flowed downward over centuries. A specific careful calculation showed that is not possible. Two-thousand-year-old Roman glass has not sagged.

what-ninety-seven-percent-counted.context_blurb: The slogan is familiar. Ninety-seven percent of climate scientists agree. In 2013 the researcher John Cook and colleagues published a paper in which they and a team of volunteers rated the abstracts of eleven thousand, nine hundred and forty-four scientific papers published between 1991 and 2011. Roughly two thirds of those abstracts expressed no position on the question at all, and were set aside before the famous percentage was taken. The ninety-seven percent is a percentage of the remaining third. A paper saying humans contribute and a paper saying humans are the dominant cause both landed in the same category.

what-the-thermometers-actually-say.context_blurb: The surface temperature record is the messiest dataset in all of science. A thermometer that has read faithfully for a century is still a problem if the town grew around it, or if the hour at which the thermometer was read changed. A physicist named Richard Muller, publicly doubtful of the mainstream temperature record, founded a specific independent project in 2010 with funding that included money from one of the Koch foundations, and reported a specific result that went against his starting position.

what-they-wrote-and-what-they-were-sayin.context_blurb: In late January and February 2020 a small group of senior virologists exchanged specific private emails about what the newly-sequenced genome of SARS-CoV-2 looked like to them. Several of them wrote that specific features of the genome looked potentially engineered, and said so to the US National Institutes of Health director. A specific teleconference was then convened by the head of the Wellcome Trust in Britain. A specific private Slack channel was opened in which one of the researchers wrote that a laboratory escape looked, in his own words, so likely that he could not see how it was anything else. On 17 March 2020 the same group of researchers published a paper in Nature Medicine stating flatly that the virus was not a laboratory construct.

what-two-teams-of-horses-could-not-pull-.context_blurb: Around 1650 the burgomaster of the German city of Magdeburg, a man named Otto von Guericke, invented one of the first working air pumps. He used it in a specific public demonstration that made the physics of the atmosphere visible to anyone watching. He had two copper half-spheres about fifty centimetres across, their rims greased and simply pressed together with no bolt or catch. Once he pumped the air out of them, teams of horses could not pull them apart. When he opened a small valve to let air back in, they fell apart in his hands. The two opposing teams of horses were showmanship. One team of horses pulling against a stone wall would have proved exactly the same thing, because the wall supplies the equal and opposite pull for free.

when-eugenics-was-the-respectable-opinio.context_blurb: Eugenics was not a fringe doctrine held only by cranks. It was the respectable scientific opinion of the Western world in the early twentieth century, held by famous people a kid today would be surprised to find on the list. The man who co-founded the Bronx Zoo, saved specific stands of California redwoods, and lobbied for a specific national park also wrote one of the most popular American books of racial science of its era. The founder of the American birth-control movement joined a specific eugenics society and argued in writing for sterilising people classified as feeble-minded. The specific scientific refutation of eugenics was published in a mathematics-of-genetics journal in 1917, decades before the state programs reached their peak. Nobody who mattered acted on it.

when-the-vaccine-causes-the-disease-vapp.context_blurb: The oral polio vaccine designed by Albert Sabin is not a killed virus. It is a specific live poliovirus that has been passed through animal cells over and over until it has lost its appetite for human nerve cells. It is swallowed on a sugar cube rather than injected. Because it is alive, it reproduces in the child's gut, which is exactly what makes it so good at blocking transmission in a population. The child's gut then sheds live virus for weeks. In a specific small number of doses, measured per million, the weakened strain can revert and cause paralysis in the recipient or in a close contact.

who-paid-for-the-bat-work.context_blurb: From 2014 to 2019 the United States National Institutes of Health funded research on bat coronaviruses at a specific institute in central China, not directly but through a specific New York non-profit organisation that subcontracted part of the work to the Chinese institute.

why-crystals-have-flat-faces-and-the-pat.context_blurb: Around 1781 in Paris, a priest and mineralogist named Rene Just Hauy broke a piece of calcite and noticed that every fragment broke into the same slanted little brick shape. He concluded that a crystal is stacked out of identical repeating units, and that is why it shows flat faces and fixed angles between those faces. A specific mathematical rule says that a pattern that repeats by simple translation can only have two-fold, three-fold, four-fold, or six-fold rotational symmetry. Five-fold symmetry is impossible because regular pentagons will not tile a floor without leaving gaps. The rule was called the crystallographic restriction theorem, and for a hundred years it defined the word crystal. In 1982 an Israeli materials scientist named Dan Shechtman fired electrons through a specific rapidly cooled aluminium-manganese alloy and watched the diffraction spots repeat every thirty-six degrees. That is ten-fold symmetry, and the pattern was sharp enough to prove long-range order, yet no repeating lattice could produce it.

why-ice-is-slippery.context_blurb: The textbook answer most schoolbooks give for why ice is slippery is that a skater's blade presses down so hard on the surface that it melts a thin lubricating film of water under the blade. That specific textbook answer is wrong. The pressure a skater actually exerts lowers ice's melting point by only a tiny fraction of a degree, which is nowhere near enough to produce a film. Ice stays slippery at twenty degrees below zero and colder, where no plausible pressure would melt it. A specific Scottish physicist proposed it in 1849, and his more famous brother confirmed the direction of the effect. The physics is real. The size is just too small. There are two later alternative explanations. One of them is that the surface of ice is already somewhat disordered and liquid-like, even when the block beneath is solid. The other is that the sliding itself heats the contact and melts a very thin layer. Which mechanism dominates in which regime is still argued.

why-soap-wrecks-a-virus.context_blurb: Here is a test anyone can run in a bowl of water tonight. Sprinkle ground pepper on the surface of the water. Touch the surface with a soapy finger. The pepper flees to the rim of the bowl in an instant. A soap molecule is a two-ended thing, with a charged head that loves water and a long greasy tail that hates water. In the wash, the greasy tails hide inside droplets of grease and the heads face outward, forming specific little balls that trap dirt and rinse away. On a virus with a specific lipid envelope stolen from a cell membrane, the greasy tails slide into the envelope, pry it apart, and the virus falls to pieces. Soap does not do this to every germ. Some common viruses have no envelope at all, and against those the mechanism is a specific different one.

why-the-sky-is-blue-and-the-sunset-is-re.context_blurb: The Sun does not change colour at sunset. Your line of sight does. At noon, sunlight crosses a short slab of air to reach your eye. At the horizon, the same sunlight ploughs through many times more atmosphere, and the blue has been scattered out of the beam long before it gets to you, leaving the orange and red. The blue overhead is not the sky's own colour, because there is no blue substance up there. Air molecules, mostly nitrogen and oxygen, redirect short wavelengths of light far more strongly than long ones, and the redirected blue arrives at your eye from every direction at once.

why-we-sleep-a-third-of-your-life-unexpl.context_blurb: You spend roughly a third of your life unconscious, motionless and defenceless. That ought to be an evolutionary disaster, and yet every animal with a brain does it anyway. Nobody has worked out, in a definitive settled way, what sleep is for. In famous experiments by a Chicago psychologist named Allan Rechtschaffen, rats forced to stay awake on a slowly spinning disk over water died after about two to three weeks. The experiments proved that sleep is not optional. They did not say what it does.

william-smith-maps-a-nation.context_blurb: In the 1790s a self-taught English canal surveyor named William Smith started noticing something as he dug. The same rock layers turned up in the same order wherever he cut, and each layer carried its own particular set of fossils. The fossils identified the layer even when the rock itself looked identical. The practical value of that specific discovery was enormous because it let him predict what rocks lay underneath a field that had never been dug. His map, published in 1815, was over eight feet tall, hand-coloured on a specific national base map, and essentially the work of one man who had walked England and Wales himself.

withering-and-the-foxglove.context_blurb: In 1775 a Birmingham physician named William Withering heard that a specific family in Shropshire had a herbal tea that cured dropsy, which was the terrifying condition in which a body swelled up filling with fluid and which no physician of the day could reliably treat. Instead of dismissing it, he asked for the recipe. The recipe contained more than twenty herbs. He was also a serious botanist, and he worked out through careful experiment which single plant in that jumble was doing the work. He gave dried, weighed, carefully measured doses of the plant to patient after patient for a decade. In 1785 he published a specific book containing one hundred and sixty-three case histories, including every patient for whom the drug had done nothing or caused harm.

x-rays-through-a-crystal-the-father-and-.context_blurb: In 1912 in Munich, the German physicist Max von Laue reasoned that if X-rays are waves whose wavelength happens to be about the size of the gaps between atoms in a crystal, then a crystal should scatter X-rays in a specific sharp pattern of spots. His team shot X-rays through a crystal onto a photographic plate and got exactly that. The experiment proved two things at once, which was that X-rays are waves and that crystals are regular arrays of atoms.

you-never-suck-a-drink-up-a-straw.context_blurb: Drinking a drink through a straw involves no pulling at all. You thin the air inside your mouth, and the atmosphere pressing down on the surface of the drink outside the straw pushes the liquid up the tube. The outside air pushes it. Poke a pin-hole in the side of the straw above the liquid line. Now suck as hard as you like. You will get nothing, because the air has an easier way in through the hole. Even a perfect vacuum in your mouth could raise water only about ten metres at sea level, which is roughly a three-storey house, because that is the tallest column of water the atmosphere's push can balance. A twelve-metre straw is impossible for anyone, forever.
